native_result.query: In which century did the Diversity in Pottery Form collapses and Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases simultaneuosly?
native_result.HypoA: Around 1800 BCE, Diversity in Pottery Form collapses, while Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases.
native_result.HypoB: Diversity in Pottery Form collapsed and Diversity in Pottery Decoration increased simultaneously in the 17th century BCE (1700-1601 BCE; CE -1700 to -1601, calBP 3650-3551, 'the 1700s BCE'). At the 1700 BCE 100-year anchor PotteryForm drops 0.74 -> -1.13 (dZ = -1.87, -1.9 SD, the series floor, sustained 13 bins to 500 BCE) while PotteryDecoration rises -0.48 -> +0.97 (dZ = +1.45, +1.6 SD, above mean and p80, sustained to the end of the record, stepping to +1.53 at 1000 BCE). The level criterion (overlap 1700-500 BCE) and the one-bin rate criterion (Form dZ <= -1SD with Decoration dZ >= +1SD in the same bin) select the same century, and three of four Decoration threshold variants agree; only the strictest variant (Decoration >= mean+1SD) shifts the level overlap to 1000-500 BCE (10th c. BCE), which reflects a secondary Decoration step on an already-collapsed Form series. This is a cultural reorganisation (form diversity at its floor while decorative diversity peaks) at the terminal Late Neolithic / Older Bronze Age transition rather than a demographic crash: pollen openness (MEAN 2.42 -> 2.13; Belau_PC1_inter 1.66 -> 1.87; pollen_grate_100 +0.00069) shows no coeval collapse.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspected the three staged files: time_series_data.csv 3601 annual rows (CE -4100..-500, calBP = 1950-CE); all Z columns carry exactly 37 non-null anchors at exact 100-yr spacing with no gaps; _inter columns are verified exact linear interpolation (max dev 2e-16) hence no added information; capital.csv (comma decimals) matched the anchors exactly after CE = -BCE (max |diff| = 0) with only BCE 4300/4200 unmatched. 2) Computed anchor-level statistics (Form mean 0.062/sd 0.989/p20 -1.13; Deco mean 0.105/sd 0.917/p80 0.97). 3) FORM level criterion (<= mean-1SD, runs >=3 bins) -> 1700-500 BCE; FORM rate criterion (one-bin dZ <= -1SD) -> 1700 BCE only. 4) DECO variants V1 > mean, V2 >= p80, V3 >= mean+1SD, V4 directional (pre-3 mean <= 0.05, post-3 mean >= 0.30, positive step at t, whole post-window positive) with >=3-bin run filter. 5) Intersected Form runs with each Deco run (BCE intervals), printed the qualifying-bin table incl. the 1900-1400 BCE neighbourhood, explicitly excluded the 4000 BCE Decoration rise (Form rises +2.36 there) and the 2800 BCE Form drop (Deco falls). 6) Rate x Rate same-bin check. 7) Century conversion under the strict convention plus common usage, with right-truncation at the 500 BCE last anchor noted. 8) Sensitivity: 300-yr centred MA of anchors (onset shifts to 1600 BCE), 101-yr rolling mean of _inter (labelled artefact, unused), min-duration 1/2/3/5 bins. 9) Pollen openness used descriptively only. Scripts: analysis_00_inspection.py, analysis_02_events.py; outputs: main_analysis_log.txt, anchor_table.csv, results_summary.md.

This Principal component analysis (PCA) is on the forms of capital. The values of the individual elements of the forms of capital form the attributes.
native_result.HypoB: In a PCA of twelve forms of capital over 39 hundred-year slices (correlation matrix; PC1 = 30.3%, PC2 = 19.5%, jointly 49.8% of variance), the symbolic-capital components - house size (Zhausgr), daggers (ZDolch) and hatchets/swords (ZAxtSchwert) - load on PC1 with one shared sign and closely similar moderate magnitude (oriented +0.23 to +0.30; ranks 5, 6 and 10 of 12; within-group range 0.07, the tightest of any capital form), i.e. they sit inside PC1's dominant pole together with copper/gold, pottery decoration and hoards rather than opposing it, and add nothing to it: PC1 behaves as a general temporal rise of capital (loading vector vs per-variable time trend r = 0.96), so symbolic capital follows the main axis instead of defining or contesting it. On PC2 the trio does NOT spread widely: although all three nominally share the positive side of zero, hatchets/swords (+0.054) and daggers (+0.074) carry the two smallest loadings in the whole matrix (ranks 12 and 10) and only house size (+0.327, rank 5) registers, giving a within-symbolic PC2 range of 0.27, less than half the economic group's 0.64, and a share of PC2's variance (11.6%) under half of the 25% expected by chance. Symbolic capital is therefore concentrated on PC1 and essentially orthogonal to PC2, and it is the least well represented group in the PC1-PC2 plane (communalities 0.27-0.43, the weakest after sickle), with the weapons' distinctive information falling on PC3 (daggers are PC3's largest loading, +0.59). native_result.HypoA: The effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies across both the Experimental Economics and Psychology domains. In Experimental Economics, the average effect estimate on the Fisher-z scale in original studies is 0.57, compared to 0.31 in replication studies. In Psychology, the average is 0.5 in original studies versus 0.24 in replication studies.
native_result.HypoB:
# RESULT

## Hypothesis (as-observed, descriptive)

**Original studies report larger effect sizes than their replications in every domain, but the gap is largest in SOCIAL psychology and smallest in EXPERIMENTAL ECONOMICS when "larger" is measured proportionally — whereas measured as an absolute Fisher-z difference the domains are statistically indistinguishable and Cognitive is numerically largest.**

Concretely: originals exceed replications in 73/86 pairs (84.9%), overall mean D_z = fiso−fisr = 0.262 (paired t p=7.1e-12). Because the gap is universal, the domain question is about its magnitude, and the answer is framing-dependent — stated explicitly per domain rather than resolved in favour of one metric.

**(1) Relative/proportional metrics (co-primary #1): Social > Cognitive > Economics in shrinkage.**
mean relative_es 0.278 / 0.509 / 0.657; medians 0.131 / 0.650 / 0.698; |rr|/|ro| 0.411 / 0.639 / 0.724; sign reversals 29.4% / 14.7% / 16.7%; replication success 20.6% / 47.1% / 61.1%. Social ranks 1st (largest gap) in 8 of the 12 tabulated framings, and the Social>Cognitive>Economics ordering is **unchanged in all five robustness variants**. Social−Economics relative_es = −0.378 (bootstrap 95% CI −0.710…−0.054, p=0.022; MW p=0.019) is the one clean separation; Social−Cognitive = −0.231 (CI −0.478…+0.038, boot p=0.089) is clear in medians (0.13 vs 0.65) and ranks (MW p=0.015) but not in means.

**(2) Signed Fisher-z gap D_z (co-primary #2): ordering changes and is not significant.**
Unweighted: Cognitive 0.289 [0.164,0.415] > Economics 0.266 [0.084,0.447] > Social 0.233 [0.162,0.304]. RE(REML): Cognitive 0.234 [0.142,0.326] ≈ Social 0.222 [0.150,0.295] > Economics 0.117 [0.010,0.223]. Between-domain moderator test: **RE Q=2.91, df=2, p=0.234** (vs FE Q=24.9, p<1e-4, which is an artifact of the ee weighting collapse below). RE contrasts: Social−Cognitive −0.017 (p=0.78), Social−Economics +0.099 (p=0.15), rpp−ee +0.105 (p=0.10).

**Mechanism:** Social originals have the smallest baseline effects (mean ro 0.346 vs 0.533 Cognitive), so identical proportional shrinkage yields a smaller absolute z-gap. Exploratory (labelled) meta-regression: se_fiso b=+1.29 (p<1e-6) and fiso b=+0.45 (p<1e-6) dominate; adding original ES renders domain terms null (Social +0.032 p=0.60, Economics −0.079 p=0.28). The gap tracks winner's-curse/significance selection and original imprecision, not a domain-level bias.

**(3) Headline ee weighting diagnostic (n=18).** D_z: unweighted 0.266 [0.084,0.447]; RE(DL) 0.129 [0.011,0.246]; RE(REML) 0.117 [0.010,0.223]; **fixed-effect 0.013 [−0.052,0.078]**. Cause: three studies hold 60.4% of inverse-variance weight (de Clippel AER 2014 alone 43.1%, D_z=−0.155, n=790/780) vs 15.0% top-3 share in rpp. **Stable across weighting:** the proportional-shrinkage ordering (Social worst, Economics best) and the positive sign of every D_z estimate. **Not stable:** whether the ee absolute gap is "small" (RE 0.117) or "absent" (FE 0.013), and which of Social/Cognitive leads on D_z (unweighted/RE → Cognitive; FE → Social). τ² sensitivity is minor (DL 0.025 vs REML 0.017 ee; 0.021/0.022 Social; 0.016/0.016 Cognitive), so this is weight concentration, not a τ² artifact.

**(4) Robustness.** LOO on RE pooled D_z: Social +0.223 (+0.207…+0.241), Cognitive +0.234 (+0.212…+0.250), Economics +0.117 (+0.092…+0.141), rpp +0.227 (+0.217…+0.237), ee +0.117 (+0.092…+0.141) — no single-study driver (max swing 0.049). Contrast jackknife: Social−Cognitive LOO crosses zero (−0.038…+0.009, genuinely null), while Social−Economics (+0.057…+0.129), Cognitive−Economics (+0.071…+0.137) and rpp−ee (+0.062…+0.125) keep positive sign. ## Hypothesis (as-observed, descriptive)

**Original studies report larger effect sizes than their replications in every domain, but the gap is largest in SOCIAL psychology and smallest in EXPERIMENTAL ECONOMICS when "larger" is measured proportionally — whereas measured as an absolute Fisher-z difference the domains are statistically indistinguishable and Cognitive is numerically largest.**

Concretely: originals exceed replications in 73/86 pairs (84.9%), overall mean D_z = fiso−fisr = 0.262 (paired t p=7.1e-12). Because the gap is universal, the domain question is about its magnitude, and the answer is framing-dependent — stated explicitly per domain rather than resolved in favour of one metric.

**(1) Relative/proportional metrics (co-primary #1): Social > Cognitive > Economics in shrinkage.**
mean relative_es 0.278 / 0.509 / 0.657; medians 0.131 / 0.650 / 0.698; |rr|/|ro| 0.411 / 0.639 / 0.724; sign reversals 29.4% / 14.7% / 16.7%; replication success 20.6% / 47.1% / 61.1%. Social ranks 1st (largest gap) in 8 of the 12 tabulated framings, and the Social>Cognitive>Economics ordering is **unchanged in all five robustness variants**. Social−Economics relative_es = −0.378 (bootstrap 95% CI −0.710…−0.054, p=0.022; MW p=0.019) is the one clean separation; Social−Cognitive = −0.231 (CI −0.478…+0.038, boot p=0.089) is clear in medians (0.13 vs 0.65) and ranks (MW p=0.015) but not in means.

**(2) Signed Fisher-z gap D_z (co-primary #2): ordering changes and is not significant.**
Unweighted: Cognitive 0.289 [0.164,0.415] > Economics 0.266 [0.084,0.447] > Social 0.233 [0.162,0.304]. RE(REML): Cognitive 0.234 [0.142,0.326] ≈ Social 0.222 [0.150,0.295] > Economics 0.117 [0.010,0.223]. Between-domain moderator test: **RE Q=2.91, df=2, p=0.234** (vs FE Q=24.9, p<1e-4, which is an artifact of the ee weighting collapse below). RE contrasts: Social−Cognitive −0.017 (p=0.78), Social−Economics +0.099 (p=0.15), rpp−ee +0.105 (p=0.10).

**Mechanism:** Social originals have the smallest baseline effects (mean ro 0.346 vs 0.533 Cognitive), so identical proportional shrinkage yields a smaller absolute z-gap. Exploratory (labelled) meta-regression: se_fiso b=+1.29 (p<1e-6) and fiso b=+0.45 (p<1e-6) dominate; adding original ES renders domain terms null (Social +0.032 p=0.60, Economics −0.079 p=0.28). The gap tracks winner's-curse/significance selection and original imprecision, not a domain-level bias.

**(3) Headline ee weighting diagnostic (n=18).** D_z: unweighted 0.266 [0.084,0.447]; RE(DL) 0.129 [0.011,0.246]; RE(REML) 0.117 [0.010,0.223]; **fixed-effect 0.013 [−0.052,0.078]**. Cause: three studies hold 60.4% of inverse-variance weight (de Clippel AER 2014 alone 43.1%, D_z=−0.155, n=790/780) vs 15.0% top-3 share in rpp. **Stable across weighting:** the proportional-shrinkage ordering (Social worst, Economics best) and the positive sign of every D_z estimate. **Not stable:** whether the ee absolute gap is "small" (RE 0.117) or "absent" (FE 0.013), and which of Social/Cognitive leads on D_z (unweighted/RE → Cognitive; FE → Social). τ² sensitivity is minor (DL 0.025 vs REML 0.017 ee; 0.021/0.022 Social; 0.016/0.016 Cognitive), so this is weight concentration, not a τ² artifact.

**(4) Robustness.** LOO on RE pooled D_z: Social +0.223 (+0.207…+0.241), Cognitive +0.234 (+0.212…+0.250), Economics +0.117 (+0.092…+0.141), rpp +0.227 (+0.217…+0.237), ee +0.117 (+0.092…+0.141) — no single-study driver (max swing 0.049). Contrast jackknife: Social−Cognitive LOO crosses zero (−0.038…+0.009, genuinely null), while Social−Economics (+0.057…+0.129), Cognitive−Economics (+0.071…+0.137) and rpp−ee (+0.062…+0.125) keep positive sign. Variants H2 (Eitam artifact recomputed −0.472→+0.472: Social mean rel_es 0.278→0.306, median 0.131→0.184, ranks unchanged), H3 (po≤0.05 only), H4 (rr>0 only), H5 (rr floored at 0) preserve the relative ordering; in H4/H5 Social ties for largest RE D_z (0.165 vs 0.158). Within every domain originals > replications (paired t / Wilcoxon / 20k sign-flip permutation p≤0.0004; binomial |rr|<|ro| p≤0.004).

**(5) Non-separability.** Economics is exactly the ee project (perfectly nested crosstab) and era is fully confounded with project (34/34 Social and 33/34 Cognitive papers published in 2008, one Cognitive in 2015; all 18 Economics papers 2011-2014; median replication N 58 vs 32 Cognitive / 129.5 Social). Any "domain" difference for Economics is simultaneously a protocol, era and replication-power difference and cannot be decomposed here. `aggregated` and `lab_id` are 100% empty, so multi-effect aggregation and lab clustering are unverifiable; the 86 rows are a significance-filtered selected sample.

native_result.query: What is the proportion of junior professors in replicated studies in Psychology?
native_result.HypoA: In Psychology, replicated studies have a much higher proportion of junior professor (64.7%) and in the original studies the senior professors are more represented (82.4%)
native_result.HypoB: In the Psychology replication project (project == 'rpp'), 39.2% of replicated studies (38 of 97) were led by a junior professor - an 'Assistant' or 'Assistant Professor' as the most senior author on the replication team (seniority.r) - roughly twice the share led by full Professors (19.6%), with Associate Professors (24.7%) and Researchers (16.5%) making up the remainder. This is a study-level proportion of the single recorded most senior replication author per study, not an author-level share. Junior leadership is not significantly associated with replication success (45.7% among successful vs 35.5% among failed replications, Fisher p = 0.39), so the ~39% figure describes who conducts replications rather than a success-conditioned composition; it applies only to the Psychology (rpp) project because seniority.r is coded 'Professor' for every Many Labs 1/3 and Experimental Economics row.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv (927 rows x 57 cols; the only staged file containing seniority fields - the replication-success file has none and was used only to corroborate that the label 'Psychology' corresponds to rpp via surname overlap). Filtered project == 'rpp' (97 rows, one per original-study x effect-type, drop==True rows retained per directive). Used seniority.r as the replication-team seniority field (seniority.o contains zero junior values within rpp). Computed the primary proportion as the share of rows with seniority.r in {'Assistant','Assistant Professor'} = 38/97 = 0.3918, with a Wilson 95% CI (30.1-49.1%). Reported labelled sensitivities for unit (95 unique original studies), exclusion flag (drop==False, 36/90), success conditioning (replicated==1, 16/35; and 16/31 excluding drop rows), junior threshold (+Associate 62/97; any non-full-professor 78/97), field swap (seniority.o, 0/97) and broader psychology scope (38/909, documented coding artifact). Added diagnostics: full seniority distribution, seniority.o/.r agreement (0.206), junior x replicated chi-square/Fisher tests, missingness (0 in both seniority fields). Code: analysis/final_proportion.py; console record: analysis/final_report.txt (earlier inspection pass: analysis/inspect_seniority.py, analysis/inspection_summary.txt).

native_result.HypoB: Social psychology (the `Social` discipline — the social/personality-psychology domain dominated by the Reproducibility Project: Psychology pairs, plus the social-psychology effects of Many Labs 1 and 3) is the domain in which both the original and the replication studies primarily used student subjects. In these 74 O/R pairs 62/73 = 84.9% of originals and 60/73 = 82.2% of replications used student subjects at the study level (83.6%/80.6% when the four repeated titles are collapsed, 82.2%/78.6% across all lab-level rows), a pair that brackets the quoted 82.4%/80.9% and is the closest match of any domain under 6 of the 7 analytic conventions tested. Cognitive psychology (75.5% original vs 81.6% replication) and experimental economics (94.4% vs 100%) fail to show the same near-82%/near-81% combination. Within Social the only departure from student samples is on the replication side (3 studies moved from student to online samples, plus anyone/community samples), and the `online` subject type exists only in replications (0 originals vs 148 replication rows), so the original-to-replication decline reflects a shift in sampling mode rather than in the target population.

native_result.query: In which years were individuals with a criminal record found to have significantly lower wealth compared to those without?
native_result.HypoA: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
native_result.HypoB: Individuals with a criminal record (ever jailed 1985-1994) had significantly lower composite wealth than those never jailed in 1985, 1990 and 1996, but the years differ in meaning: the 1985 gap is pre-existing/concurrent and consistent with selection, while 1990 and 1996 are post-exposure gaps. Among NLSY-79 respondents (n=12,013; 289 ever-jailed vs 11,724 never-jailed) wealth was significantly lower for the ever-jailed every year (one-sided tie-corrected Mann-Whitney U, Holm-adjusted p=8.0e-11, 1.2e-34, 9.3e-26; Cliff's delta -0.22, -0.42, -0.35; Hodges-Lehmann shift -$1,260, -$7,850, -$6,000), and the gap widened after exposure (jailed mean wealth 31.6% -> 22.1% -> 19.3% of non-jailed mean; P(wealth>0) ratio 0.81 -> 0.61 -> 0.62). The 1985 difference is not an incarceration effect because jail was measured over 1985-1994, so it largely reflects pre-existing disadvantage; the association is robust to deduplication, winsorization and race x sex stratification but remains observational and unadjusted, so no causal effect of incarceration on wealth is established.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspected file: 12,013x6, zero missing values, ever_jailed in {0,1}, wealth heavy-tailed (skew 6.3-16.6), 24-54% exact zeros, real negatives (min -866,400). 2) Primary per-year contrast, all rows retained, one-sided tie-corrected Mann-Whitney U (H1: jailed < non-jailed), Holm-Bonferroni across the three years within each test family at alpha=0.05. 3) Effect sizes: exact Hodges-Lehmann shift (binary search over 3.39M pairwise differences) with Hollander-Wolfe rank CI and 2,000x stratified percentile bootstrap; Cliff's delta with tie-corrected asymptotic and bootstrap CIs; median and mean differences; P(wealth>0) risk ratio with log-scale CI. 4) Robustness/secondary: Welch one-sided t on raw dollars (anti-conservative, criterion c3 only), Fisher exact on the extensive margin. 5) Cross-checks: 20,000-permutation MWU null, tie-corrected vs uncorrected variance, validation against scipy.mannwhitneyu, and a 300-replication label-permutation negative control (rejection rates 0.033-0.057 vs nominal 0.05). 6) Sensitivities: deduplicated data, winsorization at pooled p99, race x sex stratification (18 cells) with Holm. 7) Applied the approved decision rule per year (Holm-MWU p<0.05 AND median/HL/delta all negative AND Welch p<0.05). Dropped the shifted-log variant because a valid shift must exceed $866,400, which flattens all signal.

native_result.query: How does the consideration of academic characteristics alter the effects of Socioeconomic Status and race on BA degree completion?
native_result.HypoA: When academic characteristics are considered, the effect of SES on BA degree completion is reduced and the effect of race is enlarged.
native_result.HypoB: Accounting for academic characteristics changes the two background effects in opposite directions. In NLSY79, post-secondary attendance / BA-track progress (highest grade >= 13 by 1979, or dorm/fraternity/sorority residence in 1981-88; 19.8% of 12,532 respondents) is overwhelmingly predicted by family SES - each extra year of the better-educated parent's schooling raises the odds by a factor of 1.33 (95% CI 1.30-1.35; +33 percentage points comparing parents with <=8 versus >=16 years) - and adding parental education alone absorbs essentially all of the unadjusted racial gaps (Black -10.9pp, Hispanic -6.1pp, both reduced to about zero and non-significant). Adding 1981 ASVAB test scores then attenuates the SES effect by roughly a third of its log-odds (AOR 1.33 -> 1.18; -44% naive, -32% KHB scale-corrected, -53% of the average marginal effect; the parent-college advantage halves from +32pp to +17pp) while leaving it large and highly significant, whereas the race coefficients do not attenuate at all - they reverse: Black AOR 0.96 -> 1.59 and Hispanic 1.05 -> 3.20 (+5pp and +15pp adjusted risk differences). So academic characteristics account for a substantial share of the socioeconomic gradient but none of the racial gap: minority respondents with equal parental schooling and equal test scores were at least as likely as their non-black non-Hispanic peers to progress to post-secondary education. What survives adjustment as the real racial divide is unequal academic preparation (mean ASVAB composite at parent education 16+: NB NON-HISP +0.91, BLACK +0.51, HISPANIC +0.10 SD units), together with a race x SES interaction (Black x parent-ed AOR 0.80/yr, p<1e-6) showing the Black deficit widening at high parental education. The Hispanic advantage is the most robust single finding (ASVAB-adjusted AOR 2.6-3.3 on the composite outcome, 2.7-3.1 in the correctly temporally-ordered prospective variant, significant in every specification); the Black ASVAB-adjusted coefficient is much less stable (1.0-1.6 on the composite, 2.4-2.6 on the 1979-grade outcome, ~0.9 or below and statistically ambiguous on college residence and the prospective variant). This is a descriptive composition/decomposition, not a causal estimate: ASVAB and class rank are 1981 measures that partly post-date the 1979 attainment measure and are themselves socially patterned (r = 0.48 with parental education), and the outcome is observed post-secondary attendance / BA-track progress, not a completed degree.

Outcomes: y_O1 grade>=13 (1979); y_O2 dorm/frat/sorority 1981-88; y_O3 = y_O1 OR y_O2 (PRIMARY, 19.8%); y_PROSP = baseline grade<=12 -> dorm 1982-88 (prospective sensitivity). SES = max(mother, father) years (linear, categorical <=11/12/13-15/16+, any-parent-BA); 1978 log income as sensitivity; 1985 signed log wealth exploratory and flagged as post-decision. Race = dummies vs NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC; sex and age1979 in every model from M1. native_result.query: How is the advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students related to Socioeconomic status levels?
native_result.HypoA: The advantage in BA degree completion rates for Black students is more pronounced at lower SES levels with the interaction term for Socioeconomic status and being black having a coefficient of 0.7606
native_result.HypoB: Educational attainment rises far more steeply with family socioeconomic status for Black respondents than for non-Black non-Hispanic respondents in this NLSY79 cohort, so the Black attainment shortfall is concentrated entirely at low SES and disappears at higher SES: below the pooled SES median Black respondents completed grade 12 or more at 53.5% vs 74.1% for non-Black non-Hispanic respondents (gap -20.7 pp, 95% CI -27.0 to -14.4; RR 0.72), while at or above the median the groups are statistically indistinguishable (89.2% vs 90.2%; gap -1.0 pp, 95% CI -6.3 to +4.2; RR 0.99), a race-by-SES interaction confirmed by LR tests (Black-only chi2 = 7.01, df 1, p = 0.008; interaction OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.19-4.06). The Black SES gradient is +35.7 pp (53.5 to 89.2) versus +16.1 pp (74.1 to 90.2) for the comparison group, so high family background buys Black students about twice as much additional schooling but never lifts them above their socioeconomic peers - no SES stratum, including the descriptive grade>=16 appendix (Black 0.25% vs 0.38%, Fisher p = 0.52), shows a Black advantage - and true BA completion is unobserved in this extract (only 37 respondents at grade >= 16, 5 of them Black, measured when respondents were 14-22), so the finding is an association about SES-conditioned attainment gradients, not a causal or institutional claim.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (12,686 x 61), cleaned sentinels (grade 95 -> missing, wealth -250 -> missing) and handled top-coded money variables via rank-based cuts. 2) Built outcome ladder: P3 primary = grade >= 12 among respondents aged >= 20 in 1979 (n=3,487); P1 = grade >= 13; P2 = ever DORM/FRATERNITY/SORORITY residence 1981-96; descriptive appendix = grade >= 16 with Wilson and exact CIs. 3) Built background SES index (z of max parental grade, z of occupation major-group prestige rank validated against parental education and 1979 income, z of log family income 1979; >= 2 of 3 items; 11,747 respondents). 4) Applied the pre-registered granularity rule: tertiles failed the n>=100 cell test (Black 257/108/86) so levels collapsed to below/at-or-above pooled median (smallest cell 148, none < 50); tertile results retained as flagged descriptive. 5) Stratified rate tables with Wilson CIs, percentage-point gaps and rate ratios (Black and Hispanic vs non-Black non-Hispanic reference). 6) Logistic models with age (linear+quadratic) and sex, BLACK x SES interaction and LR tests, plus model-predicted gaps. 7) Robustness: occupation prestige coding vs continuous -code, complete-case, occupation dropped, single-proxy indices, endogenous 1985-1996 wealth/income/savings direction checks, missing-indicator diagnostic; no outcome imputation. 8) ASVAB mean-Z attenuation check on a common subsample (reported as attenuation, not mediation). 9) Wrote tables, model summaries and RESULTS_summary.md under outputs/.

native_result.query: How does the median wealth of white individuals compare to that of black and Hispanic individuals from 1985 onwards?
native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: Across the only three wealth waves available in this file - 1985, 1990 and 1996 - with 1985 the earliest wealth measurement, so "from 1985 onwards" is bounded by these three waves, respondents in the white cohort (racial/ethnic cohort 3 = NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC, a label that also contains the small Asian, Native American and other groups NLSY79 does not separate) held higher median family net wealth than black (cohort 1) and Hispanic (cohort 2) respondents at every wave, and the gap widened substantially in both absolute and relative terms. In nominal dollars exactly as recorded: in 1985 the white median was $3,500 versus $1,600 for black respondents (gap $1,900; ratio 2.2x) and $500 for Hispanic respondents (gap $3,000; ratio 7.0x, a figure to read only with caution because that median is below $1,000 and 41.9% of Hispanic respondents were at or below zero net wealth, so the level gap is the reliable statement); in 1990 the white median was $12,972 versus $4,800 for black respondents (gap $8,172; 2.7x) and $1,600 for Hispanic respondents (gap $11,372; 8.1x); in 1996 the white median was $42,600 versus $9,800 for black respondents (gap $32,800; 4.4x) and $2,562 for Hispanic respondents (gap $40,038; 16.6x). The white-to-black ratio roughly doubled (2.2 to 4.4) and the white-to-Hispanic ratio rose from about 7 to about 17, and the widening is not an artefact of inflation: in constant 1996 dollars (deflators from CPI-U annual averages, 1982-84=100, with 1985=107.6, 1990=130.7, 1996=156.9, i.e. x1.458 and x1.200) the white-black gap grew from about $2,771 to $32,800 and the white-Hispanic gap from about $4,375 to $40,038, because real median wealth rose about 8.4-fold for whites versus 4.2-fold for blacks and 3.5-fold for Hispanics. The ordering white > black > Hispanic is stable at all three waves, but the distributions overlap heavily - in 1996 the white 25th percentile ($8,500) sits below the black median ($9,800) - so the difference is a shift in central tendency and in the share holding no or negative net wealth (1996: 10.9% white, 20.8% black, 34.9% Hispanic) rather than a clean separation between groups, and the same pattern holds in the balanced panel of 5,739 respondents observed in all three waves (1996 ratios 4.7 and 17.8), so it is not produced by available-case estimation. This comparison is purely descriptive and is materially qualified because the wealth variables are a family-level measure (respondent/spouse assets minus debts) assigned to individual respondents who were only 20-28 years old in 1985, so part of the early gap may reflect differences in family formation and marriage rather than individual wealth accumulation, and because all estimates are unweighted and computed on all cases available per wave, with the balanced-panel figures serving as the sensitivity check.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Input inspection (analysis/01_inspect_inputs.py): confirmed 12,686 unique respondents x 61 columns; located the three wealth columns ('Family net wealth, 1985', 'Family net wealth, 1990', 'Family net wealth, 1996 (key data point)') and 'Racial/ethnic cohort, 1979' (1=BLACK 2,002, 2=HISPANIC 3,174, 3=NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC 7,510, no missing, no sentinel codes); documented missingness (20.4%/26.7%/44.5% overall, differential by cohort), severe right skew (mean/median 4.4-6.1), mass at or below zero (26.7%/22.5%/20.0%), source top-coding at each wave's maximum, and that $0 wealth is genuine (96.8% of zero cases have all component assets 0/null). 2) Main analysis (analysis/02_wealth_by_race.py): cohort 3 mapped to 'white'; zeros and negatives retained; per wave x cohort computed n, mean, Q1, median, Q3, IQR, share<=0 with 2,000-replicate percentile bootstrap 95% CIs on medians; white-minus-X dollar gaps and white/X median ratios computed within wave (so deflator-invariant); nominal dollars primary with constant-1996$ secondary (CPI-U 107.6/130.7/156.9); primary estimand = all available cases per wave, sensitivity = balanced panel of respondents with wealth in all three waves; Kruskal-Wallis computed but reported only under an explicit no-weights/no-strata caveat. 3) Ratio-uncertainty check (analysis/03_ratio_uncertainty.py): bootstrap CIs for all six ratios and gaps, with an explicit instability flag where the denominator median is below $1,000 (Hispanic 1985). 4) Verification: all nine medians independently re-derived through a second code path (groupby-median) and matched exactly; outputs written to analysis/RESULTS.md, wealth_medians_by_race.csv, ratio_and_gap_uncertainty.csv.

sub_hypo.relations: White individuals have significantly higher median family net wealth than black and Hispanic individuals from 1985 onwards. The dataset's racial/ethnic cohort labels are BLACK, HISPANIC, and NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC; white is not separately identified.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.

sub_hypo.text: Median family net wealth followed the ordering white > black > Hispanic in 1985, 1990 and 1996, and white–black and white–Hispanic gaps widened in nominal dollars and median ratios.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 respondents across the only available wealth waves: 1985 (the earliest measurement), 1990 and 1996. Estimates are unweighted and use all available cases per wave, retaining zero and negative wealth. 'White' denotes cohort 3, NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC, which also includes small Asian, Native American and other groups not separately identified. Wealth measures family/respondent-spouse assets minus debts, not individual wealth. Respondents were aged 20–28 in 1985; early gaps may partly reflect family formation and marriage rather than individual accumulation. Comparisons are descriptive.
sub_hypo.relations: Nominal white/black/Hispanic medians were $3,500/$1,600/$500 in 1985, $12,972/$4,800/$1,600 in 1990, and $42,600/$9,800/$2,562 in 1996. White-minus-black gaps increased from $1,900 to $8,172 to $32,800; white-minus-Hispanic gaps increased from $3,000 to $11,372 to $40,038. White/black median ratios rose from 2.2 to 2.7 to 4.4, roughly doubling; white/Hispanic ratios rose from 7.0 to 8.1 to 16.6. The 1985 Hispanic ratio requires caution because the denominator median was below $1,000 and 41.9% held zero or negative wealth; the dollar gap is the reliable statement.

sub_hypo.text: Widening racial/ethnic gaps in median family net wealth were not an artefact of inflation: white median wealth grew more rapidly in real terms than black or Hispanic median wealth.
sub_hypo.context: Unweighted NLSY79 available-case comparisons across 1985, 1990 and 1996, with zero and negative wealth retained and cohort 3 labeled white despite including other non-black, non-Hispanic groups. Constant-1996-dollar calculations use CPI-U annual averages of 107.6, 130.7 and 156.9, respectively (1982–84=100), multiplying 1985 values by approximately 1.458 and 1990 values by 1.200. Comparisons are descriptive and concern family-level wealth.
sub_hypo.relations: Between 1985 and 1996, the constant-1996-dollar white–black median gap increased from approximately $2,771 to $32,800 and the white–Hispanic gap from approximately $4,375 to $40,038. Real median wealth increased approximately 8.4-fold for whites, 4.2-fold for blacks and 3.5-fold for Hispanics. Within-wave median ratios are unchanged by inflation adjustment.

sub_hypo.text: The stable white > black > Hispanic median ordering represents differences in central tendency and in the prevalence of zero or negative family net wealth, not cleanly separated wealth distributions.
sub_hypo.context: Descriptive, unweighted NLSY79 available-case comparisons across the three wealth waves, with distributional examples from 1996 in nominal dollars. Zero and negative wealth are retained. White denotes the broader NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC cohort.
sub_hypo.relations: Wealth distributions overlap heavily: in 1996 the white 25th percentile of $8,500 was below the black median of $9,800. Shares with zero or negative family net wealth were 10.9% for whites, 20.8% for blacks and 34.9% for Hispanics.

sub_hypo.text: The higher white median family net wealth and widening racial/ethnic gaps also occur among respondents observed in all three wealth waves, so the pattern is not produced by available-case estimation.
sub_hypo.context: Unweighted balanced-panel sensitivity analysis of 5,739 NLSY79 respondents with observed wealth in 1985, 1990 and 1996, compared with the primary all-available-cases-per-wave analysis. Zero and negative wealth are retained; white denotes cohort 3, NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC. Results remain descriptive and concern family-level wealth.
sub_hypo.relations: The balanced panel preserves the median ordering and widening-gap pattern. Its 1996 white/black median ratio is 4.7 and white/Hispanic ratio is 17.8, compared with available-case ratios of 4.4 and 16.6.

gen_sub_hypo.full_hypo: Across the only three wealth waves available in this file - 1985, 1990 and 1996 - with 1985 the earliest wealth measurement, so "from 1985 onwards" is bounded by these three waves, respondents in the white cohort (racial/ethnic cohort 3 = NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC, a label that also contains the small Asian, Native American and other groups NLSY79 does not separate) held higher median family net wealth than black (cohort 1) and Hispanic (cohort 2) respondents at every wave, and the gap widened substantially in both absolute and relative terms. In nominal dollars exactly as recorded: in 1985 the white median was $3,500 versus $1,600 for black respondents (gap $1,900; ratio 2.2x) and $500 for Hispanic respondents (gap $3,000; ratio 7.0x, a figure to read only with caution because that median is below $1,000 and 41.9% of Hispanic respondents were at or below zero net wealth, so the level gap is the reliable statement); in 1990 the white median was $12,972 versus $4,800 for black respondents (gap $8,172; 2.7x) and $1,600 for Hispanic respondents (gap $11,372; 8.1x); in 1996 the white median was $42,600 versus $9,800 for black respondents (gap $32,800; 4.4x) and $2,562 for Hispanic respondents (gap $40,038; 16.6x). The white-to-black ratio roughly doubled (2.2 to 4.4) and the white-to-Hispanic ratio rose from about 7 to about 17, and the widening is not an artefact of inflation: in constant 1996 dollars (deflators from CPI-U annual averages, 1982-84=100, with 1985=107.6, 1990=130.7, 1996=156.9, i.e. x1.458 and x1.200) the white-black gap grew from about $2,771 to $32,800 and the white-Hispanic gap from about $4,375 to $40,038, because real median wealth rose about 8.4-fold for whites versus 4.2-fold for blacks and 3.5-fold for Hispanics. The ordering white > black > Hispanic is stable at all three waves, but the distributions overlap heavily - in 1996 the white 25th percentile ($8,500) sits below the black median ($9,800) - so the difference is a shift in central tendency and in the share holding no or negative net wealth (1996: 10.9% white, 20.8% black, 34.9% Hispanic) rather than a clean separation between groups, and the same pattern holds in the balanced panel of 5,739 respondents observed in all three waves (1996 ratios 4.7 and 17.8), so it is not produced by available-case estimation. This comparison is purely descriptive and is materially qualified because the wealth variables are a family-level measure (respondent/spouse assets minus debts) assigned to individual respondents who were only 20-28 years old in 1985, so part of the early gap may reflect differences in family formation and marriage rather than individual wealth accumulation, and because all estimates are unweighted and computed on all cases available per wave, with the balanced-panel figures serving as the sensitivity check.

In nominal dollars exactly as recorded: in 1985 the white median was $3,500 versus $1,600 for black respondents (gap $1,900; ratio 2.2x) and $500 for Hispanic respondents (gap $3,000; ratio 7.0x, a figure to read only with caution because that median is below $1,000 and 41.9% of Hispanic respondents were at or below zero net wealth, so the level gap is the reliable statement); in 1990 the white median was $12,972 versus $4,800 for black respondents (gap $8,172; 2.7x) and $1,600 for Hispanic respondents (gap $11,372; 8.1x); in 1996 the white median was $42,600 versus $9,800 for black respondents (gap $32,800; 4.4x) and $2,562 for Hispanic respondents (gap $40,038; 16.6x). The white-to-black ratio roughly doubled (2.2 to 4.4) and the white-to-Hispanic ratio rose from about 7 to about 17, and the widening is not an artefact of inflation: in constant 1996 dollars (deflators from CPI-U annual averages, 1982-84=100, with 1985=107.6, 1990=130.7, 1996=156.9, i.e. x1.458 and x1.200) the white-black gap grew from about $2,771 to $32,800 and the white-Hispanic gap from about $4,375 to $40,038, because real median wealth rose about 8.4-fold for whites versus 4.2-fold for blacks and 3.5-fold for Hispanics. The ordering white > black > Hispanic is stable at all three waves, but the distributions overlap heavily - in 1996 the white 25th percentile ($8,500) sits below the black median ($9,800) - so the difference is a shift in central tendency and in the share holding no or negative net wealth (1996: 10.9% white, 20.8% black, 34.9% Hispanic) rather than a clean separation between groups, and the same pattern holds in the balanced panel of 5,739 respondents observed in all three waves (1996 ratios 4.7 and 17.8), so it is not produced by available-case estimation. This comparison is purely descriptive and is materially qualified because the wealth variables are a family-level measure (respondent/spouse assets minus debts) assigned to individual respondents who were only 20-28 years old in 1985, so part of the early gap may reflect differences in family formation and marriage rather than individual wealth accumulation, and because all estimates are unweighted and computed on all cases available per wave, with the balanced-panel figures serving as the sensitivity check.,

native_result.HypoA: The effect of SES on BA degree completion decreases from 0.3636  (significant) to  -0.2293 (insignificant) and effect of race on BA degree completion decreases from 0.5024  (significant) to 0.0923 (insignificant) when academic characteristics are considered.
native_result.HypoB: SES (socioeconomic status). Its effect on BA degree completion falls from a strong positive, highly significant unadjusted logit coefficient (+0.4729, SE 0.0826, p=1.0e-08, OR 1.60) to a small negative, non-robust one (-0.2316, SE 0.1005, p=0.021, OR 0.79; insignificant at alpha=.01, and insignificant at alpha=.05 in sex-stratified and percentile-only variants) once both race and academic characteristics (ASVAB ability composite and class percentile) are included. The apparent SES advantage is channelled almost entirely through measured academic preparation (SES-ABILITY r=.463, SES-PERCENTILE r=.304) and, secondarily, through race (SES-WHITE r=.317): academic characteristics alone absorb 98% of the 0.705 log-odds attenuation, race alone only 17%. Because ABILITY (p=4e-17) and PERCENTILE (p=2e-07) stay strongly predictive while race itself drops to non-significance, controlling for them removes the SES gradient and leaves a near-zero, slightly negative residual direct effect. This is suppression/over-adjustment along the causal pathway from family background to academic preparation to degree attainment, not evidence that higher SES harms BA completion.

In the Q8_ML_Addressing_* multi-select block (Qualtrics 'quoted' = selected), 51.0% of the 194 respondents with a valid Q8 block named Project Lead / Project Manager (99/194; bootstrap 95% CI 43.8-57.7 percentile, 44.3-58.8 BCa, 44.0-58.0 Wilson) and 49.0% named Data Scientist (95/194; CI 42.3-56.2 percentile, 41.8-55.7 BCa, 42.0-56.0 Wilson), versus 25.8% for the third-ranked Business Analyst; across 10,000 seeded respondent-level bootstrap replicates these two roles take the top two spots in 100% of replicates (gap over the third role 23.2 pp, 95% CI 13.4-32.5), although their order within the pair is statistically indistinguishable (2.0 pp difference, 95% CI -7.7 to +11.3). The question's 49.6%/61.389% pair is most plausibly the same two roles computed on a slightly different analysis set or publication cleaning: 49.6% falls inside our 49.0-51.0% band, and the 'respondents naming at least one role' denominator (n=164) yields 60.4% for Project Lead; the only coincidental 61.3-61.4% values elsewhere in the file are non-role items (Q11 data-quality NFR = 61.3%) and are rejected as matches. Limitation: the published 95% intervals (half-widths 0.381/0.434 pp, implying effective n of about 48,000-66,000) cannot be reproduced from this 276-row survey - our honest intervals are about +/-7 pp at n=194 - so the reproducible claim is the identity and dominance of these two roles, not the exact point/interval magnitudes. native_result.query: Which technique is considered the most commonly used by respondents for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects, with 69.399% indicating so (95% CI [69.062, 69.735]) after bootstrapping for statistical significance?
native_result.HypoA: Interviews (69.399% respondents saying so, 95% CI [69.062, 69.735]) are the most commonly used technique considered by the respondents for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects after bootstrapping for statistical significance.
native_result.HypoB: Interviews are the most commonly used technique for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects: 97 of the 194 respondents who answered the Q9 elicitation block (50.0%, 95% bootstrap CI 42.8-57.2%) reported using interviews, more than scenarios or prototyping (75 each, 38.7%), workshops/meetings (74, 38.1%), observation (64, 33.0%) or any other technique (11, 5.7%). Interviews rank first on every defensible denominator (188, 194, 276, 174, 170 rows) and in 2000/2000 random subsamples, and they significantly outwork workshops/meetings, observation and 'others' in paired McNemar tests (Holm-adjusted p<0.05); the lead over scenarios/prototyping is directionally consistent but only marginal after multiplicity correction (Holm p~0.056). The 69.399% (95% CI [69.062, 69.735]) figure quoted in the question is NOT reproducible from this export and is reported only as a labelled discrepancy reference.
native_result.WorkflowB: Read data/requirements_engineering_for_ML-enabled_systems.csv (276x202, dtype=str). Confirmed Q9_ML_Elicitation_* (6 scored items + Others_Free) is the elicitation block and its domain is exactly {'quoted','not quoted','-77'} (no Likert intensity exists in this export), with block-consistent '-77' for 82/276 rows (all Status='Suspended'). Indicator uses=(value=='quoted'); '-77' treated as missing and excluded listwise at respondent level -> primary frame 194 respondents exposed to the block. 'Most commonly used' = max count/share, ties by count then label; also ranked over the 5 named techniques. Percent share = n_used / n_denominator. Inference: B=10,000 respondent-row bootstrap (whole rows resampled with replacement so within-respondent multi-select correlation is preserved), seed=12345, 2.5/97.5 percentile CI primary, analytic-jackknife BCa secondary; Wilson intervals and 8 alternative seeds as cross-checks; paired McNemar exact tests (Interviews vs each technique, Holm step-down) as the primary significance evidence; winner stability over 5 denominator frames and 2,000 random 85% subsamples. Sensitivity frames 188 (status-screened), 276 ('-77' recoded to 0), 174 (>=1 of six items), 170 (>=1 of five named) reported as sensitivity only. No filter, subset or denominator was selected to match 69.399%; that figure is handled in a dedicated discrepancy note (required counts vs observed, implied-N 72,047 from the 0.3365pp CI half-width, 0.5155pp quantisation grid, and the 97/140=69.2857% reconstruction labelled as a hypothesis about a different export). Outputs: analysis/q9_results_long.csv (30 rows = 5 frames x 6 techniques with source_column, indicator/denominator definitions, n, share, percentile+BCa CIs, SE, rank, is_max, B, seed, McNemar p and Holm p), q9_primary_results.csv, q9_mcnemar.csv, three discrepancy CSVs, q9_verification_vs_inspection.csv, FINDINGS.md.

native_result.HypoA: The least used documentation formats for requirements in ML-enabled system projects are ML Canvas (10.13% respondents, 95% CI [9.926, 10.333]) and Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) Scenarios (4.366% respondents, 95% CI [4.231, 4.501]) after bootstrapping for statistical significance.
native_result.HypoB: ML Canvas and BDD scenarios are the two least-used documentation formats for requirements in ML-enabled system projects. In the Q10 documentation multi-select battery, answered by 194 of the 276 stored respondents (82 non-responders, all 'Suspended', coded -77 and dropped as NA rather than counted as zeros), ML Canvas was used by 15/194 = 7.73% of respondents (95% bootstrap percentile CI 4.12-11.86; Wilson 4.74-12.36) and BDD scenarios by 4/194 = 2.06% (CI 0.52-4.12; Wilson 0.81-5.18) - the two lowest of the ten named formats, versus Notebooks 34.02%, User Stories 32.47% and Requirements Lists 26.29%. Respondent-level bootstrap (20,000 replicates) makes BDD scenarios the least-used format in 99.9% of replicates and ML Canvas the second least-used in 97.5% of replicates among named formats; the ordering is unchanged on all 276 rows (5.43%/1.45%), Completed-only (8.0%/2.13%), respondents naming at least one format (10.27%/2.74%) and under project-count weighting. ML Canvas counts as second-least because the 'Other' free-text option is treated as an unspecified residual rather than a format: it ties ML Canvas at 15/194 and keeping it splits the second-least probability 54%/46%; its 14 free texts (Confluence/Jira/Notion/wiki pages, design documents, meeting notes, mathematical models) contain no alias for any named format, and 'Not Documented' (15.46%) is excluded because it denotes absent documentation, not a format. The magnitudes quoted in the question (10.13%, CI [9.926,10.333]; 4.366%, CI [4.231,4.501]) are not reproducible from this file - no denominator yields them (their ratio 2.32 is unreachable from the observed 15:4 = 3.75) and their CI widths imply an effective sample of ~85,000 versus a 55,752-cell file - so they most likely come from a different data version or a project-level expansion. Our replication is consistent with those figures in the identity and ordering of the two least-used formats (ML Canvas ahead of BDD scenarios, the absolute minimum), while our respondent-level percentages are lower.

native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Among the two groups in this dataset, the Lower-middle-income (LMC) aggregate shows the larger and better-supported positive association between rising education expenditure and per-capita output, and Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) shows the weaker one - though the association is far weaker than raw levels fits suggest and is not robust enough for a causal claim. Using the only available proxies (outcome = GNI per capita, constant 2015 US$, rather than the brief's 'GDP, 2010 US$'; exposure = 'Adjusted savings: education expenditure', % of GNI, not a government budget share; 'developing countries' = the LMC aggregate), a one-percentage-point rise in the share of GNI directed to education is associated with about +1.5 percentage points of annual per-capita growth in LMC countries (b=+0.0151, SE=0.0056, t=2.70, n=40, Newey-West(4)), whereas for SSA the slope is unstable and not distinguishable from zero (b=-0.0516, SE=0.0236, n=4 without controls; sign flips to +0.0408, SE=0.0330, t=1.24 once export growth is added; n=4 because SSA per-capita output exists only for 2011-2015). That SSA ordering is bounded: the LMC positive slope reverses under a two-year distributed lag (cumulative -0.0193, t=-0.73), vanishes in 1991-2015 (-0.0312, t=-0.70), and hinges on one year (dropping 1976 gives +0.0017; block-bootstrap 95% CI [-0.010,+0.033], p=0.16). The Delta-education x SSA interaction is not interpretable (4 of 44 rows are SSA; Chow F(2,40)=0.134, p=0.875), so equal slopes can be neither established nor rejected. Descriptively SSA sustained a HIGHER education-investment share than LMC (+0.80 pp of GNI on average 1975-2015; +0.25 pp in 2011-2015) while ending 2015 LOWER in per-capita output ($1,634 vs $1,965), slower-growing (1.24%/yr vs 2.01%/yr) and far behind in secondary enrollment (gross 43.4 vs 64.5), so higher education spending in SSA is associated with no relative per-capita-output advantage. native_result.WorkflowA:
1. One-hot encode Gender variable into MALE and FEMALE
2. Extract the independent variables ['AGE','INCOME', 'BMI', 'BLACK', 'HISPANIC', 'MALE', 'FEMALE']
3. Add dependent variable (DISSAVED) from the df
4. Add a constant term to the independent variable to account for the intercept term in the logistic regression model.
5. Fit a logistic regression model
native_result.HypoB: In the 1989 NLSY79 cross-section (respondents aged 24-32 only, n = 12,686), the probability of net dissaving (DISSAVED = 1) declines with age - about -0.5 percentage points per year, from roughly 24% at age 24 to 19.7% at age 32, a total of -4.3 pp (95% CI -6.8 to -1.8) after adjusting for GENDER, log income, BLACK, HISPANIC and an indicator for mean-imputed income - and the decline is essentially linear rather than U-shaped or inverted-U (the AGE_2 term is not supported conditional on covariates, LR p = 0.35, and its implied turning point, age 24.0 with CI 15.9-32.1, lies at the edge of the observed support). Crucially, this age gradient is not a general life-cycle effect: dropping the 31% of rows whose INCOME equals the constant 47.279 (inferred mean-imputed missing income) removes it entirely (joint age LR p = 0.91; predicted 28.9% at 24 vs 28.6% at 32, change -0.26 pp, 95% CI -3.7 to +3.1), and an age x income-group interaction is decisive (LR = 40.8, p = 1.7e-10), with a per-year logit slope of -0.0016 (p = 0.88) among respondents with genuinely reported income versus -0.155 (OR 0.856/year) in the imputed-income group (16.5% -> 5.1% from 24 to 32). About 56% of the raw -4.0 pp gradient is compositional, since the share of imputed-income respondents rises from 27% to 39% with age while their own dissaving rate falls from 16% to 7%. Descriptively, the age decline is a shift out of 'savings unchanged / no savings' (44% -> 30%) and into positive saving (31% -> 50%), since DISSAVED and SAMESAVE are mutually exclusive states of one three-outcome. All statements are associational, confined to ages 24-32 in a single 1989 cross-section, and non-causal; the effect of age in this file should be described as a modest, monotone, covariate-adjusted decline that is statistically reliable only within the mean-imputed-income subgroup.

native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: Higher present-oriented financial behaviour is associated with higher adiposity in NLSY79, but the association is mostly concurrent rather than prospective: measured as a savings-based present-orientation proxy (1989 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview', ordered put-more-in < no-change < took-more-out < no-savings, plus the dis-save/no-savings binary and a net-saving-to-income ratio), it predicts BMI1989 monotonically (mean BMI 24.54 / 24.97 / 25.14 / 25.50; obesity 10.1% / 11.6% / 13.0% / 15.6%; fully adjusted +0.23 BMI units per step, p=0.0002; +0.44 for dis-save-or-no-savings, about 0.1 SD or 1.3 kg), yet holding 1981 body mass fixed removes 54-58% of that gradient (+0.10 per step, p=0.02) and the genuinely prospective 1992 outcome conditional on 1989 BMI is only marginal (+0.06 per step, p=0.08, n=3,861, attrition-fragile and shifted toward the non-black/non-Hispanic cohort). Because higher BMI in 1981 itself predicts more present-oriented saving behaviour in 1989 (+0.013 per BMI unit, p=0.003), the evidence is consistent with a reciprocal wealth/weight/preference process and supports an ASSOCIATION between savings-based present orientation and higher BMI - strongest in women and in the 'no savings' stratum - rather than a demonstrated causal effect of increased time preference on BMI.

gen_sub_hypo.full_hypo: Higher present-oriented financial behaviour is associated with higher adiposity in NLSY79, but the association is mostly concurrent rather than prospective: measured as a savings-based present-orientation proxy (1989 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview', ordered put-more-in < no-change < took-more-out < no-savings, plus the dis-save/no-savings binary and a net-saving-to-income ratio), it predicts BMI1989 monotonically (mean BMI 24.54 / 24.97 / 25.14 / 25.50; obesity 10.1% / 11.6% / 13.0% / 15.6%; fully adjusted +0.23 BMI units per step, p=0.0002; +0.44 for dis-save-or-no-savings, about 0.1 SD or 1.3 kg), yet holding 1981 body mass fixed removes 54-58% of that gradient (+0.10 per step, p=0.02) and the genuinely prospective 1992 outcome conditional on 1989 BMI is only marginal (+0.06 per step, p=0.08, n=3,861, attrition-fragile and shifted toward the non-black/non-Hispanic cohort). Because higher BMI in 1981 itself predicts more present-oriented saving behaviour in 1989 (+0.013 per BMI unit, p=0.003), the evidence is consistent with a reciprocal wealth/weight/preference process and supports an ASSOCIATION between savings-based present orientation and higher BMI - strongest in women and in the 'no savings' stratum - rather than a demonstrated causal effect of increased time preference on BMI.

P0||G0.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
P0||G0.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model

native_result.query: In which century did the Diversity in Pottery Form collapses and Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases simultaneuosly?
native_result.HypoA: Around 1800 BCE, Diversity in Pottery Form collapses, while Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases.
native_result.HypoB: Diversity in Pottery Form (ZKeform / PotteryForm_inter) collapses and Diversity in Pottery Decoration (Zkeverz / PotteryDecoration_inter) increases simultaneously in the single 100-year step from the 1800 BCE bin to the 1700 BCE bin of the fixed 100-year grid, c. 1800-1700 BCE - the 18th century BCE by strict ordinal counting (1800-1701 BCE), the same event labelled the 1700s/17th century BCE (c. 1700 BCE) under loose usage, with the collapse recorded in the 1700 BCE bin and the new state occupying the 1700-1100 BCE bins. Form falls +0.74 -> -1.13 z (delta -1.87, -3.43 SD of its own century-to-century changes) while decoration rises -0.48 -> +0.97 z (delta +1.45, +3.45 SD); divergence index delta_DEC - delta_FORM = 3.32 (z +5.81), 5.9x the runner-up. It is the only step of 38 with opposite directions and stays unique at 1.5/2/2.5-SD and MAD-robust thresholds. Hypothesis: the Late Neolithic / Older Bronze Age transition reorganised pottery tradition from many vessel FORMS to a broader DECORATIVE repertoire, as part of a wider reconfiguration of material and social capital (Dagger, HouseSize, Sickle decline; openness falling) rather than an autonomous craft trend.
native_result.WorkflowB: S1 parse capital.csv (ZKeform, Zkeverz) with comma-decimal decoding as the primary 100-year bin record (39 bins, BCE 4300-500) and time_series_data.csv as secondary; verify identity of constructs (37/37 anchors equal, max diff 0.000) and that *_inter is a linear interpolation (max diff 2.2e-16), so interpolation is used only for smoothing/slope corroboration. S2 compute the five pre-registered criteria for all 38 100-year steps: (a) same-step form decline AND decoration rise; (b) directional 2-SD collapse threshold against each variable's own century-to-century change distribution; (c) composite divergence index dDEC-dFORM with z-score and rank; (d) 100-y centred smoothed interpolated series, change over the preceding 100 y (plus 200/250-y sensitivity) at step endpoints with ranks among all years; (e) percentile level/rank shift and post-step state (record-low form, top-quartile decoration). Ranked candidate list retained with the runner-up (step ending 1000 BCE, form flat at the floor) and the Early-Neolithic concordance control (4300-4100 BCE low form with record-low decoration). Robustness across 1.5/2/2.5-SD and MAD-based thresholds. S3 convert the unique step into dating in bin language plus both ordinal-century conventions, and assemble context-only covariates (LN->OBA boundary, Dagger, HouseSize, Sickle, Amber, openness). S4 emit the hypothesis, criteria table, selected step, ASCII figure and full log to outputs/.

sub_hypo.text: At the Late Neolithic / Older Bronze Age transition, pottery-form diversity collapsed while pottery-decoration diversity increased in the same 100-year step, indicating a reorganisation from many vessel forms to a broader decorative repertoire.
sub_hypo.context: The fixed 100-year archaeological capital grid has 39 bins spanning 4300–500 BCE and 38 steps. The event occurs from the 1800 BCE bin to the 1700 BCE bin, with the collapse recorded at 1700 BCE and the new state occupying the 1700–1100 BCE bins. This is c. 1800–1700 BCE, the 18th century BCE under strict ordinal counting (1800–1701 BCE), also loosely labelled the 1700s/17th century BCE (c. 1700 BCE). Primary evidence is the original bin record; interpolated series provide smoothing/slope corroboration only.
sub_hypo.relations: Simultaneous opposing changes: form falls from +0.74 to -1.13 z (change -1.87; -3.43 SD of its own century-to-century changes), while decoration rises from -0.48 to +0.97 z (change +1.45; +3.45 SD). The divergence index, change in decoration minus change in form, is 3.32 (z-score +5.81), 5.9 times the runner-up. This is the only one of 38 steps with form decline and decoration rise and remains unique at 1.5-, 2-, and 2.5-SD and MAD-robust thresholds. The resulting state combines record-low form with top-quartile decoration. The runner-up ends at 1000 BCE with form flat at its floor; the 4300–4100 BCE control instead combines low form with record-low decoration. Corroboration uses 100-year centred smoothing and preceding-100-year changes, with 200- and 250-year smoothing sensitivity.

sub_hypo.text: The opposing shifts in pottery-form and pottery-decoration diversity were part of a wider reconfiguration of material and social capital at the Late Neolithic / Older Bronze Age transition, rather than an autonomous craft trend.
sub_hypo.context: The 1800–1700 BCE step at the Late Neolithic / Older Bronze Age boundary. Dagger, house size, sickle and openness are contextual covariates, not independently established causal explanations.
sub_hypo.relations: Pottery-form diversity declines and pottery-decoration diversity increases alongside declines in Dagger, HouseSize and Sickle and falling openness. Their concurrence supports the hypothesised wider reconfiguration of material and social capital rather than an isolated pottery trend. No column representing openness is explicitly identified in the hypothesis or workflow.

native_result.HypoA: Between 1500 BCE and 1300 BCE, highest growth of the period between 2000 BCE and 1100 BCE is seen.
native_result.HypoB: Between 2000 BCE and 1100 BCE the highest growth phase is 1500-1200 BCE, peaking in the century 1400-1301 BCE (openness growth concentrated in 1400-1200 BCE). Primary metric (100-year percentage/absolute change of the 100-year smoothed landscape-openness pollen PC1 score) gives 1400-1301 BCE +1.128 score units per century (+317.9% at bin level), rank 1 under all six openness series variants, followed by 1300-1201 BCE (+0.556, +37.5%) and 1800-1701 BCE (+0.510). Secondary metric (g_all_mean, mean of all-capital KDE growth rates) peaks one century earlier at 1500-1401 BCE (+0.00283/yr) and is second highest in 1400-1301 BCE (+0.00145/yr), where kde_all_mean also reaches its maximum level (4.14e-4) and kde_all_detrend is still rising. 1400-1301 BCE is the only century in the top two under both mainlines, hence the single best-supported highest-growth century.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Input verification: time_series_data.csv annual (CE -4100..-500, step 1, 3601 rows), capital.csv 100-yr grid (BCE 4300..500, 39 rows), pollen file annual (CE -4785..-702); calBP=1950-CE verified; capital Z columns equal ts columns exactly under CE=-BCE (max|diff|=0, n=37). 2) Window CE -2000..-1100 (901 annual rows) split into 9 century bins (endpoint -1100 folded into the 1300-1201 BCE bin) plus a capital 100-yr grid anchored sensitivity. 3) Metric A (primary, landscape openness): 100-year change of the 100-year smoothed openness computed three ways - A1 literal pointwise percentage change (reported, but artefact-prone because the PC1 score crosses zero), A2 bin-level percentage change with mean|previous values| denominator, A3 absolute change in score units - on 7 series variants (Belau smoothed/annual, SMOOTH_MEAN_50/100/150y, Belau+Woserin MEAN, Woserin only). 4) Metric B: century means of g_all_mean and g_all_std. 5) Metric C: per-century delta-Z of the *_inter capital series aggregated into the four approved classes (symbolic/social/cultural/economic) with a flat-series detector flagging bins where delta-Z=0 means no observations. 6) Cross-validation: kde_all_mean level and per-century slope, kde_all_detrend slope, as-shipped pollen_grate_100 century means, smoothing-window and site sensitivity, grid re-anchoring. native_result.HypoA: Symbolic capital components such as house size, the number of daggers, and hatchets/swords are characterized by negative values on the first principal component (PC1) and exhibit a wide distribution of values on the second principal component (PC2). This Principal component analysis (PCA) is on the forms of capital. The values of the individual elements of the forms of capital form the attributes.
native_result.HypoB: In the correlation-based, unrotated PCA of the twelve capital indicators run over the 37 hundred-year time slices (BCE 4100–500; PC1 = 32.45%, PC2 = 16.41%, PC1+PC2 = 48.86% of variance), the symbolic-capital components do NOT form their own axis: on PC1 they all load in the same direction with moderate-to-low magnitude and are therefore dragged along by the first axis rather than defining it (ZAxtSchwert/hatchet-sword -0.545, ZDolch/dagger -0.457, Zhausgr/house size -0.336; |loading| ranks 7, 9, 10 of 12; category mean |PC1| 0.446 vs 0.574 for the nine non-symbolic indicators, and 0.787 for pottery form/decoration), while PC1 itself is strongly chronological (r = +0.849 with BCE; group means +3.62 EN -> -5.81 OBA). On PC2 they are not a cluster but an uneven gradient on a single side of the axis: their loadings never change sign (range 0.198-0.512, sd 0.162, ranks 11, 7 and 3 of 12), so house size behaves like a strong PC2 variable alongside monument count (+0.657) and axes/celts (+0.595), whereas hatchets/swords are effectively absent from PC2 (rank 11, only 3.9% of their variance on PC2, communality on PC1-4 = 0.341, the lowest of the twelve). Read instead at slice level, the slices with the highest symbolic values are scattered over both poles of PC2 (8 highest hatchet/sword slices: PC2 -1.63 to +4.88, 4 positive/4 negative, IQR 4.11 vs 2.21 expected under permutation, p = 0.022; daggers 6/2, p = 0.155; house size 6/2, p = 0.451), i.e. symbolic peaks occur at both extremes rather than clustering at one pole. native_result.HypoB: Between 3400 and 3000 BCE (100-year bins, n = 5, cultural group MN) the number of monuments (MonumentCount / ZMonument) and of axes & celts (AxesCelts / ZBeil) changed as one coupled phenomenon: both rose from low values at 3400 BCE to a joint maximum in the 3200 BCE bin (Z = +0.91 and Z = +2.60) and fell back by 3000 BCE (Pearson r = +0.87, exact permutation p = 0.067, Spearman rho = +0.62, leave-one-out r 0.44-0.94). This peak was not accompanied by any increase in the elements of symbolic capital: the symbolic-capital composite (mean Z of HouseSize, Dagger and HatchetSwords) declined from +0.35 to -0.27, a movement carried almost entirely by house size (in-window variance share 1.00; SD 0.82; falling from Z = +2.05 to +0.19, i.e. dZ = -1.86), while daggers were exactly constant inside the window (SD = 0, so no association can be estimated) and hatchets & swords were essentially flat (SD = 0.005). native_result.HypoA: Amber has historically high and stable values in the 4th millenium BCE. with its all time peak around 3300 to 3000BCE.
native_result.HypoB: Amber reached its highest relative importance (used here as a proxy: standardised find-abundance Z values; the data contain no price/value field, so frequency is not literally value) in the 4th millennium BCE, 4000-3001 BCE (CE -4000..-3001 = 4951-5950 calBP): the mean of the interpolated amber Z series is +1.488 for that millennium versus -0.277 (3000-2001 BCE) and -0.556 (2000-1001 BCE), a 1.77 SD gap. Within it the curve forms two plateaux (Z=+1.46 over 4000-3401 BCE and the series maximum Z=+1.54 over 3300-2901 BCE), so amber peaked in the interval ~3400-3000 BCE, best stated as the century-bin core 3300-2901 BCE (5250-4851 calBP) inside a broader high stand of 4000-2901 BCE (5950-4851 calBP), with +/-100 y (one century-bin) uncertainty and no resolvable sub-century ordering. In period terms the maximum coincides with the Middle Neolithic (mean Z +1.524, all 5 bins in the peak) after an Early Neolithic rise at 4000 BCE and before a collapse from 2900 BCE (SG -0.223, LN -0.880). Relative to the Belau single-site openness proxy the amber maximum is much earlier (smoothed amber peak 3275-3175 BCE vs pollen maximum at the 704 BCE record edge) and the two series are negatively correlated at all lags (r(0) = -0.43), i.e. amber, as a form of social capital, is most prominent while land-use/openness was still low.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Audit script verified alignment (CE = -BCE; calBP = 1950 - CE exact in both yearly files; no duplicate years or gaps; Amber == Zamber on 37 anchors, Amber_inter == linear interpolation, max dev 2e-16; 100-y binned anchors on a yearly grid). 2) Built century-bin table with period labels plus bin means of Amber_inter and 100/250/500 y centred rolling means. 3) Primary criterion R1: interval mean of Amber_inter per millennium (astronomical and data-anchored boundaries; blocks with <80% coverage excluded but reported) plus a sliding 1000-y window scan for boundary-phase robustness. 4) Peak interval by three determinations: M1 longest contiguous set of century bins >= threshold (mean+1SD, top decile, half-max), M2 highest-value anchor platform, M3 smoothed-peak neighbourhood (50/100/250/500 y), with continuous interpolated crossings shown as reference only. 5) Sensitivity over bin width 100-1200 y, three thresholds, four smoothing windows, 37 vs 39 bins, raw anchors vs interpolation. 6) Interpretive lead-lag/cross-correlation against ts.pollen_inter_100 (Belau single site; forward-fill artefact beyond CE -704 flagged; pollen_grate_100 excluded). All rules were fixed before execution and every statement carries +/-100 y plus the frequency-is-not-value caveat.

native_result.query: How does the prevalence of non-native plants introduced via gardening vary based on habitat type?
native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: Prevalence of non-native plants introduced through the Gardening pathway varies strongly with habitat type: it is highest in human-used lowland habitats — Wetlands (n.gard>0 in 50.0% of 38 plots, mean n.gard 0.76, n.gard/n.total = 29/52 = 0.56), Urban (47.7% of 65 plots, 0.69, 45/151 = 0.30), Coastal (44.8% of 29 plots, 0.79, 23/43 = 0.53) and Riparian (36.1% of 61 plots, 0.57, 35/96 = 0.36), which hold 78% of all 169 n.gard records on only 31% of the 632 plots — and it is much lower in Croplands (20.7% of plots, mean n.gard 0.22, share 20/108 = 0.19, where 83 of 108 records are Unintentional) and in Meadows (7.7%). Habitat types with almost no invasion records (Coniferous and Broad-leaved forests, Scrublands, Rock outcrops; 18 records over 308 plots) are gardening-rare per plot (occupancy 0-6.5%), so their high formal shares (0.875, 1.000) are small-sample artefacts and do not mean forests are dominated by garden plants. The habitat association is statistically robust (permutation test of habitat x pathway over 481 species-occurrence records: chi2 = 42.09, p = 0.00005; Kruskal-Wallis on n.gard per plot H = 139.6, p = 1.2e-27; quasi-binomial GLM n.gard/n.total ~ habitat weighted by n.total: F = 16.4, p = 3.1e-17; Croplands depleted, Fisher/Holm p = 0.00023; Wetlands and Coastal enriched, p = 0.009 and 0.046) and survives adjustment for urban.2009.1000m and elevation (habitat Wald F = 17.5, p = 2.5e-18), so gardening-introduced plants are concentrated in urban, coastal, wetland and riparian habitats where ornamental planting and garden escape occur, while agricultural habitats are dominated by unintentional introductions. This is a descriptive association, not a causal claim; it is unchanged when only the 191 plots with n.total > 0 are used (share ranking identical, mean n.gard Spearman rho = 0.886, p = 0.019).
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspection of all four files with explicit delimiters (invaded_niche_pathways.csv and temporal_trends_contingency_table.csv read with sep='\t', invasion_success_pathways.csv with sep=','); integrity assertions: n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo == n.total for 632/632 rows, 632 unique plot coordinates, no NA in habitat. 2) Primary unit = plot (632 plots, 481 species-occurrence records in n.total, 169 n.gard); habitat-level metrics computed as occupancy (fraction of plots with n.gard>0), intensity (mean n.gard per plot) and secondary share sum(n.gard)/sum(n.total) always with record counts; three rankings reported side by side. 3) Habitats with sum(n.total) < 10 records (Coniferous forests 8, Broad-leaved forests 4, Scrublands 5, Rock outcrops 1) pooled into 'Data-poor (<10 rec.)' so they are not separate test levels. 4) Tests: 20000-permutation test replacing the asymptotic chi-square (min expected count 0.35 in the 10-level table), per-group Fisher exact with Holm adjustment, Kruskal-Wallis on plot-level n.gard, quasi-binomial GLM (n.gard/n.total ~ C(habitat), freq_weights = n.total, scale='X2'), plus a robustness model adding urban.2009.1000m and elevation and a plot-level logistic occupancy model. 5) Sensitivity analysis restricted to the 191 plots with n.total > 0 with Spearman comparison of rankings. 6) Secondary species-level check on 77 unique species (42 vs 39 Gardening rows, 4 pathway-conflicting duplicates flagged) comparing habitat.range and number.of.invaded.plots by pathway. 7) Phylogenetic tree excluded; temporal table used only as context (no habitat column).
