native_result.query: In what context does the gardening pathway for introducing non-native plants show different prevalence styles across habitat types?
native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: The gardening pathway shows different prevalence styles according to the intensity and heterogeneity of the surrounding land use, not according to climate. In warm, low-elevation, humid coastal-plain habitats with a heterogeneous, only partly converted matrix (Wetlands and Coastal: ~182 m, 14.6 °C, 645 mm, 22-26% urban and 17-26% cropland cover at 500 m), gardening is the dominant style, supplying the majority of established non-native occurrences (0.56 [0.42-0.69] and 0.54 [0.39-0.68]) at the highest absolute intensity recorded (76-79 gardening occurrences per 100 plots). In habitats governed by a single intensive land use the gardening style is diluted by unintentional contaminant introductions: Croplands (62% cropland at 50 m) falls to 0.19 [0.12-0.27] with 77% unintentional, and the built-up Urban habitat to 0.30 [0.23-0.37] with 69% unintentional - although Urban still receives high absolute gardening propagule input (69 occurrences per 100 plots), so its low share is compositional dilution rather than absence of garden-origin species. Riparian constitutes a third style: intermediate gardening share (0.36 [0.27-0.46], not different from the pooled mean) plus a strong concentration of the AgriForest pathway (13 of 23 occurrences, standardised residual +3.93, MC p=0.0006), i.e. a legacy agro-silvopastoral signature along watercourses. Measured context acts as a modifier in the same direction at both scales - each SD more urban cover reduces the gardening odds by ~27% among habitats (p=0.005) and by ~26% within habitats (p=0.018), cropland cover similarly (p=0.002), and plots with both urban and cropland cover above 15% have a gardening share of 0.245 versus 0.448 where both are below - whereas elevation, rainfall, distance to roads/streams and post-1993 landscape change add nothing once habitat is accounted for. Because habitat labels still improve fit beyond all measured context (quasi-F=7.01, p=5e-06) while context adds only marginally beyond habitat (p=0.12), we hypothesise that the residual differences reflect proximity to the ornamental propagule source (gardens, nurseries, plantings) interacting with habitat, rather than abional conditions: gardening-derived invasion becomes the dominant style in thermally benign, low-lying, structurally open wet/coastal habitats embedded in a mixed low-intensity matrix, and a minority style wherever cropland or dense urban fabric concentrates contaminant propagule pressure. All shares are shares of plot occurrences (plot-level unit), and the apparent gardening excess of the pooled remote seminatural habitats is a denominator artifact (OR 5.34 under invaded-plot denominator vs 0.15 under all-plots denominator) rather than an ecological signal.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspection (analysis/01_inspection.py): shapes, categorical levels, missingness, duplicate flags; established that invaded_niche_pathways.csv is one row per plot (632 unique coordinates, 0 NAs), that n.total == n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo, and that habitat totals are plot-weighted species occurrences (481 occurrences) rather than species richness; confirmed no crosswalk between the plot file and the 81-species trait file. 2) Data setup (analysis/02_main_analysis.py): success=n.gard, trials=n.total (AgriForest folded into non-gardening); primary frame = 191 invaded plots; sensitivities = all-plots denominator (any plot hosting >=1 gardening species, 632 plots) and AgriForest dropped (n.gard vs n.unint, 396 occurrences); all 10 habitats kept descriptively, five habitats with <=13 occurrences pooled into 'Seminatural-pooled' for confirmatory inference; Clopper-Pearson intervals for shares. 3) Models: quasi-binomial GLM on grouped binomial endog (statsmodels GLM, scale='X2', t-tests) for habitat-only, unpooled 10-level, both sensitivities, context-only, context+habitat, within-habitat (habitat fixed effects), 3-group contrasts, leave-one-habitat-out and leave-one-5km-cell-out refits; home-likelihood beta-binomial MLE (scipy, numerical Hessian SEs) for habitat means, context model and nested comparisons. 4) Permutation inference: Monte-Carlo multinomial G-test (B=20000, fixed row totals and pooled column proportions) on 10x3, 6x3 and 6x2 tables with simulated standardised residuals and per-cell two-sided MC p-values against a Bonferroni threshold, plus a plot-level permutation test in which pathway counts are shuffled across plots (habitat occurrence totals not held fixed). 5) Context characterisation: per-habitat means of elevation, temperature, rainfall, urban and cropland cover at 50 m and 500 m, distance to road/stream, progressive-minus-regressive landscape change, with one variable retained per collinear pair; two-axis style table (composition share vs occurrences per 100 plots); urban and cropland binned shares and a 2x2 cover mosaic; quadratic-term tests for monotonicity. 6) Robustness flagging and exports (results_*.csv, FINDINGS.md). 7) Temporal contingency table used only as one-sentence framing (no habitat key); Наибольшее превосходство оригиналов — в социальной психологии: репликация сохраняет в медиане 18% эффекта (relative_es 0.184 [0.016;0.330]), mean|ro| 0.346 → mean|rr| 0.154, |ro|>|rr| в 88.2% случаев, воспроизведено 20.6%. Далее — когнитивная психология (relative_es 0.650 [0.302;0.769], 0.533 → 0.344, воспроизведено 47.1%), наименьшее превосходство — экспериментальная экономика (0.698 [0.437;0.926], 0.474 → 0.305, воспроизведено 61.1%). Различие проявляется в относительном, а не абсолютном сжатии: контрасты Social−Cognitive (−0.466 [−0.695;−0.123], p_boot=0.007) и Social−Economics (−0.514 [−0.789;−0.228], p_boot=0.006) различимы, Cognitive и Economics статистически между собой не различимы (p_boot=0.52), а все контрасты по шкале Фишера лежат в доверительных интервалах (p_boot 0.14–0.86); по абсолютному падению лидирует когнитивная психология (d_fisher −0.249 [−0.341;−0.207]). Это не объясняется исключительно регрессией к среднему или низкой мощностью: наклон fisr~fiso = 0.586 (p=0.020) подтверждает RTM во всех доменах, но в социальной психологии наименьшие исходные ro при наибольшем пропорциональном падении, а ранжирование сохраняется на подвыборке power_planned.r ≥ 0.8 (n=69; Social−Cognitive −0.472 [−0.732;−0.106], p_boot=0.012). Ограничения: домен смешан с журналом и годом публикации (психология 2008 г., экономика 2011–2014 гг.), экономика представлена 18 наблюдениями, поэтому атрибуция именно области исследования остаётся условной.

sub_hypo.text: Proportional effect shrinkage is greatest in social psychology, followed by cognitive psychology and experimental economics. Median relative_es is 0.184 [0.016, 0.330], 0.650 [0.302, 0.769], and 0.698 [0.437, 0.926], respectively.
sub_hypo.context: All 86 pairs grouped by discipline; relative_es for B Eitam was corrected from −0.472 to rr/ro = +0.472. Four sensitivity variants yielded Social medians of 0.184, 0.164, 0.131, and 0.184.

sub_hypo.text: Replication success is lowest in social psychology (20.6%), intermediate in cognitive psychology (47.1%), and highest in experimental economics (61.1%).

sub_hypo.relations: Replication success rates increase from Social to Cognitive to Economics; the workflow verified replicated = (pr ≤ 0.05 and rr > 0).

sub_hypo.text: Domain differences are statistically distinguishable for relative shrinkage, but not for Fisher-scale shrinkage. Social differs from both Cognitive and Economics, whereas Cognitive and Economics are not statistically distinguishable.

native_result.query: What is the proportion of junior professors in replicated studies in Psychology?
native_result.HypoA: In Psychology, replicated studies have a much higher proportion of junior professor (64.7%) and in the original studies the senior professors are more represented (82.4%)
native_result.HypoB: In the Psychology replication project (project = "rpp"), 40.0% of the replicated studies (36 of 90 usable replication attempts; 95% Wilson interval 30.5-50.3%) were led by a junior professor - their most senior author being an Assistant Professor (22) or an Assistant (14) - so junior faculty ran roughly two in five RPP replications; the share rises to 51.6% (16/31) among the studies that actually replicated and is 39.2% (38/97) without the drop filter, and because "junior professor" is not a label in the data it is bounded between 15.6% (Assistant only) and 66.7% (also counting Associate Professors). Seniority is coded only for the most senior author of each team, so this is the share of studies led by junior faculty rather than a share of individual authors, and the original-study side shows no junior professors at all in rpp (Professor 76, Associate Professor 9, Researcher 5 of 90), so the figure describes the people who ran the replications. Descriptively, replication teams were far less senior than the originals they tested (mean author citations 463 vs 2,957) and junior-led attempts replicated at 44.4% versus 27.8% for the rest - a pattern in 90 studies, not evidence of an effect of seniority on replication success.
native_result.WorkflowB: File A (927 rows, study x lab) filtered to project=='rpp' (97 rows, one per study id), deduplicated by id, aggregated==True excluded (none in rpp; ml1/ml3 lab rows would have to be collapsed first), drop==True excluded (7 rows) -> n=90 usable replication attempts, no missing seniority. Junior professor = seniority.r in {Assistant Professor, Assistant}: 36/90 = 40.0% (Wilson 30.5-50.3%, Clopper-Pearson 29.8-50.9%). Parallel denominators: replicated==1 (16/31 = 51.6%) and all 97 rows (38/97 = 39.2%). Sensitivity grid across 3 rank definitions x 2 seniority columns x 3 denominators; seniority distribution table for both columns; discipline split (Cognitive 19/42 = 45.2%, Social 17/48 = 35.4%); descriptive context on replication success by rank and citation/author-count contrasts; light cross-check of rpp outcomes against File B on 63 unambiguously matched ids (100% outcome agreement, corr(log10 p)=0.999), which does not alter the estimate. native_result.HypoB: In the sample of original papers underlying these replication projects — table 1 study_data (927 rows / 141 unique O/R pairs), where original-paper length is the field `length` (pages of the original paper) and the two categories are defined solely by `project` (`ee` = Experimental Economics, n=18, exactly matching discipline=='Economics'; `rpp` = Psychology, n=97; `journal` not used for screening) — Experimental Economics original papers average 28.0 pages, whereas Psychology (rpp) original papers average 11.22 pages, a difference of 16.78 pages or about 2.5x (bootstrap 95% CI for the difference 13.3-20.4 pages; for the ratio 2.12-2.95; Welch t=9.06, p=7.4e-09; Mann-Whitney U=1681.5, p=4.5e-10). Medians are 27.5 vs 9.0 pages (SD 7.37 vs 6.30; IQR 23.5-30.0 vs 7-16; range 16-45 vs 1-31, right-skewed on the psychology side). Overall, ever-incarcerated individuals had a median 1985 composite wealth of about $720 versus $3,600 for the never-jailed (difference -$2,880; bootstrap 95% CI [-3,600, -2,300]; 0.20x, i.e. roughly 80% lower; Mann-Whitney p=1.6e-10). native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Among black respondents (NLSY-79 processed file), incarceration (ever_jailed = 1, jailed 1985–1994) is associated with substantially lower wealth by 1996 at every economic-status level, where 'income levels' are proxied — as a stated assumption, since no income variable exists — by rank-based quartiles of baseline composite_wealth_1985. Within every baseline-wealth quartile, jailed black respondents gained far less wealth from 1985 to 1996 than non-jailed peers (mean jailed-minus-non-jailed gaps: −$19,003 in Q1, −$16,061 in Q2, −$41,742 in Q3, −$58,317 in Q4; pooled −$33,489), while at baseline the groups were nearly equal (gaps of roughly $0 to −$16,000). In absolute dollars the wealth penalty of incarceration is largest for high-baseline black respondents — the top-quartile jailed group's mean wealth actually fell (Δ = −$5,043) while non-jailed top-quartile peers gained +$53,274 (median DiD −$14,876) — whereas for low-baseline respondents the penalty manifests as floor-level stagnation: medians of composite_wealth_1996 are $0 for both groups (median DiD ≈ 0 due to ties at zero), yet jailed means remain only ~21–35% of non-jailed means and 57% of jailed respondents sit at exactly zero wealth in 1996 versus 33% of non-jailed. The jailed/non-jailed mean-wealth ratio falls from 0.34–0.86 in 1985 to 0.19–0.35 by 1996 in every quartile. Male-only results (n=143 jailed vs 1,322 non-jailed) show the same pattern with larger gaps (Q4 mean DiD −$76,192); the black jailed female cell (n=16, all wealth medians $0) is reported but too small for separate inference. A jail wealth penalty also appears for white respondents (mean Δ96 DiD −$92,678), so the direction is not black-specific; it is especially consequential for black respondents because jail incidence is far higher (159/3,013 ≈ 5.3%, vs 69/7,099 ≈ 1.0% for white). This is an observational association, not a causal effect: mechanical wealth suppression during 1985–1994 incarceration, baseline imbalance ($320 vs $764 median composite_wealth_1985), small jailed cells, absence of income/age/incarceration-timing fields, duplicate rows treated one-per-respondent, and ever_jailed being the only incarceration indicator (no residence field exists) all preclude a causal reading.

native_result.HypoA: The largest increases in median wealth from 1985 to 1990 were among black females, with a percentage increase of 1385.71%.

All three metrics (absolute dollars, percent growth, dollars per year) agree on 1985-1990, although the percentage metric is unstable because the 1985 base is near zero. The finding is NOT robust to how zero-valued composites are treated: in this subsample zeros are most frequent in 1985 (618/1,548 = 39.9%) versus 29.4% in 1990 and 31.7% in 1996, so excluding year-wise zeros yields medians of $3,832 / $8,100 / $19,800 and reverses the ranking to 1990-1996 (+$11,700 vs +$4,268); excluding respondents with a zero in any year (fixed sample, n = 675; medians $4,000 / $12,300 / $30,050) also gives 1990-1996 (+$17,750 vs +$8,300). Restricting to ever_jailed == 0 (n = 1,532; medians $200 / $2,888 / $4,000) reproduces the primary answer (1985-1990, +$2,688 vs +$1,112), while ever_jailed == 1 (n = 16) has medians of $0 in all three years and is uninformative. native_result.HypoB: Between 1990 and 1996 wealth inequality increased for both white males and white females, driven by upper-tail expansion rather than top concentration: for both groups the mean rose (+49.5% and +29.3%) while SD, IQR, P90-P50, P75/P90/P99 levels, the P90/P50 ratio (from ~12-14 to ~37) and the zero-truncated Gini (+1.3-1.6 pp) rose concordantly, alongside a 16-19 percentage-point growth in the share at or below zero wealth. The rise is not visible at the median (whose apparent fall is a duplication artefact), the top-1% share of positive wealth declined slightly, and among positive-wealth holders the distribution flattened; the change is best described as a hollowing-out of the bottom combined with strong nominal gains at the 75th percentile and above.

native_result.query: In which years were individuals with a criminal record found to have significantly lower wealth compared to those without?
native_result.HypoA: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
native_result.HypoB: In all three observed years - 1985, 1990 and 1996 - respondents with a criminal record (ever_jailed = 1, jailed between 1985 and 1994; n = 289) held significantly lower composite wealth than those never jailed (n = 11,724), and the gap widened over time. In 1985 mean wealth was $7,929 vs $25,086 (difference -$17,157; 95% CI -20,603 to -13,711; bootstrap -20,364 to -13,621; one-sided Welch p = 3.2e-21, Holm-adjusted 9.5e-21; Mann-Whitney p = 8.0e-11; Cliff's delta = -0.22; medians $720 vs $3,600); in 1990 $16,350 vs $73,948 (-$57,598; CI -69,428 to -45,768; p = 7.8e-20, Holm 7.8e-20; MWU 3.9e-35; delta = -0.42; medians $0 vs $10,500); in 1996 $20,383 vs $105,447 (-$85,063; CI -102,274 to -67,853; p = 3.6e-20, Holm 7.3e-20; MWU 4.6e-26; delta = -0.35; medians $0 vs $8,500). The pattern survives adjustment for sex and race (asinh-wealth beta = -0.49, -1.45, -1.63; all p <= 1.7e-06), median regression (-$1,100, -$3,800, -$6,000), permutation tests, and every sensitivity variant (zeros treated as missing, wealth>0 only, deduplicated rows, winsorized, trimmed means); the wealth ratio fell from 0.32 to 0.22 to 0.19, and both the share with wealth <= 0 (45/57/63% vs 32/29/40%) and mean wealth among positive-wealth respondents (difference -$22k, -$67k, -$121k) contributed. The association is descriptive, not causal: the exposure window is 1985-1994, so the 1985 difference reflects a pre-existing wealth gap / selection into incarceration rather than a consequence of it, and the unweighted data (1,899 exact duplicate rows; wealth zeros that may include survey nonresponse) are not representative of the U.S. population.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) QC of data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 x 6, no missing values, race label 'hipanic' kept, ever_jailed 289 vs 11,724, 1,899 exact duplicate rows noted). 2) Main sample = full file; exposure = ever_jailed only, no derived features. 3) Primary per-year contrasts on raw dollars (1985, 1990, 1996): one-sided Welch t-test (H1: jailed < never) and one-sided Mann-Whitney U, with Holm correction across the 3 years within each test family at alpha = 0.05; two-sided p-values and 95% t CIs reported alongside; 10,000-replicate percentile bootstrap CIs for differences in means and medians; 10,000-swap permutation test as a distribution-free check. 4) Effect sizes: Cliff's delta on raw wealth, Hedges g on asinh(wealth/1000). 5) Confirmatory regressions: OLS asinh(wealth/1000) ~ ever_jailed + C(sex) + C(race) with HC3 SEs (unadjusted coefficient shown in the same table) and median (quantile) regression with the same covariates. 6) Decision rule: a year counts as robust if direction agrees in all analyses (mean difference, median difference, adjusted asinh beta, median-regression beta, Cliff's delta) AND Holm-adjusted p < 0.05 in both primary families. 7) Decomposition of the gap into the extensive margin (share with wealth <= 0; chi-square and logistic regression adjusted for sex+race) and the intensive margin E[wealth | wealth > 0] with bootstrap CI, showing the finding is not produced by zero-filled attrition. 8) Sensitivity: A main (zeros+duplicates kept), B zeros as missing, C wealth>0 only, D exact duplicate rows dropped, E winsorized at 1st/99th percentile, plus Yuen-Welch 10%-trimmed means. 9) Exploratory sex x race appendix with cell sizes (n_jailed 9-16 in female cells) flagged as low power and excluded from the answer wording. 10) Outputs: results_table_primary.csv, results_table_sensitivity.csv, results_table_appendix_sexrace.csv, results_summary.md.

sub_hypo.context: Participants in the National Longitudinal Study of Youth's 1979 cohort, with wealth measured in 1985, 1990, and 1996.
sub_hypo.relations: Individuals with a criminal record, operationalized as having been jailed between 1985 and 1994 (ever_jailed = 1), have significantly lower composite wealth in each of 1985, 1990, and 1996 than those without (ever_jailed = 0).

sub_hypo.context: Full unweighted National Longitudinal Study of Youth 1979 cohort dataset: 12,013 rows, including 289 ever-jailed and 11,724 never-jailed respondents. Observed wealth years are 1985, 1990, and 1996. The main analysis retains zeros and 1,899 exact duplicate rows; zeros may include survey nonresponse. Findings are descriptive, not causal or representative of the U.S. population. The 1985 gap reflects pre-existing differences or selection into incarceration, not a consequence of incarceration during the 1985–1994 exposure window.
sub_hypo.relations: Ever-jailed versus never-jailed mean wealth was $7,929 versus $25,086 in 1985, $16,350 versus $73,948 in 1990, and $20,383 versus $105,447 in 1996; reported differences were -$17,157, -$57,598, and -$85,063. Wealth ratios declined from 0.32 to 0.22 to 0.19. Medians were $720 versus $3,600, $0 versus $10,500, and $0 versus $8,500. Both one-sided Welch and Mann–Whitney tests were significant after Holm correction across years at alpha = 0.05, with Cliff's delta of -0.22, -0.42, and -0.35.

sub_hypo.text: The negative association between incarceration status and wealth in all three years persists after adjustment for sex and race and across distribution-free checks and sensitivity analyses.
sub_hypo.context: Same NLSY 1979 cohort sample and 1985, 1990, and 1996 wealth observations. Adjusted analyses use sex and race as covariates. Sensitivity analyses treat zeros as missing, restrict wealth to positive values, remove exact duplicate rows, winsorize at the 1st and 99th percentiles, or use 10%-trimmed means. Associations remain descriptive rather than causal.
sub_hypo.relations: Sex- and race-adjusted OLS coefficients for ever_jailed on asinh(wealth/1000) were -0.49, -1.45, and -1.63 in chronological order, all with p <= 1.7e-06. Adjusted median-regression coefficients were -$1,100, -$3,800, and -$6,000. Negative directions agree across mean and median differences, adjusted regressions, and Cliff's delta; permutation tests and every specified sensitivity variant support the pattern.

sub_hypo.text: Both a higher share of respondents with nonpositive wealth and lower mean wealth among positive-wealth respondents contribute to the wealth disadvantage of ever-jailed respondents.
sub_hypo.context: Same NLSY 1979 cohort dataset, comparing ever-jailed and never-jailed respondents in 1985, 1990, and 1996. The extensive margin uses wealth <= 0; the intensive margin restricts each year's comparison to wealth > 0. Extensive-margin analyses include logistic regression adjusted for sex and race.
sub_hypo.relations: Shares with wealth <= 0 were 45%, 57%, and 63% among ever-jailed respondents versus 32%, 29%, and 40% among never-jailed respondents in 1985, 1990, and 1996. Among respondents with positive wealth, ever-jailed minus never-jailed mean differences were approximately -$22,000, -$67,000, and -$121,000. native_result.query: Is the relation between socioeconomic status and chances of degree completion affected by racial lines of the individual?
native_result.HypoA: The strength and significance of the relationship between socioeconomic status (SES) and BA degree completion differ across racial groups. For Whites, SES has a positive coefficient of 0.2169 (p = 0.031). For Blacks SES has a larger positive coefficient of 0.9775 (p < 0.001). For Hispanics, SES has a positive coefficient of 0.6724 (p = 0.013).
native_result.HypoB: Among NLS respondents, socioeconomic status is positively associated with the chance of completing a BA degree, but this socioeconomic gradient is not modified by the race of the individual once ability, sex and family size are held constant. Each additional standard deviation of SES raises the odds of degree completion by about 1.23 (95% CI 1.05-1.45, p = 0.013), and the SES slope is statistically indistinguishable across Hispanic, Black and White respondents (LRT for the SES-by-race interaction chi2(2) = 1.33, p = 0.513; Wald p = 0.503; AIC worsens by 2.67; parametric-bootstrap p = 0.514; Firth-penalised Wald p = 0.478; race-specific odds ratios per SD of SES: White 1.19, 95% CI 0.99-1.43; Black 1.50, 1.04-2.17; Hispanic 1.19, 0.75-1.88). Race instead acts chiefly as a difference in level rather than a difference in slope: Black and Hispanic respondents complete degrees far less often than White respondents (1.32% and 1.44% vs 3.54%), and race keeps an independent association with completion after adjustment (joint LRT chi2(2) = 6.10, p = 0.047) whose direction reverses once ability, sex and family size are held constant (Black OR 1.86, 1.20-2.89; Hispanic OR 1.34, 0.81-2.23). A proportional gradient therefore coexists with a persistent absolute gap: moving from one SD below to one SD above mean SES raises the modelled probability of a degree by 1.45-fold in every group, yet a high-SES Black or Hispanic respondent (about 1.6-1.8%) remains below a low-SES White respondent (2.75%). An SES-by-race interaction is visible in the unadjusted data (crude LRT p = 0.008) but it does not survive adjustment and is largely compositional, since SES tracks ability and family size differently within the minority groups than within the White group; it is reported descriptively and not claimed as effect modification. The Hispanic-by-SES term is imprecisely estimated on 19 degrees among 1,323 respondents and is underpowered (differences below about 0.60 log-odds per SD are undetectable at 80% power), so it is characterised as uninformative rather than as evidence of equality. The same conclusion holds in the companion percentile-adjusted (partially direct) estimand (interaction p = 0.418), so the finding does not depend on the mediator adjustment. These are associations under an assumed simple-random-sampling design in a complete-case subset of the cohort with no weights, strata or curriculum measure, and no causal claim is made.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspection of data/nls_ses_processed.csv (8,773 records x 8 variables, unique CASE ID, no missing values or sentinel codes, no curriculum variable present). 2) Logistic regression of BA DEGREE COMPLETED on standardised SES with a three-level race factor (White reference) and heteroskedasticity-robust HC1 standard errors, on all 8,773 complete cases (236 events). 3) Two estimands kept strictly separate: TOTAL effect (ability, sex, family size) as headline and PARTIALLY DIRECT effect (additionally adjusting for PERCENTILE IN CLASS, a plausible mediator), each as a nested pair of main-effects vs SES-by-race interaction models. 4) Pre-specified primary criterion: likelihood-ratio test of the 2 interaction terms, cross-checked with a joint Wald test, delta-AIC, race-specific slopes with confidence intervals (linear combinations), and g-computed marginal probabilities at SES = -1/0/+1 SD standardised within each racial group. 5) Robustness: Firth penalised likelihood (with the penalised LR reported but not chi2-calibrated), a B=800 parametric bootstrap of the interaction LRT under the main-effects null, categorical-quartile and quadratic SES specifications, re-levelling with Black as reference, a fully race-specific model, stratified fits, a pooled-minority sensitivity, a one-cell influence check and an explicit minimum-detectable-effect calculation. 6) All steps executed in analysis/01..04 python scripts with logged output and CSV result tables; written hypothesis in analysis/HYPOTHESIS.md.

In the transparent race-only logit the Black-vs-White log-odds ratio is -1.0057 (OR 0.366, 95% CI 0.245-0.546, p = 8.4e-07) and the Hispanic-vs-White one is -0.9241 (OR 0.397, 95% CI 0.247-0.639, p = 1.4e-04), with crude BA completion shares of 1.33% (Black), 1.44% (Hispanic) and 3.54% (White); the Black-White pair is the answer under every specification checked (crude, race+SES, race*SES contrasts at SES quartiles and ATC, Firth/ridge refits), and among 252 race terms scanned across 42 formulas and 3 reference categories only the Black-vs-White term in the race x SES model rounds to -0.9568, so the Hispanic-White reading is rejected.

native_result.HypoB: Requirements work in ML-enabled systems is perceived as being carried mainly by the Project Lead / Project Manager and the Data Scientist: among the 194 respondents who completed the role block, 51.031% (95% bootstrap CI 43.814-58.247; BCa 43.299-57.217) reported that ML/requirements aspects are addressed by the Project Lead / Project Manager and 48.969% (95% CI 42.268-56.186; BCa 41.753-55.670) by the Data Scientist, versus at most 25.773% for any other role (Requirements Engineer 10.309%, Tester 1.031%). This pair is the top-2 in 9 of 9 pre-registered specifications and in 100% of 10,000 respondent-level bootstrap replicates, although the two leaders are statistically indistinguishable from each other (difference 2.06 pp, 95% CI -7.73 to +11.86). The numbers 61.389% and 49.6% quoted in the question are not reproduced: the second is close to the reproduced Data Scientist share (48.97%, delta 0.63 pp) while the first exceeds every legitimate estimate for the Project Lead (max 56.1%), and the quoted 95% CIs (half-widths 0.381/0.434 pp, implying an effective sample of ~66,000/48,000 units) are 15.8-18.5 times narrower than any statistically valid respondent-level bootstrap of these 194 respondents (SE ~3.6 pp, CI +/-7.1 pp) - they are consistent only with resampling a much smaller unit (e.g. the flattened 276x202 = 55,752-cell table, SE 0.212 pp) or with a scaling error. These shares describe respondents' perceived organizational division of labour on ML/requirements aspects (survey self-reports, non-random dropout of 82 suspended questionnaires), not a measured or causal contribution of the roles; conditional role->requirements probabilities are uninformative for Requirements Engineer and Tester (n=2 each), so the superficially similar (Project Lead 62.5%, Business Analyst 50.0%) pair based on n=32 and n=10 (interval widths 34 and 60 pp) is only an illustration of fragility.

sub_hypo.text: BDD scenarios and ML Canvas are respectively the least-used and second least-used requirements documentation formats in ML-enabled system projects. The stated reference shares are 4.366% (95% CI [4.231, 4.501]) and 10.13% (95% CI [9.926, 10.333]). Among 194 valid respondents, 4 (2.06%) reported using BDD scenarios and 15 (7.73%) reported using ML Canvas. Both usage shares are significantly below all other documentation formats, while notebooks and user stories are used by roughly a third of respondents.

Notebooks and user stories each have roughly one-third respondent usage. The stated reference percentages are distinct from the observed shares using the 194-respondent denominator.

native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB:
口径声明（与结论不可分离）：本数据的核心解释变量实为 Adjusted savings: education expenditure (% of GNI)（NY.ADJ.AEDU.GN.ZS），并非文档所述的政府教育支出占财政总支出比重；被解释变量实为 GNI per capita, constant 2015 US$（NY.GNP.PCAP.KD），既非 GDP 亦非 2010 年基期；"developing countries" 以 Lower middle income (LMC) 组为代理，结论不外推至全部发展中国家；面板为分组聚合层面（仅 SSA 与 LMC 两个单位、T=41），不支持国家固定效应，标准误一律 Newey-West HAC(4) 且无聚类稳健选项；缺失值按 complete-case 处理，未插补、未外推。

结论：在 1975–2015 这两个分组聚合序列上，本数据没有为"某一组增加教育支出对人均收入的效应更强"提供统计支持；两组可识别的关联在经济量级上都很小，其符号与显著性取决于是否扣除共同趋势以及使用哪个窗口与控制变量集合。就唯一可直接估计的 LMC 而言，教育支出与人均收入增长之间的总（条件）关联在一阶差分（增长率）口径下为小幅正：教育储蓄率（占 GNI）每变动 1 个百分点，人均 GNI 年增长率相应高约 2.2 个百分点（+0.0219，HAC se 0.0104，p=0.035，n=40；加入小学与中学毛入学率控制后 +0.0266，se 0.0111，p=0.017，n=40）；长期水平形式为负（含时间趋势 −0.2002，se 0.0658，p=0.002，n=41；含入学率控制 −0.1205，p=0.040），但 ADF 显示人均 GNI 含单位根而教育支出平稳、Engle-Granger 协整不成立（1975–2015 p=0.285；1991–2015 p=0.533），长期方程 DW=0.20 且误差修正项系数为正（+0.0568），说明水平负号是共同趋势造成的伪相关，故主结论取差分口径。

必须区分两个口径，不可互相替代：+0.0219/+0.0266 是教育支出与人均 GNI 增长之间的总（条件）关联；移植法得到的 LMC −0.00229（bootstrap 95% CI [−0.02273, +0.01311]）只是总关联中经由小学与中学毛入学率的那部分（partial/indirect）关联——它之所以为负，是因为差分口径下 LMC 的渠道斜率本身为负（小学 −0.781、中学 −0.786）而第二阶段"入学率→收入"系数为正（prim 0.00757、sec 0.02899）。按同一度量比较，该渠道部分仅相当于总关联的约 −10.5%，即入学率渠道只承载总关联中极小且反向的一块，两者口径不同、符号相反完全可解释，绝不意味着"LMC 的效应为负"。

对 Sub-Saharan Africa，其自身收入方程不可估计：人均 GNI 仅有 2011–2015 共 5 个观测，主设定（教育支出＋劳动力参与率＋小学/中学毛入学率＋出口年增长）参数 k=6、剩余自由度 −1；即便只保留入学率控制，被解释变量仍只有 5 年（n=5 的拟合 −0.1000 仅作展示）。经渠道回归（教育支出→小学/中学毛入学率，两组 1975–2015 全覆盖）并移植 LMC 的"入学率→收入"系数，得到 SSA 隐含（间接、非因果）的部分关联 −0.00052（配对移动分块 bootstrap se 0.00390，95% CI [−0.00952, +0.00513]）。组间比较须同时看两个层面：一是渠道斜率的 SSA×edu 交互（水平+趋势口径小学 −3.329，se 1.736，p=0.055；一阶差分口径 +1.030，se 0.649，p=0.112；符号相反，属设定依赖；中学交互两口径均不显著，p=0.635 与 p=0.147），二是合成效应的组间差（差分口径 +0.00178，se 0.00943，95% CI [−0.01555, +0.02260]；水平+趋势口径 −0.00182，95% CI [−0.09978, +0.14131]）。两个层面的显著性与置信区间都没有给出稳定的组间差异，故"无统计支持的组间差异"这一结论对设定与口径均稳健；差分口径下 SSA 的隐含部分关联比 LMC 更接近零（即略偏大）只是点估计层面的倾向，不得单独强调。辅助性反事实（仅用 SSA 可得的入学率与时间趋势，剔除 SSA 缺失的劳动力与出口）显示，把 LMC 的入学率—收入对应关系套到 SSA 回归元上，2011–2015 预测人均 926–1024 美元，明显低于实际 1555–1634 美元（实际/预测均值 1.639），说明两组人均收入水平差距主要由该对应关系之外的水平项承载，而非教育支出或入学率差异（SSA 教育储蓄率均值 4.30% 高于 LMC 的 3.50%，但 2015 年人均 GNI 1634 美元低于 LMC 的 1965 美元）。

最后如实标注稳健性边界：LMC 显著为正的总关联只出现在 1976–2015 长窗口、控制变量较少或无控制的差分设定中；在作为组间比较主窗口的 1991–2015 且含全部控制变量（劳动力参与率、小学与中学毛入学率、出口年增长）时，短期差分系数为 −0.0271（p=0.589，n=24）、水平为 −0.1536（p=0.171，n=25），均不显著，因此 +0.022 的 p<0.05 并不像其字面那样稳健。鉴于反向因果占优（LMC 水平口径中收入 Granger 引起教育支出，lag1 F=14.59，p=0.0005，而教育→收入不显著 p=0.231；差分口径两者均不显著）且无外部工具变量，以上全部数字应理解为目的性关联与弹性，而非"教育支出导致/提升人均收入"的因果论断。

口径声明（与结论不可分离）：本数据的核心解释变量实为 Adjusted savings: education expenditure (% of GNI)（NY.ADJ.AEDU.GN.ZS），并非文档所述的政府教育支出占财政总支出比重；被解释变量实为 GNI per capita, constant 2015 US$（NY.GNP.PCAP.KD），既非 GDP 亦非 2010 年基期；"developing countries" 以 Lower middle income (LMC) 组为代理，结论不外推至全部发展中国家；面板为分组聚合层面（仅 SSA 与 LMC 两个单位、T=41），不支持国家固定效应，标准误一律 Newey-West HAC(4) 且无聚类稳健选项；缺失值按 complete-case 处理，未插补、未外推。

结论：在 1975–2015 这两个分组聚合序列上，本数据没有为"某一组增加教育支出对人均收入的效应更强"提供统计支持；两组可识别的关联在经济量级上都很小，其符号与显著性取决于是否扣除共同趋势以及使用哪个窗口与控制变量集合。就唯一可直接估计的 LMC 而言，教育支出与人均收入增长之间的总（条件）关联在一阶差分（增长率）口径下为小幅正：教育储蓄率（占 GNI）每变动 1 个百分点，人均 GNI 年增长率相应高约 2.2 个百分点（+0.0219，HAC se 0.0104，p=0.035，n=40；加入小学与中学毛入学率控制后 +0.0266，se 0.0111，p=0.017，n=40）；长期水平形式为负（含时间趋势 −0.2002，se 0.0658，p=0.002，n=41；含入学率控制 −0.1205，p=0.040），但 ADF 显示人均 GNI 含单位根而教育支出平稳、Engle-Granger 协整不成立（1975–2015 p=0.285；1991–2015 p=0.533），长期方程 DW=0.20 且误差修正项系数为正（+0.0568），说明水平负号是共同趋势造成的伪相关，故主结论取差分口径。

必须区分两个口径，不可互相替代：+0.0219/+0.0266 是教育支出与人均 GNI 增长之间的总（条件）关联；移植法得到的 LMC −0.00229（bootstrap 95% CI [−0.02273, +0.01311]）只是总关联中经由小学与中学毛入学率的那部分（partial/indirect）关联——它之所以为负，是因为差分口径下 LMC 的渠道斜率本身为负（小学 −0.781、中学 −0.786）而第二阶段"入学率→收入"系数为正（prim 0.00757、sec 0.02899）。按同一度量比较，该渠道部分仅相当于总关联的约 −10.5%，即入学率渠道只承载总关联中极小且反向的一块，两者口径不同、符号相反完全可解释，绝不意味着"LMC 的效应为负"。

对 Sub-Saharan Africa，其自身收入方程不可估计：人均 GNI 仅有 2011–2015 共 5 个观测，主设定（教育支出＋劳动力参与率＋小学/中学毛入学率＋出口年增长）参数 k=6、剩余自由度 −1；即便只保留入学率控制，被解释变量仍只有 5 年（n=5 的拟合 −0.1000 仅作展示）。经渠道回归（教育支出→小学/中学毛入学率，两组 1975–2015 全覆盖）并移植 LMC 的"入学率→收入"系数，得到 SSA 隐含（间接、非因果）的部分关联 −0.00052（配对移动分块 bootstrap se 0.00390，95% CI [−0.00952, +0.00513]）。组间比较须同时看两个层面：一是渠道斜率的 SSA×edu 交互（水平+趋势口径小学 −3.329，se 1.736，p=0.055；一阶差分口径 +1.030，se 0.649，p=0.112；符号相反，属设定依赖；中学交互两口径均不显著，p=0.635 与 p=0.147），二是合成效应的组间差（差分口径 +0.00178，se 0.00943，95% CI [−0.01555, +0.02260]；水平+趋势口径 −0.00182，95% CI [−0.09978, +0.14131]）。两个层面的显著性与置信区间都没有给出稳定的组间差异，故"无统计支持的组间差异"这一结论对设定与口径均稳健；差分口径下 SSA 的隐含部分关联比 LMC 更接近零（即略偏大）只是点估计层面的倾向，不得单独强调。辅助性反事实（仅用 SSA 可得的入学率与时间趋势，剔除 SSA 缺失的劳动力与出口）显示，把 LMC 的入学率—收入对应关系套到 SSA 回归元上，2011–2015 预测人均 926–1024 美元，明显低于实际 1555–1634 美元（实际/预测均值 1.639），说明两组人均收入水平差距主要由该对应关系之外的水平项承载，而非教育支出或入学率差异（SSA 教育储蓄率均值 4.30% 高于 LMC 的 3.50%，但 2015 年人均 GNI 1634 美元低于 LMC 的 1965 美元）。

最后如实标注稳健性边界：LMC 显著为正的总关联只出现在 1976–2015 长窗口、控制变量较少或无控制的差分设定中；在作为组间比较主窗口的 1991–2015 且含全部控制变量（劳动力参与率、小学与中学毛入学率、出口年增长）时，短期差分系数为 −0.0271（p=0.589，n=24）、水平为 −0.1536（p=0.171，n=25），均不显著，因此 +0.022 的 p<0.05 并不像其字面那样稳健。鉴于反向因果占优（LMC 水平口径中收入 Granger 引起教育支出，lag1 F=14.59，p=0.0005，而教育→收入不显著 p=0.231；差分口径两者均不显著）且无外部工具变量，以上全部数字应理解为目的性关联与弹性，而非"教育支出导致/提升人均收入"的因果论断。

native_result.query: In which century did the Diversity in Pottery Form collapses and Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases simultaneuosly?
native_result.HypoA: Around 1800 BCE, Diversity in Pottery Form collapses, while Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases.
native_result.HypoB: In the 17th century BCE (the 100-year bin 1700-1600 BCE, calBP ~3650-3551; step registered between the 1800 BCE and 1700 BCE bins) pottery FORM diversity collapsed while pottery DECORATION diversity increased simultaneously: form Z fell from +0.74 to -1.13 (delta = -1.87, -3.3 SD of ordinary century-to-century change) while decoration Z rose from -0.48 to +0.97 (delta = +1.45, +3.4 SD). This is the only bin in the 4100-500 BCE record with opposite-signed large changes, it is unique at every threshold (0.75/1.0/1.5/2.0) and under MAD-z, rank-based and percentile-break variants, and it is visible identically on the interpolated annual series (form crossing its mean 1765 BCE, decoration 1759 BCE). Form thereafter stays pinned at its floor value (-1.13, the only distinct value in the remaining 13 bins, so the sustained low level is confirmed but its magnitude may be a Z-transform floor), while decoration remains above its mean and rises again at 1000 BCE. Because the two diversity components normally co-vary positively (r = +0.361 across the 36 transitions), this decoupling indicates a reorganisation of ceramic cultural capital - a shift of variability-generating investment from vessel form to surface treatment - rather than an overall decline in cultural capital. The finding is descriptive and correlational: it identifies timing and direction only. The contemporaneous pollen openness proxy (Belau_PC1 / pollen_inter_100) shows elevated but directionless values with a NEGATIVE growth rate at 1700 BCE, so it does not line up with the pottery transition and provides no support for a demographic or landscape-opening explanation.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded the three staged files (time_series_data.csv 3601x36 annual grid CE -4100..-500; capital.csv 39x15 100-yr grid, decimal=','; pollen file 4084 rows, reverse-ordered, decimal=','). 2) Confirmed 100-year binning in the data: raw pottery columns populated at exactly 37 dates spaced 100 yr apart, *_inter 0 missing and linearly interpolated between them; cross-validated raw values against capital.csv ZKeform/Zkeverz (max abs diff 0.0). 3) Built the primary 37-point binned series for 4100-500 BCE. 4) Computed 100-yr differences, standardised them by sd(Delta) per series, and applied the approved primary criterion (|Delta z| >= 1 + level vs series mean + persistence over >= 3 bins) to both series; simultaneity required at the same bin. 5) Printed the complete 36-row transition table (levels, deltas, z, contrast, percentiles) and the opposite-signed subset. 6) Swept thresholds 0.75/1.0/1.5/2.0 with and without level/persistence conditions. 7) Ran variants: contrast score, percentile breaks (P10/P75 strict plus three tie-robust forms, with a tie diagnostic), 2-bin and 3-bin smoothing, median-based levels, robust MAD-z of changes, rank-of-changes, window trimmed to 4000-500 BCE, and addition of capital's 4300/4200 BCE bins. 8) Reported distinct post-1700 BCE form values to test whether the plateau is real or a transform floor. 9) Resolution-invariance check on the derived *_inter annual series (50-yr changes, max-contrast year, mean-crossing years) reported as confirmatory only. 10) Converted the winning bin to a century with explicit BCE span, calBP, and the bin-label caveat. 11) Merged pollen openness on CE (reverse-ordered file) and reported level, trend, growth-rate sign and contextual correlations for 2000-1500 BCE, concluding non-contemporaneity in direction. 12) Wrote results.txt and a tidy per-bin CSV; ASCII charts used because matplotlib is unavailable.

native_result.HypoB: Between 3400 and 3000 BCE monuments and axes increase together while elements of symbolic capital do not: MonumentCount rises +0.10 Z (-0.47 -> -0.36, peaking at +0.91 in 3200 BCE) and AxesCelts +0.43 Z (+0.37 -> +0.80, peaking at +2.60 in 3200 BCE), the two tracking each other (descriptive r = 0.87), whereas Hatchets&Swords stay pinned at the floor of their record (~-0.43 Z, dZ 0.00), Daggers are constant at their record minimum (-0.58 Z, zero variance) and House Size falls steeply (dZ -1.86, ~-0.46 Z/century) from the highest value in the whole dataset (2.05 Z) to near average. native_result.query: How does the prevalence of non-native plants introduced via gardening vary based on habitat type?
native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: Prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants varies strongly and systematically by habitat type in the Barcelona province plot network (632 plots): it is highest in low-elevation, human-subsidised and hydric habitats - Wetlands (50.0% of plots, 95% CI 34.8-65.2) and Urban (47.7%, 36.0-59.6), then Coastal (44.8%) and Riparian (36.1%) - intermediate in Croplands (20.7%), and lowest in upland semi-natural habitats, Coniferous forests (6.5%), Broad-leaved forests (4.4%) and Meadows (7.7%), with Scrublands (1.9%) and Rock outcrops (0%) too sparsely colonised to support a rate. The four lowland-disturbed habitats hold 44.0% garden-occupied plots (85/193) versus 6.0% (11/184) in the forest/meadow set - risk difference 38.1 percentage points (30.3-45.9), risk ratio 7.4x, odds ratio 12.4 (6.3-24.2), Fisher p = 9e-19 - and habitat x pathway heterogeneity in plot occupancy is significant beyond chance (chi2 = 139.4, df = 9, Monte-Carlo p <= 0.0001 with 10,000 permutations, seed 20261023; unchanged in direction under the >=20-record restriction, p = 0.002, and under effort rarefaction to 29 plots/habitat, rank rho = 1.00). Because the gardening pathway supplies ~75% of regional introductions in the most recent period (397 of 528 species; 18 -> 54 -> 142 -> 397 across periods) while gardening species occupy fewer habitat types (mean habitat.range 1.95) than unintentional ones (2.77), we hypothesise the habitat gradient is propagule-pressure and disturbance mediated - largely expressed through elevation (occupancy 37.3% in the lowest elevation quartile vs 3.2% in the highest; rho = -0.37) and urban cover within 1 km (rho = +0.38) - but with habitat retaining an independent effect after elevation adjustment (Wetlands/Urban/Coastal/Riparian 8-10x odds vs broad-leaved forest, all p <= 0.004). Prediction: garden-origin species will keep accumulating in urban, wetland, coastal and riparian plots while upland forest, meadow, scrub and rock habitats stay comparatively free of garden introductions.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Confirmed primary source: invaded_niche_pathways.csv (632 plots x 37 cols; row = plot with 632 unique coordinate pairs; n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo = n.total in 632/632 rows); habitat identity is absent from invasion_success_pathways.csv (habitat.range is a count), so per-habitat species lists are not recoverable and were not approximated. 2) PRIMARY prevalence = fraction of all sampled plots per habitat with n.gard >= 1, with Wilson 95% CIs. 3) SECONDARY, reported separately and never blended: occurrence-conditioned share sum(n.gard)/sum(n.total) per habitat, plus occupancy restricted to colonised plots; rank agreement between views quantified (Spearman rho = 0.08). 4) FORMAL TEST: 2 x 10 plot-level Gardening-occupied vs not table, primary p from 10,000-permutation Monte-Carlo chi-square (labels permuted across plots, seed 20261023), asymptotic chi-square reported alongside, plot-level standardised residuals for the gardening column. 5) ROBUSTNESS: restriction to habitats with >=20 occurrence records; exclusion of uninformative habitats (<=5 records); both compared for direction agreement. 6) DESCRIPTIVE ONLY: 10 x 3 occurrence standardised residuals, labelled non-inferential because species recur across plots. 7) SENSITIVITY: effort rarefaction to the smallest habitat sample (29 plots, 5,000 draws) and elevation checks (quartile occupancy, Spearman, and a small logistic comparison of habitat vs habitat+elevation LRTs, dropping perfectly separated habitats) - no full GLM. 8) CONTEXT (region-wide, not from the plots): pathway species counts and mean habitat.range from invasion_success_pathways.csv (4 duplicated=TRUE dual-pathway rows retained), and the temporal rise of the gardening pathway. 9) phylogenetic_tree.txt deliberately out of scope. 10) Validation: Wilson CIs recomputed with statsmodels, chi2 recomputed against scipy, permutation p reproduced on a second RNG stream (20,000 permutations), occupancy counts recomputed by an independent groupby.

The four lowland-disturbed habitats hold 44.0% garden-occupied plots (85/193) versus 6.0% (11/184) in the forest/meadow set - risk difference 38.1 percentage points (30.3-45.9), risk ratio 7.4x, odds ratio 12.4 (6.3-24.2), Fisher p = 9e-19 - and habitat x pathway heterogeneity in plot occupancy is significant beyond chance (chi2 = 139.4, df = 9, Monte-Carlo p <= 0.0001 with 10,000 permutations, seed 20261023; unchanged in direction under the >=20-record restriction, p = 0.002, and under effort rarefaction to 29 plots/habitat, rank rho = 1.00). Because the gardening pathway supplies ~75% of regional introductions in the most recent period (397 of 528 species; 18 -> 54 -> 142 -> 397 across periods) while gardening species occupy fewer habitat types (mean habitat.range 1.95) than unintentional ones (2.77), we hypothesise the habitat gradient is propagule-pressure and disturbance mediated - largely expressed through elevation (occupancy 37.3% in the lowest elevation quartile vs 3.2% in the highest; rho = -0.37) and urban cover within 1 km (rho = +0.38) - but with habitat retaining an independent effect after elevation adjustment (Wetlands/Urban/Coastal/Riparian 8-10x odds vs broad-leaved forest, all p <= 0.004). Prediction: garden-origin species will keep accumulating in urban, wetland, coastal and riparian plots while upland forest, meadow, scrub and rock habitats stay comparatively free of garden introductions.

rank agreement between views quantified (Spearman rho = 0.08). 4) FORMAL TEST: 2 x 10 plot-level Gardening-occupied vs not table, primary p from 10,000-permutation Monte-Carlo chi-square (labels permuted across plots, seed 20261023), asymptotic chi-square reported alongside, plot-level standardised residuals for the gardening column. 5) ROBUSTNESS: restriction to habitats with >=20 occurrence records; exclusion of uninformative habitats (<=5 records); both compared for direction agreement. 6) DESCRIPTIVE ONLY: 10 x 3 occurrence standardised residuals, labelled non-inferential because species recur across plots. 7) SENSITIVITY: effort rarefaction to the smallest habitat sample (29 plots, 5,000 draws) and elevation checks (quartile occupancy, Spearman, and a small logistic comparison of habitat vs habitat+elevation LRTs, dropping perfectly separated habitats) - no full GLM. 8) CONTEXT (region-wide, not from the plots): pathway species counts and mean habitat.range from invasion_success_pathways.csv (4 duplicated=TRUE dual-pathway rows retained), and the temporal rise of the gardening pathway. 9) phylogenetic_tree.txt deliberately out of scope. 10) Validation: Wilson CIs recomputed with statsmodels, chi2 recomputed against scipy, permutation p reproduced on a second RNG stream (20,000 permutations), occupancy counts recomputed by an independent groupby.

native_result.query: In what context does the gardening pathway for introducing non-native plants show different prevalence styles across habitat types?
native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: The gardening pathway shows different prevalence styles across habitat types specifically in the low-urban-cover, low-elevation part of the landscape: in moist, disturbed azonal habitats (Wetlands and Coastal, with Riparian intermediate) gardening is frequent AND co-dominant (occupancy 0.45-0.50; gardening supplies 54-56% of pathway-coded invader records, Holm p=0.005/0.061 vs the regional 35%), whereas in intensively human-held Urban and Croplands plots it is frequent but subordinate (equally often encountered - Urban 0.477 vs Wetlands+Coastal 0.478, OR 1.00 - yet only 19-30% of records, outnumbered by unintentional introductions 0.24-0.43:1, p<=7e-07). The contrast is not a richness or detectability artefact (invaded-plot richness p=0.089) and survives conditioning on urban cover, elevation, road proximity, historical cropland and CMH stratification (pooled dominance OR 2.50 [1.67,3.72]; adjusted 2.90 [2.06,4.09]), but it exists only outside the urbanisation saturation zone: the OR is 14.4 where 1000 m urban cover <0.02 and 1.43 (p=0.20) where it exceeds 0.20, and it decays from 7.35 to 1.81 as plot invader richness rises, because heavy unintentional introduction pressure homogenises pathway composition. In the dry upland habitats (Rock outcrops, Scrublands, both forest types, Meadows) there is too little gardening signal to assign any style (1-5 invaded plots, 1-13 records): no evidence of gardening, not demonstrated absence. Because frequency and dominance rank the ten habitats almost independently (Spearman rho=0.079, p=0.83; rho=0.985 restricted to invaded plots), the conclusion depends on using both metrics: frequency alone would class Urban with Wetlands, while share alone would put Broad-leaved forests first on 4 records.
native_result.WorkflowB: Plot-level pathway-richness data only (632 plots; species-level table used solely as corroboration; temporal table cited as background; tree unused). (1) Prevalence-style table per habitat: frequency = occupancy P(n.gard>0) with Wilson CI; dominance = n.gard/n.total with Holm-adjusted leave-one-out binomial test plus within-habitat gardening-vs-unintentional binomial test; intensity = mean n.gard per occupied plot; reliability gate >=15 occurrences and >=15 invaded plots; labels frequent-and-co-dominant / frequent-but-subordinate / frequent-and-proportional / rare-but-exclusive / absent-or-undetermined. (2) Plot-weighted and occurrence-weighted versions of every habitat table. (3) Permutation Fisher-Freeman-Halton for habitat(10)xpathway(3) and habitat(3)xpathway(2) (plain chi-square not used; 17/30 expected cells <5); collapsed Fisher exact contrasts with OR, 95% CI, Cramer V, both weightings. (4) Firth penalised logistic for occupancy (own implementation, validated) with nested LR tests of habitat vs context (urban cover 50 m/1000 m, elevation, log distance to road, land-cover change, 1956 cropland), invaded-plot-only models, quasi-binomial dominance model on invaded plots, Poisson/NB2 count check, CMH stratified tests and stratum-specific ORs, sensitivity to style thresholds and to habitat grouping. (5) Species-level habitat.range ~ pathway with and without duplicated rows, labelled corroboration only.

native_result.query: For which domains do the effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies?
native_result.HypoA: The effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies across both the Experimental Economics and Psychology domains. In Experimental Economics, the average effect estimate on the Fisher-z scale in original studies is 0.57, compared to 0.31 in replication studies. In Psychology, the average is 0.5 in original studies versus 0.24 in replication studies.
native_result.HypoB: Original studies report larger effects than their replications in all three domains in this data (Social psychology, Cognitive psychology, Economics), so no domain is exempt; what differs is robustness. Social psychology is the most consistent (ro > rr in 88.2% of 34 studies; mean Fisher-z gap 0.233 [0.162,0.304]; paired p=1.3e-07) and shows by far the largest proportional shrinkage (median rr/ro 0.131 vs 0.650 Cognitive and 0.698 Economics; only 20.6% replicated vs 47.1% Cognitive and 61.1% Economics). Cognitive has the largest per-study gap (0.289 [0.164,0.415], 82.4%, p=4.5e-05). Economics - which in these data is identical to the Experimental Economics project, since discipline is perfectly nested in project - also tends to favour originals at study level (0.266 [0.084,0.447], 83.3%, p=0.0067) but the gap is weighting-dependent and not robust: precision-weighted it is 0.013 [-0.052,0.078] against 0.208 [0.161,0.255] Social and 0.206 [0.132,0.279] Cognitive (Social-Economics +0.195 [0.086,0.304] p=0.0006; Cognitive-Economics +0.193 [0.060,0.325] p=0.005; discipline Wald F(2)=7.03 p=0.0015). It is not an artifact of tiny originals (only 2 of the 5 studies with no<10 are Experimental Economics; trimmed EE stays at 0.190 [0.063,0.316], 85.7%, p=0.0065), but within EE the gap falls as sample size rises (correlation with replication SE +0.65; 0.436 in the low replication-N half vs 0.096 in the high-N half), so well-powered economics replications reproduce originals almost exactly. At project level Psychology (0.261 [0.191,0.332], 85.3%) and Experimental Economics (0.266 [0.084,0.447], 83.3%) are indistinguishable unweighted (diff +0.004, p=0.96; Mann-Whitney p=0.28) and differ only under precision weighting (IV diff -0.194, p=0.0003, exploratory).
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded the joined CSV as-is (86 studies, 0 duplicates, 0 missing effect values; aggregated/lab_id/n.r/pm_belief unused). Built per-study paired difference d = fiso - fisr with SE_pair = sqrt(se_fiso^2 + se_fisr^2). PRIMARY scale = unweighted study-level tendency per domain (mean/median d, t-based CI, 10k seeded bootstrap CI, paired t-test, Wilcoxon, %ro>rr with Clopper-Pearson CI) for the three disciplines (primary grain) and both projects (secondary/exploratory). Equally prominent sensitivity: inverse-variance weighted pooled estimate per group plus IV-weighted meta-regression d ~ 1 + Social + Cognitive (ref = Economics) with joint Wald test, and a matching unweighted HC3 OLS. Sensitivity runs: trimmed (no<10 and |ro|<0.2 removed) for every estimator, tiny-N composition by project, gap-vs-precision correlations and EE median-N split, and relative_es = rr/ro (median, trimmed, |ro|>0.2). Holm correction over the pre-registered family (3 discipline paired tests + meta-regression); project-level comparisons flagged exploratory. Results written to analysis/summary_table.csv and analysis/results_log.txt; hypothesis in analysis/hypothesis.md.

native_result.HypoA: Studies in Experimental Economics tend to have longer original papers compared to Psychology. The average length of original papers in Experimental Economics is 28 pages, whereas in Psychology, the average is 11 pages.
native_result.HypoB: In this replication-project sample, the recorded original papers in Experimental Economics are substantially longer than those in Psychology: the 18 original papers from the Experimental Economics replication project (project='ee') average 28.0 pages (median 27.5, SD 7.4, 95% bootstrap CI 24.8-31.4), whereas the 95 original papers from the Reproducibility Project: Psychology (project='rpp', the headline definition of Psychology) average 11.2 pages (median 9.0, SD 6.3, 95% bootstrap CI 10.0-12.5) - a difference of 16.8 pages (about 2.5x; Welch p = 7.3e-09, Mann-Whitney p = 5.2e-10, Cohen's d = 2.57, 95% CI 1.97-3.18). The same figures hold under the broader pooled definition of Psychology (ml1+ml3+rpp, 117 papers, 11.16 pages, gap 16.8 pages), under id-level de-duplication, and after excluding or winsorising short brief reports (gap 13.4-17.9 pages). This is a difference in recorded page counts within this sample of replication targets, not evidence that economics papers are generally longer than psychology papers: the economics side is 18 papers from only two journals (American Economic Review 16, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2) whose page conventions are a format artefact, while the psychology side reflects RPP sampling short-format outlets (PS 39, JPSP 29, JEPLMC 27; 8 of 95 papers are 3 pages or shorter).

native_result.query: What kind of demographic disparities exist in median wealth in 1985 among individuals who were ever incarcerated?
native_result.HypoA: Gender disparities exist in median wealth in 1985 among individuals who were ever incarcerated, with males having higher median wealth than females.
native_result.HypoB: Among the 289 NLSY79 respondents ever incarcerated (jailed 1985-1994), 1985 wealth was essentially nil - median $720 (95% bootstrap CI $0-$1,200) with 45.0% holding zero or negative assets - and the disparities within this group run mainly along race, with a second, bottom-of-the-distribution divide along sex. Median 1985 wealth was $2,200 for ever-incarcerated white respondents, $320 for black respondents, and exactly $0 for hispanic respondents (asset poverty 31.9%, 47.8% and 52.5% respectively); the white-black gap is +$1,880 (permutation p=0.010 but bootstrap CI -127 to +$4,950, so suggestive rather than established) and the black-hispanic difference is negligible ($320, p=0.79). Among men, the only adequately powered race contrast, white men ($2,000, 29.8% at or below zero) held roughly 2.5 times the median wealth of black men ($800, 44.1%) and hispanic men ($700, 46.2%), though neither difference is statistically secure at n=252. The ever-incarcerated female median is literally $0 (n=37; CI degenerate because 64.9% have exactly zero wealth) versus $1,000 for men, and the female-male asset-poverty gap (70.3% vs 41.3%) is the more stable signal than the median gap itself. Race-specific results for women (n=16, 9, 12) are reported but not interpretable, and no race x sex interaction can be supported. Because q10 and q25 are $0 in every race group, the racial gap is invisible at the bottom and appears only as a level shift in the share with nothing, widening in dollars above the median (median -$1,880, q75 -$4,400, p90 -$14,104 for black vs white) while positive-wealth medians nearly converge ($4,400 vs $6,000). Race accounts for somewhat more spread than sex (median range $2,200 vs $1,000; both cuts explain only ~2% of rank variation, Kruskal-Wallis p=0.07 and p=0.02). These are descriptive, within-sample disparities measured at the start of the 1985-1994 incarceration window, so they characterise the wealth profile of people who are incarcerated during the window rather than an effect of incarceration; the flag cannot be cross-validated (no place-of-residence or detention-facility field exists in this file), jail cannot be distinguished from prison or short from long spells, and with no sampling weights and a household survey frame the results do not generalise beyond this NLSY79 sample.

For the primary population computed, overall and by race, sex and race x sex: n, q25, median, q75, p90, IQR, mean, min/max, share with wealth <=0 / ==0 / <0 / >0, and percentile-bootstrap 95% CIs for medians (B=2,000) and for asset-poverty shares (B=4,000; seed 20261022). Added medians restricted to strictly positive wealth, dollar differences and ratios vs the never-incarcerated group in the same demographic cell (ratios only where both medians >0), a q10-q25-median-q75-p90 ladder by race to locate the gap in the distribution, Kruskal-Wallis and rank eta-squared to compare the race and sex cuts, B=20,000 permutation tests for median differences, Mann-Whitney male-only race contrasts, threshold tail shares ($0/$1k/$10k/$50k/$100k), and a clearly-labelled nominal-dollar 1990/1996 trend as robustness only. native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB: Among Black men in this NLSY-79 cohort, incarceration is associated with a large, persistent wealth deficit whose dollar size scales with pre-jail economic position while its relative size is roughly constant. "Income level" is proxied by baseline composite_wealth_1985 because the file contains no income, earnings, wage or employment variable, grouped into rank tertiles. Of 1,465 Black men, the 143 ever jailed 1985-1994 gained only $4,601 in composite wealth from 1985 to 1996 versus $44,127 for the never-jailed (gap -$39,526; bootstrap 95% CI -$53,072 to -$27,724) and held $11,164 versus $55,544 in composite_wealth_1996 (gap -$44,380; CI -$57,251 to -$32,652), with 63.6% versus 37.7% holding zero-or-negative assets. Relative to baseline wealth the penalty is uniform: ever jailed raises the risk of ending with no positive assets by 23.8 percentage points (95% CI 15.7-32.0; OR 2.92, CI 2.00-4.26) and drops a man 14.5 percentile points down the 1996 wealth distribution (p=5e-13), with no moderation on the relative scale (asinh interaction p=0.37; odds-ratio interaction p=0.63). In nominal dollars the gap widens monotonically with 1985 wealth: -$11.5k in the bottom tertile, -$33.1k in the middle, -$85.7k in the top tertile of 1996 wealth (ever_jailed x stratum F=7.92, p=0.0004; tail-robust winsorised gaps -$10.7k, -$22.8k, -$63.7k with permutation p=0.17, 0.011, <0.001). Jail therefore appears to destroy accumulated, otherwise transferable assets rather than merely depressing a negligible stock: at the bottom of the income distribution the deficit is compressed toward zero dollars because even non-jailed Black men accumulated almost nothing (median 1996 wealth $0 in both groups), whereas among the third who entered the jail window with the most resources it is associated with roughly $60k-$86k less nominal wealth (median -$22,900) and a doubling of the share left with no assets (44% versus 20%). This is an association, not a causal estimate: the ever-jailed were already 43% poorer in 1985 ($6,564 vs $11,417), no covariates or jail timing/duration exist in the file, and within-stratum raw-mean permutation tests are non-significant after Holm (p=0.34-0.53) because a few multi-million-dollar observations dominate cell means; the robust signals are the distributional and assetlessness results.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Audit (12,013x6; zero missingness; 289 ever jailed = 2.41%; 1,899 exact duplicate rows; 37.97% of composite_wealth_1996 exactly zero; confirmed no income/earnings field). 2) Primary sample Black men (n=1,465; 143 jailed); co-primary outcomes = change in composite wealth 1985->1996 and 1996 level, always with means AND medians. 3) Income proxy = composite_wealth_1985 in rank-based tertiles with a seeded random tie-break (value-based quantiles collapse since ~40% of values tie at <=0); quartiles and a demoted 1990-wealth stratifier as robustness. 4) Within-stratum jailed-vs-not contrasts: means/medians/percentages, stratified bootstrap CIs (2,000), two-sided label permutation tests (10,000), Mann-Whitney, plus Hodges-Lehmann shifts, probability of superiority and 1%/99% winsorised means for tail robustness. 5) Effect modification: ever_jailed x stratum on the dollar scale (OLS on the 1985->1996 change, HC3; joint F test and linear-in-stratum trend) and on the asinh/rank scale (asinh(wealth/1000) adjusted for rank of 1985 wealth; percentile-rank regression), plus P(wealth<=0 in 1996) by logit and linear probability. 6) Holm correction within the 6-test primary family. 7) White men, Hispanic men and pooled Black respondents run identically as labelled comparison groups only. 8) Sensitivity: deduplicated rows, quartile strata, 1990 strata, winsorised means.

native_result.HypoB:
FINAL SUBMISSION — all six instructions implemented.

ANSWER (primary, zeros at face value): the largest increase in median wealth among black females occurred between 1985 and 1990.

HYPOTHESIS (verbatim, as written to result_payload.json):
"Among black females, median wealth grew in both windows but the largest increase came between 1985 and 1990: for the 1,548 black women in the sample (complete on all three survey years) median composite wealth rose from $175 in 1985 to $2,600 in 1990, a gain of $2,425 (14.9x; $485/year), against $4,000 by 1996, a further gain of only $1,400 (1.5x; $233/year) - and this holds on the assumption, taken from the supplied file itself, that the zeros in the wealth columns are genuine zero-wealth values rather than missing data. That assumption is what pins the answer down: if those zeros are instead read as zero-filled nonresponse (the file reports no missing values anywhere in its 12,013 rows) and are set missing, the largest increase shifts to 1990→1996, with a median gain of $14,135 versus $7,834 for 1985→1990 ($20,500 versus $10,295 among women holding positive wealth in both years), while treating only the negative values as missing leaves the answer at 1985→1990 ($3,250 versus $2,000). Under the primary coding every secondary measure agrees on 1985→1990: the median within-person gain is $1,000 versus $0 for 1990→1996, 54.6% versus 47.9% of black women gained wealth, and the paired bootstrap of the difference between the two interval gains is $1,025 (95% CI −$175 to $2,450; P(1985→1990 larger) = 0.95) - a bootstrap interval that straddles zero, so the defensible claim is only that both windows brought gains and the earlier brought the larger one, not that the two windows are cleanly separable. Nor is this an artefact of window length: 1985→1990 spans 5 years against 6 for 1990→1996, so the per-year normalisation ($485/year versus $233/year) points the same way rather than qualifying the result. Incarceration status does not drive it - among never-jailed black women the gains are $2,688 versus $1,112 - and the 16 ever-jailed black women, whose wealth is almost entirely $0, are reported descriptively only and support no inferential claim. For context only: black females held the lowest median wealth of all six race x sex cells in every wave, and theirs kept climbing after 1990 even as white women's median fell from $20,100 to $8,825 and white men's from $15,601 to $8,900 over 1990→1996; their median reached 45% of white women's by 1996 (from 3% in 1985 and 13% in 1990), so their fastest proportional gains came earliest, in 1985→1990, from a near-zero base, while the level gap narrowed mainly before 1990 and then plateaued. Limitations: unweighted medians (no survey weights supplied), nominal non-deflated dollars (no price index supplied), and no documented construction rules for the five-component wealth composite."

HOW EACH INSTRUCTION WAS MET
1. Sentence 1 names the interval, all three medians, and the zero-handling assumption. 2. Sentence 2 states the zeros→NA reversal with both numbers ($14,135 vs $7,834) plus positives-only ($20,500 vs $10,295). 3. Per-year normalisation visible ($485/yr vs $233/yr) with a one-line "points the same way" note. 4. ever_jailed is a descriptive table + never-jailed footnote only; no incarceration claim. 5. Cross-race/sex appears strictly in a context sentence; the answer sentence names black females and the years. 6. One consolidated script (analysis_black_female_median_wealth.py) regenerates all three tables plus the hypothesis and workflow; the four loose inspection files were deleted.
DROPPED as instructed: winsorised medians reduced to a one-line note; no weights, no deflation (kept as limitations).

THREE DEFECTS I FOUND AND FIXED IN MY OWN OUTPUT (worth your attention):
(a) The first draft's sensitivity numbers were hand-typed from the older pairwise-complete variant; the consolidated script uses complete-case pairs, so the correct zeros→NA figures are $14,135/$7,834 (not $11,700/$4,268). The hypothesis is now built from f-strings over the generated tables, so no figure can drift.
(b) My earlier claim "the bootstrap CI excludes zero only for 1985→1990" was wrong — the correct same-respondent test of the actual headline claim gives $1,025 (95% CI −$175 to $2,450), which straddles zero. The hypothesis now says the two windows are not cleanly separable; the ranking rests on point estimates plus four concordant secondary measures, not on a significant difference.
(c) My draft claimed black females were "the only group whose median kept rising after 1990" — false (black males +$900, hipanic females +$9,101, hipanic males +$5,600 also rose). Rewritten to the verifiable claim (lowest level in every wave; 3%→13%→45% of white females' median).

native_result.query: What changes occurred in the wealth inequality for white males and females between 1990 and 1996?
native_result.HypoA: Wealth inequality increases among white people (both men and women) in the 1990-1996 period, with the Gini coefficients for white females increasing from 0.775593 in 1990 to 0.781602 in 1996, and for white males increasing from 0.792018 in 1990 to 0.797468 in 1996.
native_result.HypoB: Between 1990 and 1996 wealth inequality narrowed substantially for both white men and white women in this NLSY79 cohort, driven by compression at the top and rapid gains in the middle of the wealth-holding distribution, and the two groups moved in parallel rather than diverging. Among respondents reporting positive wealth (headline basis: composite>0, zeros treated as missing-by-convention non-response, negatives/debt excluded) the Gini fell from 0.688 to 0.623 (-0.066, 95% CI -0.094..-0.036) for white males and 0.681 to 0.599 (-0.082, CI -0.110..-0.052) for white females; p90/p50 fell 5.68->3.89 and 4.89->3.74; the top-10% wealth share fell 53.8%->47.8% and 52.1%->45.6% and the top-1% share roughly halved (18.5%->11.4%; 19.0%->11.7%), while median holdings among wealth-holders roughly tripled (~$48k->~$132k male; ~$58k->~$132k female) and mean/median ratios fell (2.61->1.83; 2.30->1.76). Inequality therefore compressed top-down: the middle and lower-middle of the wealth-holding distribution grew fastest and the top pulled away less. The same narrowing holds within respondents observed with positive wealth in both years (dGini -0.063 male, -0.077 female, both CIs excluding zero) and when debtors are retained at zero (dGini -0.068/-0.089), so it is not an artifact of selection into the positive-wealth sample. native_result.query: In which years were individuals with a criminal record found to have significantly lower wealth compared to those without?
native_result.HypoA: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
native_result.HypoB:
## Result: 1985, 1990 और 1996 — तीनों वर्षों में jailed समूह का wealth significantly lower है (कोई split decision नहीं)

### PRIMARY (crude unadjusted, सारे 12,013 rows, zeros retained)
Decision rule: Welch-asinh 1-sided **Holm p<.05** + Mann-Whitney 1-sided **Holm p<.05** + bootstrap (2000, stratified) mean-diff 95% CI का **upper bound < 0**.

| Year | mean jailed (n=289) | mean non-jailed (n=11,724) | **raw-dollar ratio** | median 1 vs 0 | Δ mean ($) [95% boot CI] | Welch t (df) | p_1s / **p_Holm** | MW **p_Holm** | **Hedges' g** | **Cliff's δ** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1985 | 7,929 | 25,086 | **0.32** (68.4% lower) | 720 vs 3,600 | −17,157 [−20,284, −13,695] | −5.24 (303.6) | 1.5e−07 / **1.5e−07** | **8.0e−11** | **−0.30** | **−0.22** |
| 1990 | 16,350 | 73,948 | **0.22** (77.9% lower) | 0 vs 10,500 | −57,598 [−67,275, −44,289] | −11.48 (302.4) | 7.5e−26 / **2.3e−25** | **1.2e−34** | **−0.68** | **−0.42** |
| 1996 | 20,383 | 105,447 | **0.19** (80.7% lower) | 0 vs 8,500 | −85,063 [−98,551, −65,962] | −10.37 (303.7) | 4.6e−22 / **9.2e−22** | **9.3e−26** | **−0.59** | **−0.35** |

**तीनों वर्ष = तीनों criterion pass (AGREE_all3 = True), split_decision_years = []** — कोई वर्ष direction-yes/track-no mismatch नहीं दिया, इसलिए कोई ambiguity छिपाने का प्रश्न नहीं उठता। Median-diff bootstrap CI भी तीनों वर्ष negative: 1985 −2,880 [−3,600, −2,300]; 1990 −10,500 [−11,100, −10,000]; 1996 −8,500 [−10,000, −7,140]। Hodges–Lehmann (asinh) −0.97 / −3.22 / −1.70।

### Statistical vs practical significance (आपका point #1)
n-ratio 1:40 होने के कारण छोटा gap भी significant आ सकता था — यहाँ gap छोटा नहीं है: jailed समूह का mean non-jailed का **सिर्फ़ 32%/22%/19%** है, median 1990 और 1996 में **शून्य** है, और jailed समूह का 45%/57%/63% लोगों sample के bottom decile में हैं बनाम 32%/29%/40%। Effect size small→large range में है: g = −0.30 (1985, small–medium), −0.68 (1990), −0.59 (1996); Cliff's δ = −0.22/−0.42/−0.35 (अर्थात यादृच्छिक रूप से चुना गया jailed व्यक्ति के कम wealth होने की संभावना ~61%/71%/68%)। यह magnitude-aware conclusion है, केवल p-based नहीं।

### SENSITIVITY — conclusion कहीं नहीं बदला (एक table, direction + pass/fail)
| Spec | 1985 | 1990 | 1996 | Direction lower? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 dedupe exact duplicates (n₁=239) | pass | pass | pass | हाँ (g −0.38/−0.84/−0.70) |
| S2 exclude zeros within-year (n₁=175/157/132) | pass | pass | pass | हाँ (g −0.20/−0.74/−0.91) |
| S3 winsorize 1st/99th | pass | pass | pass | हाँ (g −0.30/−0.69/−0.59) |
| S4 positive-only within-year (n₁=159/125/107) | pass | pass | pass | हाँ (g −0.38/−0.81/−0.88) |
| S5 extensive margin P(wealth>0) | RR 0.81, p=1.4e−03 | RR 0.61, p=8.1e−07 | RR 0.62, p=8.4e−05 | हाँ |

Bootstrap CI seed-stability (seeds 1/2/99): 1985 [−20.4k,−13.5k], 1990 [−67.8k,−44.1k], 1996 [−98.5k,−65.7k] — CI location ~0.5% भी नहीं हिला। ग़ौरतलब: **zeros हटाने से gap घटा नहीं, बल्कि effect size बड़ा हुआ** — यानी finding zero-coding artifact पर निर्भर नहीं करती।

### EXPLORATORY (side-by-side, primary को override नहीं करता)
- OLS on asinh wealth + sex + race (HC3): jailed coefficient −1.09 (p=2e−04), −3.38, −3.53 — तीनों वर्ष significant। Dollars-outcome OLS: −$9,441 / −$35,394 / −$60,911 (सब p<.001)। यानी crude gap_sex/race confounding से नहीं बन रहा (याद रखें: jailed समूह 87% male, 55% black)।
- Male-only (n_jailed=252): तीनों वर्ष significant।
- Race-stratified: white 1985/1990/1996 pass, hipanic तीनों pass, black 1990/1996 pass — **एकमात्र cell fail: black/1985 (est −0.30, p_Holm = 0.229, n_jailed=159)**। यह primary conclusion को नहीं बदलता, पर honest caveat है कि 1985 का gap black sub-sample में अकेले detect नहीं हुआ (power सीमित)।

### Final data-grounded hypothesis (deliverable)
"Individuals with a criminal record — operationalized here as `ever_jailed` = 1 (jailed at any time 1985–1994), the only criminal-record proxy in the supplied data — had significantly lower wealth than those without in **all three measured years: 1985, 1990, and 1996**. The wealth gap widened over time in relative terms (jailed mean = 32%, 22% and 19% of non-jailed means in 1985, 1990, 1996; Hedges' g = −0.30, −0.68, −0.59; one-sided Holm-adjusted p ≤ 1.5e−07 in every year), and it is not driven by duplicate rows, zero-coded wealth, top-coded outliers, or sex/race composition. **Timing caveat: 1985 and 1990 wealth is measured inside or adjacent to the 1985–1994 jail window, so those two gaps are consistent with pre-existing socioeconomic disadvantage and selection (reverse/ simultanous causality) rather than effects of incarceration; only 1996 is a clean post-window comparison**, so the causal reading should rest on 1996 while the descriptive answer to 'which years' remains 1985, 1990 and 1996."

### Declared assumptions (boldly, per your point #5–6)
1. **`ever_jailed` = "criminal record" — single operationalization.** कोई place-of-residence या formal-charge proxy supplied assets में नहीं है। इसका मतलब lifetime criminal records (arrests, convictions without jail, post-1994 incarceration) missing हैं; यह non-differential misclassification expected direction में **conservative** है (true offending group contaminated with unconvicted/never-caught people, जिससे gap underestimate होता है) — पर unmeasured-severity confounding नहीं ढकता।
2. Zero = genuine zero net worth in primary; zero-excluded spec sensitivity में (conclusion unchanged)।
3. **Unavailable और इसलिए assume नहीं किया गया:** NLSY79 sampling weights, respondent ID (dedupe की जाँच के अलावा कुछ नहीं), composite-wealth codebook (कौन-से five components, debt net होता है या नहीं), original analysis का test/threshold। ये unknowns unknown ही रखे गए — कोई reconstructed codebook/weighting नहीं बनाई।
4. 1,899 exact duplicate rows primary में retained; unweighted means nationally representative नहीं (NLSY79 minority/low-SES oversample)।
5. Nominal dollars; केवल within-year between-group comparison — कोई cross-year trend/inflation claim नहीं।

### Limitations
Cross-sectional per-year design, कोई covariate adjustment primary में नहीं (आपके निर्देशानुसार), n=289 subgroup power सीमित (black/1985 fail इसी का नतीजा), 25–38% exact zeros + शून्य missingness से zero-filled non-response की संभावना काटती नहीं (हालांकि exclude-zeros spec result नहीं बदलता), और jail window vs measurement-year overlap causal interpretation को 1996 तक सीमित कर देती है।

sub_hypo.text: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
sub_hypo.context: Participants in the National Longitudinal Study of Youth's 1979 cohort, with wealth measured in 1985, 1990, and 1996.
sub_hypo.relations: Individuals jailed between 1985 and 1994 (ever_jailed = 1) have significantly lower composite wealth in each of 1985, 1990, and 1996 than individuals not jailed during that period (ever_jailed = 0).

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.

sub_hypo.text: Individuals ever jailed during 1985–1994 had significantly lower wealth than those not jailed during that window in each of 1985, 1990, and 1996, with a widening relative mean wealth gap.
sub_hypo.context: National Longitudinal Study of Youth 1979 cohort; primary unweighted, unadjusted comparisons use all 12,013 rows, including 289 jailed and 11,724 non-jailed observations, retaining zeros and exact duplicates. Wealth comparisons are within-year in nominal dollars. The 1985 and 1990 measurements overlap the jail window and may reflect pre-existing disadvantage or selection; only 1996 is post-window. Criminal record is operationalized solely as ever_jailed, not lifetime arrests or convictions.
sub_hypo.relations: Jailed/non-jailed mean wealth ratios are 0.32, 0.22, and 0.19, respectively; mean differences are −$17,157, −$57,598, and −$85,063. Each year satisfies one-sided Holm-adjusted p<.05 for both Welch tests on asinh wealth and Mann–Whitney tests, with a stratified 2,000-bootstrap mean-difference 95% CI wholly below zero. Median-difference CIs are also negative. Hedges' g is −0.30, −0.68, and −0.59, so standardized effects do not widen monotonically. Lower wealth remains significant after exact deduplication, within-year exclusion of zeros, 1st/99th percentile winsorization, and restriction to positive wealth. These are descriptive associations, not established causal effects.

sub_hypo.text: Individuals ever jailed during 1985–1994 were less likely to have positive wealth in all three measured years.
sub_hypo.context: National Longitudinal Study of Youth 1979 cohort; exploratory extensive-margin sensitivity comparisons for 1985, 1990, and 1996.
