native_result.query: Which two documentation formats are the least used for requirements in ML-enabled system projects, with 10.13% (95% CI [9.926, 10.333]) and 4.366% (95% CI [4.231, 4.501]) of respondents indicating so, respectively, after bootstrapping for statistical significance?
native_result.HypoA: The least used documentation formats for requirements in ML-enabled system projects are ML Canvas (10.13% respondents, 95% CI [9.926, 10.333]) and Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) Scenarios (4.366% respondents, 95% CI [4.231, 4.501]) after bootstrapping for statistical significance.
native_result.HypoB: BDD scenarios and ML Canvas are the two least used named documentation formats for requirements in ML-enabled system projects. Among the 194 respondents who answered Q10, only 2.06% (95% bootstrap CI [0.52, 4.12]) used BDD scenarios and 7.73% (95% CI [4.12, 11.86]) used ML Canvas, compared with 34.02% for notebooks and 32.47% for user stories. Mapping the question's figures by magnitude, the first-named 10.13% [9.926, 10.333] corresponds to ML Canvas (our 7.73%, the larger of the pair) and the second-named 4.366% [4.231, 4.501] to BDD scenarios (our 2.06%, the smallest format of all); bootstrapping supports the rank, not the exact level - BDD is bottom-2 in 100.0% of 10,000 replicates and ML Canvas in 97.8%, while every other format is below 1.4%. Caveat: ML Canvas is tied at 15/194 (7.73%) with the free-text Others basket, so the second slot depends on not counting Others as a format, and the reference CIs (implied n ~ 85,000) cannot be reproduced at n = 194.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Load CSV (276 respondents, unique IDs); assert Q10 encodings are only quoted / not quoted / -77. 2) Treat -77, -66, -99, -1, NaN as missing and exclude them (never summed); the Q10 block is all-or-nothing missing for 82 respondents, so the primary sample is the 194 Q10 answerers, unit = respondent. 3) Indicator used = value equals quoted; metric = usage share = used / 194 (the complement is 66-98% and cannot match the question's magnitudes; no Likert levels exist in this export). 4) Rank the 10 named formats ascending, with Not_Documented and the free-text Others shown only as reference rows plus a full 12-column table so the MLCanvas/Others 15/194 tie is visible. 5) Non-parametric bootstrap over respondents, B = 10000, numpy default_rng(20261022), percentile 2.5/97.5, no stratification; rank significance = bottom-2 inclusion probability across replicates. 6) Sensitivity section (not primary, never used to pick the answer): Status != Suspended and Duration > 300/600/1000/1120 s, plus an explicit counter-argument block showing that under strict duration filters the 10.13% anchor sits closer to Others than to ML Canvas. 7) Anchor check: implied n from the reference CIs = p(1-p)(1.96/h)^2 = 88012 and 84452 vs n = 194, so exact CI agreement is unattainable. 8) Print tables and the hypothesis; rerun verified byte-identical (md5 of the output table).

native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Across 1975-2015, adjusted savings: education expenditure (% of GNI) is negatively associated with GNI per capita (constant 2015 US$) in raw levels, but that negative is a share-vs-base artifact because the exposure is a ratio to GNI, so the outcome sits in its own denominator. Restating exposure as an absolute per-capita education-savings flow (share x GNIpc) flips the LMC association positive (raw r=+0.958, detrended +0.622, differenced +0.506; lagged differenced elasticity +0.068 [-0.015,+0.150], p=0.109, T=38), while the same quantity for Sub-Saharan Africa is unidentifiable (n=5 levels / n=4 changes). The clearest group difference is on the input side: in LMC a rising education-savings share is associated with rising primary gross enrollment (+1.14 GER points per +1 percentage-point rise in the share, 95% CI [+0.25,+2.03], p=0.013, T=39), whereas in SSA no such association exists (-0.14 [-1.03,+0.74], p=0.753). I therefore hypothesize that the education-expenditure -> enrollment -> income association is observable but modest for developing (LMC) countries and effectively absent for SSA: SSA's enrollment expansion (primary gross 60.6 -> 98.0, secondary 14.8 -> 43.4) accelerated after its education share peaked at 6.10% in 1997 and fell to 3.15% by 2015 (primary +0.25 -> +1.33 pp/yr, secondary +0.41 -> +1.25 pp/yr), so SSA's enrollment gains are associated with something other than a rising education-expenditure share; over 2011-2015 SSA's per-capita education flow fell 9.23% while LMC's rose 7.94%, and SSA GNI per capita rose 5.08% versus 13.81% for LMC. In the primary differenced specification the cumulative LMC income elasticity is -0.297 [-0.724,+0.129] p=0.172, indistinguishable from zero, and the SSA income elasticity cannot be estimated from this file at all. Group-level aggregates only; no country-level inference; associations only, not causal effects; no GDP-per-capita series exists in the data.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Audited raw file (12x45; 2 groups x 6 series; 41 year columns) and produced the per-series/per-group percent-null table. 2) Melted 41 year columns to long, coerced blanks to NaN, mapped Series Code to short names, pivoted to an (group, year) x series analysis frame (82x8). 3) Stationarity diagnostics (ADF maxlag=2, AR1) established unit-root levels and stationary first log-differences, fixing differencing as the primary transformation. 4) Income leg on LMC only: level elasticity (labeled non-interpretable), primary first-difference-of-logs spec with lagged education regressors + linear trend + Newey-West 4, cumulative lag1-3 contrast with CI, reverse-causality probe, restricted 1991-2015 variant with LFPR and exports. 5) Enrollment leg (education savings -> primary and secondary gross enrollment) estimated in levels-with-trend and first differences for both groups, plus a Chow-style pooled group-by-savings interaction on 1991-2015 as robustness only. 6) Required denominator check: raw vs linearly-detrended vs differenced correlations, then reformulated exposure as an absolute per-capita flow to break the shared GNI base. 7) SSA income leg reported descriptively with explicit n=5 levels / n=4 changes and no p-values. 8) All coefficients registered with window, T, transformation and controls in out/results_master.csv.

native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication

native_result.query: In which century did the Diversity in Pottery Form collapses and Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases simultaneuosly?
native_result.HypoA: Around 1800 BCE, Diversity in Pottery Form collapses, while Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases.
native_result.HypoB: En el siglo XVII a.C. (bin de 100 años 1700-1601 a.C.; cruce interpolado c. 1733-1732 a.C.) la diversidad de FORMA de la cerámica (PotteryForm) colapsa y la diversidad de DECORACIÓN (PotteryDecoration) aumenta simultáneamente: PotteryForm cae de un máximo previo de Z=+0.79 a Z=-1.13 (-1.92 Z, sostenido 13 bins) mientras PotteryDecoration sube de Z=-1.15 a Z=+0.97 (+1.45 Z en un siglo, pico +1.53) en el MISMO bin, con correlación r=-0.66 entre ambas. Interpretación: reorganización antifónica del capital cultural (cambio de la variedad morfológica a la ornamental) en la transición de período LN a OBA, coincidiendo con una fuerte reducción del indicador demográfico de apertura polínica de Belau/Woserin (SMOOTH_MEAN_200y 2.26 -> 0.91, -59.8%; pollen_grate_100 negativo), compatible con una contracción demográfica que redujo la variabilidad de formas mantenida por transmisión dependiente de población y reorientó la inversión simbólica hacia la decoración.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Carga time_series_data.csv (3601 filas anuales, Z arqueológicos solo en 37 knots de 100 años; *_inter interpolación lineal) y capital.csv con decimal=',' (solo bins y group). 2) Detección primaria nivel+mínimo local: colapso forma = racha >=2 bins con Z<=-0.5 (grid -1.0), mínimo local con caída >=1.0 Z vs máximo de 500-1000 años previos; aumento decoración = espejo (Z>=+0.5). 3) Simultaneidad por gap entre onsets <= tol bins (primaria 0-1 bin = <=200 años). 4) Matriz de robustez 16 celdas primarias (crudo/suavizado 200a/suavizado 300a x umbral 0.5 y 1.0 x sustain 2 y 3 x tol 0/1/2) + 8 controles por tasa de cambio (|delta Z|>=1.0 en 200-300 años anclado al primer bin que excede el umbral). 5) Tests de truncado del registro (9 cortes) y flag de tramos planos/padding. 6) Siglo = ceil(|año|/100) con eje BCE. 7) Contexto demográfico descriptivo con pollen_inter/pollen_inter_100/pollen_grate_100 y SMOOTH_MEAN_200y de Feeser et al. 2019, sin usarlo para fechar.

sub_hypo.context: Around 1800 BCE.
sub_hypo.relations: Pottery form diversity collapses while pottery decoration diversity increases.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: Around 1800 BCE, Diversity in Pottery Form collapses, while Diversity in Pottery Decoration increases.

sub_hypo.text: En la transición LN–OBA, la diversidad de formas cerámicas colapsa mientras aumenta simultáneamente la diversidad de decoración, indicando una reorganización antifónica del capital cultural desde la variedad morfológica hacia la ornamental.
sub_hypo.context: Siglo XVII a.C., bin de 100 años 1700–1601 a.C., con cruce interpolado hacia 1733–1732 a.C. La detección se basa en los bins arqueológicos centenarios, no en la resolución anual de las interpolaciones.
sub_hypo.relations: Relación inversa (r=-0.66): PotteryForm cae de un máximo previo de Z=+0.79 a Z=-1.13 (−1.92 Z), con colapso sostenido durante 13 bins; PotteryDecoration pasa de Z=-1.15 a Z=+0.97, con un incremento declarado de +1.45 Z en un siglo y un pico de +1.53. Ambos cambios ocurren en el mismo bin. El criterio primario exige al menos 2 bins con forma Z≤−0.5 y caída ≥1.0 Z respecto al máximo de los 500–1000 años previos; decoración utiliza el criterio espejo, Z≥+0.5. La simultaneidad se evalúa mediante la separación entre inicios, con tolerancia primaria de 0–1 bin (≤200 años según el workflow).

sub_hypo.text: La reorganización de la diversidad cerámica coincide con una fuerte reducción del indicador demográfico de apertura polínica de Belau/Woserin, compatible con una contracción demográfica que redujo la variabilidad de formas mantenida por transmisión dependiente de población y reorientó la inversión simbólica hacia la decoración.
sub_hypo.context: Transición LN–OBA y episodio cerámico del bin 1700–1601 a.C.; registros polínicos de Belau/Woserin utilizados únicamente como contexto demográfico descriptivo, no para fechar el episodio.
sub_hypo.relations: El colapso de la diversidad de formas y el aumento de la diversidad decorativa coinciden con una caída de SMOOTH_MEAN_200y de 2.26 a 0.91 (−59.8%) y con pollen_grate_100 negativo. La asociación se interpreta como compatible con contracción demográfica, menor variabilidad morfológica dependiente de población y mayor inversión simbólica ornamental; el análisis polínico es descriptivo y no establece causalidad.

gen_sub_hypo.full_hypo: En el siglo XVII a.C. (bin de 100 años 1700-1601 a.C.; cruce interpolado c. 1733-1732 a.C.) la diversidad de FORMA de la cerámica (PotteryForm) colapsa y la diversidad de DECORACIÓN (PotteryDecoration) aumenta simultáneamente: PotteryForm cae de un máximo previo de Z=+0.79 a Z=-1.13 (-1.92 Z, sostenido 13 bins) mientras PotteryDecoration sube de Z=-1.15 a Z=+0.97 (+1.45 Z en un siglo, pico +1.53) en el MISMO bin, con correlación r=-0.66 entre ambas. Interpretación: reorganización antifónica del capital cultural (cambio de la variedad morfológica a la ornamental) en la transición de período LN a OBA, coincidiendo con una fuerte reducción del indicador demográfico de apertura polínica de Belau/Woserin (SMOOTH_MEAN_200y 2.26 -> 0.91, -59.8%; pollen_grate_100 negativo), compatible con una contracción demográfica que redujo la variabilidad de formas mantenida por transmisión dependiente de población y reorientó la inversión simbólica hacia la decoración.

native_result.HypoA: Between 3400 BCE to 3000 BCE, the number of monuments and axes increases along with symbolic capital
native_result.HypoB: Between 3400 and 3000 BCE (five 100-year epochs: 3400, 3300, 3200, 3100, 3000 BCE; all series are standardised Z-values, not raw counts), the number of monuments (MonumentCount/ZMonument) and of axes and celts (AxesCelts/ZBeil) does not increase with the elements the study defines as symbolic capital (HatchetSword/ZAxtschwert, Dagger/ZDolch, HouseSize/Zhausgr); the two outcomes are instead dissociated from, or weakly inversely related to, them - MonumentCount vs HouseSize r = -0.35 (Spearman rho = -0.41, n = 5; first differences r = -0.04) and vs the equal-weight symbolic composite r = -0.35, AxesCelts vs HouseSize r = -0.17 (rho = -0.37, but first differences r = +0.50) and vs the composite r = -0.17 - while MonumentCount vs HatchetSword is +0.29 and AxesCelts vs HatchetSword -0.11, values that are numerically meaningless because HatchetSword spans only 0.01 Z-units in this window (sd 0.004) and Dagger is strictly constant (-0.58), so two of the three symbolic elements carry no testable signal. The strongest and only leave-one-epoch-out stable covariation is with elements classified as economic capital: Depot (ZHort) r = +0.85 with MonumentCount and +0.93 with AxesCelts, the economic composite r = +0.97/+0.92 (partly self-referential because AxesCelts belongs to that set), and the two outcomes with each other (r = +0.87), all peaking together at 3200 BCE. Demographic openness (Belau_PC1 / pollen; higher = more clearance = higher population) declines monotonically across the window (100-year bin mean +0.45 to -1.58), so the rise in monuments and axes is not accompanied by demographic growth (contemporaneous r = +0.08 for MonumentCount, -0.08 for AxesCelts); the two peak at 3200 BCE while both symbolic capital and openness are falling. Because HouseSize itself tracks openness (r = +0.72, rho = +0.87), the apparent inverse symbolic-capital relationship is largely the declining demographic trend reappearing through the only symbolic element that varies. Averaging 3400-3200 vs 3200-3000 BCE the symbolic composite falls 0.07 to -0.23 while MonumentCount rises 0.11 to 0.30 and AxesCelts 1.10 to 1.40. Limitations: n = 5 epochs so everything is descriptive and p-values are not interpreted; Z-values are standardised, not raw counts; two of the three symbolic predictors are effectively constant; lag correlations at +/-200 years rest on n = 3; and widening the window to 3800-2800 BCE (n = 11) reverses the sign of the symbolic correlations to positive (+0.16), so the negative direction is window-specific. native_result.HypoB: El ambar alcanza su valor maximo durante el IV milenio BCE (4000-3001 BCE; ~5950-5001 calBP), dentro de una meseta de maximo que se extiende entre 4000 y 3000 BCE (~5950-4851 calBP, definida como los bins seculares contiguos con Z >= 0.9*maximo: 11 bins, Z medio 1.489), con el pico estricto en 3300-3000 BCE (~5250-4851 calBP, Z = 1.54). La meseta arranca en el Neolitico medio/bajo (EN, 4000-3500 BCE, Z=1.46) y culmina en el Neolitico medio final (MN, 3400-3000 BCE, Z=1.54) justo en la frontera EN/MN; despues cae a valores negativos desde el III milenio BCE (media -0.148) hasta minimos en el I milenio BCE (-0.727). native_result.HypoA: From 1500 BCE onwards, Monuments Count and Copper & Gold increase simultaneuosly while summer social capital peaks?
native_result.HypoB: Summed social capital (Copper & Gold + Amber + Monument Count, simple sum of raw Z) peaks in the Late Bronze Age in the 13th century BCE, i.e. the 1300-1201 BCE bin (3250-3151 calBP; CE signed -1300 to -1201); the adjacent 1400-1301 BCE bin (3350-3251 calBP) is exactly tied, so the safest phrasing is a peak spanning 1400-1201 BCE, best single century 1300-1201 BCE, which wins outright under 150/200/250-year smoothing (3 of 5 windows) and is identical in capital.csv, the raw anchors of time_series_data.csv and its annual interpolated grid. The individual social-capital components that increase are Copper & Gold (ZCU_AU: Z=+2.54, 95th percentile, 59.9% of the peak anomaly, positive 500-year trend) and Monument Count (ZMonument: Z=+1.71, 97th percentile, 40.3% of the anomaly, positive trend); together they account for essentially 100% of the peak anomaly (+4.238 exact additive decomposition). Amber (Zamber) does NOT increase: Z=-0.01 at the peak, -0.3% of the anomaly, its own maximum lying in 3300-3000 BCE with a negative long-run trend. The peak is social-specific in the 13th-century bin: cultural capital (pottery form/decoration diversity) is below its mean (28th of 39 bins) and economic capital (Depot, Sickle, Axes & Celts, Monument Size) is below its mean (34th of 39), while only symbolic capital (Hatchets & Swords, Daggers, House Size) is simultaneously high (2nd of 39) although its own maximum lies two centuries later (1800-1701 BCE); in the tied 14th-century bin economic capital is also elevated, so the 'social only' reading is strongest for 1300-1201 BCE. We therefore interpret the peak as a metallurgical plus monumental-construction phenomenon - prestige copper/gold deposition and collective labour mobilisation - rather than an across-the-board prosperity maximum or a long-distance exchange boom, since amber, the exchange proxy, is decoupled from it. Landscape openness/demography (Belau/Woserin pollen PC1) correlates only weakly (r = 0.02-0.32, n = 36 overlapping bins) and is explicitly not claimed as the mechanism.

native_result.query: How does the prevalence of non-native plants introduced via gardening vary based on habitat type?
native_result.HypoA: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs between urban/cropland habitats and natural habitats.
native_result.HypoB: Prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants differs clearly among habitat types in the Barcelona province, following the ordering Wetlands ~ Coastal > Riparian > Urban > Croplands: the wetter, low-elevation habitats hold the largest share of ornamental-origin species among the plants they contain, and croplands the smallest. Defining prevalence as sum(n.gard)/sum(n.total) over species records in plots with n.total > 0 (conditional on a plot being invaded), Wetlands (29/52 = 0.56, Wilson 95% CI 0.42-0.68), Coastal (23/43 = 0.54, CI 0.39-0.68) and Riparian (35/96 = 0.37, CI 0.28-0.46) hold the highest shares of gardening species, while Croplands is the clear minimum (20/108 = 0.19, CI 0.12-0.27) and Urban is intermediate-low (45/151 = 0.30, CI 0.23-0.38); the region-wide value is 169/481 = 0.35. The habitat effect is confirmed by a cell-means binomial GLM on cbind(n.gard, n.total - n.gard) (LR chi2 = 36.7, df = 5, p = 6.8e-07; Pearson dispersion c = 1.01, so no beta-binomial correction is needed) and by a Monte-Carlo habitat x pathway test (chi2 = 75.2 over the 10 habitats, p < 0.001) used because 57% of asymptotic cells have expected counts < 5. Wetlands and Coastal exceed Croplands by ~1.7 logits (p < 1e-4) and Urban by ~1.0-1.1 logits (p = 0.005-0.001); Wetlands and Coastal do not differ from each other (p = 0.82). Broad-leaved forests (4/4), Coniferous forests (7/8), Scrublands (2/5), Meadows (4/13) and Rock outcrops (0/1) are NOT estimable and their extreme apparent values (1.00, 0.88, 0.00) must not be read as results: each rests on 1-13 records and they were collapsed into one composite group. Adding elevation and the UTM coordinates strengthens the fit (LR chi2 = 12.3, df = 3, p = 0.006) but leaves the habitat ranking unchanged, and residual spatial autocorrelation is not significant (Moran's I = +0.06, p = 0.17), although with only 191 non-empty plots this test has limited power. Elevation enters positively as a within-habitat partial effect (+0.0033 logit per metre, p = 0.0008) yet does not explain the between-habitat ranking - Wetlands, the highest prevalence habitat, sits at only ~176 m mean elevation. A plot-level occupancy analysis over all 632 plots (success = n.gard > 0, so the 515 plots with n.gard = 0 count as failures) reproduces the two poles - Wetlands highest (0.50) and Croplands lowest (0.21) - but reverses the middle: Urban rises to 0.48 (2nd) because 83% of urban plots host at least one invader, nearly all unintentional (104/151). The two definitions therefore disagree specifically for Urban and for the collapsed rare-habitat group (0.55 conditional vs 0.04 occupancy); rank agreement across the six groups is weak and non-significant (Spearman rho = 0.26, p = 0.62, n = 6). Finally, the regional introduction pool shifted from 16.8% gardening before 1500 to 75.2% in 1985-2019, so these habitat contrasts are differences in pathway mixture within one modern snapshot, not evidence about the rate at which each habitat receives ornamental introductions.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Read invaded_niche_pathways.csv with sep='\t' (it is tab-separated despite the .csv extension) and invasion_success_pathways.csv with the default separator; verified n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo==n.total in 632/632 plots and the 'Gardening' label match between intro.pathway and n.gard. 2) Verified the taxonomic union phylo.tip.label <-> Newick tips (81<->81, zero mismatches) and that the plot table has no species column, justifying exclusion of the tree from the model. 3) Full 10-habitat descriptive panel: plots, % plots with n.total==0 (occupancy descriptive, kept outside the model), records per pathway, prevalence sum(n.gard)/sum(n.total), Wilson 95% CI and plot-level cluster bootstrap CI (20 000 resamples), explicit estimability flag for habitats with <15 records. 4) Confirmatory test: cell-means binomial GLM on cbind(n.gard, n.total-n.gard) ~ habitat over the 191 plots with n.total>0, after collapsing the 5 habitats with <15 records; overdispersion reported (Pearson c) and quasi-scaled p-values given; pairwise log-odds contrasts via t_test. 5) Monte-Carlo habitat x pathway chi-square (20 000 simulations, row totals fixed) because 57% of asymptotic cells have expected count <5. 6) Spatial sensitivity: habitat + elevation + UTM coordinates, LR/quasi-F and AIC comparison, Moran's I with k=5 nearest-neighbour weights and 4 999 permutations on Pearson residuals. 7) Sensitivity: plot-level occupancy over all 632 plots (n.gard>0 as success, 515 zeros included), plus Spearman rank agreement with the conditional prevalence. 8) Robustness of the grouping threshold (MIN_REC 10/15/20/30) and a 5-estimable-habitat-only model. 9) Mechanism context from the species table (growth.form x pathway, Mann-Whitney on invaded.niche.breadth) and temporal bias from temporal_trends_contingency_table.csv. Fixed seed 20261022; re-runs verified byte-identical.

native_result.query: For which domains do the effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies?
native_result.HypoA: The effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies across both the Experimental Economics and Psychology domains. In Experimental Economics, the average effect estimate on the Fisher-z scale in original studies is 0.57, compared to 0.31 in replication studies. In Psychology, the average is 0.5 in original studies versus 0.24 in replication studies.
native_result.HypoB: Los estimadores de tamano de efecto originales tienden a ser mas grandes que los de la replicacion en TODOS los dominios de estos proyectos de replicacion (84.9% de 86 estudios; caida media fiso-fisr = 0.262, IC95 0.196-0.328; Wilcoxon p <= 0.0009 en cada dominio), pero cual dominio esta mas afectado depende de la escala y esa inversion es el hallazgo central. En escala RELATIVA (mediana de rr/ro) la brecha es mayor en la psicologia SOCIAL (0.184), seguida del resto de Psicologia (0.316), la psicologia COGNITIVE (0.650) y, con la menor brecha, la economia experimental (0.698); ahi la heterogeneidad entre dominios es sugerente (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.024; Cognitive vs Social: diferencia de medianas 0.466 [IC95 0.118, 0.695], Mann-Whitney p = 0.022; Social vs Economia: -0.514 [-0.809, -0.229], p = 0.025). En escala ABSOLUTA (d_fisher = fiso - fisr, primaria) la mayor caida media ocurre en COGNITIVE (0.289 [IC95 pareado 0.164, 0.415]), por delante de Economia (0.266 [0.084, 0.447]) y Psicologia (0.261 [0.191, 0.332]), y es menor en SOCIAL (0.233 [0.162, 0.304]); con ponderacion por precision (meta-analisis DerSimonian-Laird) Economia pasa a ser el dominio con menor caida absoluta (0.129 [0.011, 0.246]) y las diferencias entre dominios no son significativas (Q_between = 2.19, df 1, p = 0.139 a nivel de project; 2.21, df 2, p = 0.331 a nivel de discipline). La frecuencia ro > rr es mas alta en SOCIAL (88.2%) que en Psicologia global (85.3%), Economia (83.3%) y Cognitive (82.4%), y Social concentra las inversiones de signo (29.4% de rr < 0) y la menor tasa de replicacion (20.6%). Mecanismo propuesto: los efectos originales de Cognitive son mucho mas grandes (ro media 0.533 vs 0.346 en Social), de modo que la misma contraccion relativa produce una caida absoluta mayor; en Social las replicaciones tienden a anularse o invertirse, lo que desploma el ratio. Dado que Economia tiene n = 18 (IC de caida 0.084-0.447) no podemos afirmar que Psicologia caiga mas que Economia en Fisher-z, mientras que si es plausible que la contraccion relativa sea mayor en psicologia social y menor en economia.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Carga del CSV unido (86 estudios x 60 columnas; 0 faltantes en ro/rr/fiso/fisr/se_fiso/se_fisr/project/discipline/journal; study unico, sin duplicados). 2) Validacion interna: fiso=arctanh(ro), fisr=arctanh(rr) (error <5e-15); ro>0 en las 86 filas. 3) Metricas por estudio: d_fisher=fiso-fisr con var_d=se_fiso^2+se_fisr^2; d_corr=ro-rr; ratio=rr/ro recalculado (corrige el unico signo inconsistente de relative_es, fila 'B Eitam', conservada); indicadores ro>rr, coincidencia de signo y replicated. 4) Dominios en dos niveles: project.x (Psychology n=68 vs Experimental Economics n=18) y discipline (Cognitive n=34, Social n=34, Economics n=18 = mismas filas que ee, reportado una sola vez). 5) Por dominio: media+IC95 pareado (t, n-1 gl), mediana+IC95 bootstrap percentil B=2000 con semilla determinista por datos+metrica, IQR y media recortada al 10% del ratio, frecuencias; meta-analisis de efectos mixtos (DerSimonian-Laird) con pesos 1/(se_fiso^2+se_fisr^2), tau2, Q_within e I2. 6) Contrastes: bootstrap de diferencias de medias y medianas entre dominios, t de Welch, z sobre diferencias de pooled RE, Mann-Whitney, chi2 de proporciones, Q_between entre pooled RE, permutacion (B=2000) sobre la F de ANOVA y Kruskal-Wallis. 7) Sensibilidades: journal (QJE n=2 no tratado como dominio), pub_year, rr firmado vs absoluto, ratio restringido a rr>0, exclusion de la fila atipica, correlacion ro vs d_fisher. 8) Redaccion probabilistica nombrando dominios en ambas escalas y declarando la inversion Cognitive vs Social.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: The effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies across both the Experimental Economics and Psychology domains. In Experimental Economics, the average effect estimate on the Fisher-z scale in original studies is 0.57, compared to 0.31 in replication studies. In Psychology, the average is 0.5 in original studies versus 0.24 in replication studies.

sub_hypo.text: Original effect estimates tend to exceed replication estimates across all domains: ro > rr in 84.9% of 86 studies, with a mean Fisher-z decrease of 0.262 (95% CI 0.196–0.328) and within-domain Wilcoxon p ≤ 0.0009.
sub_hypo.context: Merged data.csv and RProjects.csv: 86 unique studies with complete effect-estimate and standard-error data; Psychology n=68, Experimental Economics n=18; Cognitive n=34, Social n=34, Economics n=18. All original correlations are positive.
sub_hypo.relations: Original estimates generally exceed replication estimates in every domain; the primary absolute decrease is d_fisher = fiso - fisr.

sub_hypo.text: Relative contraction is greatest in Social psychology and smallest in Experimental Economics. Reported median rr/ro values are 0.184 for Social, 0.316 for the remaining Psychology category named in the hypothesis, 0.650 for Cognitive, and 0.698 for Experimental Economics.
sub_hypo.context: The 86 merged studies, grouped separately by project.x and discipline. The workflow defines Psychology as the full 68-study project, not as an additional mutually exclusive discipline. Ratios are recalculated from signed rr and ro, correcting the inconsistent relative_es sign for 'B Eitam' while retaining that study.
sub_hypo.relations: Lower median rr/ro indicates greater relative contraction. Between-domain heterogeneity is suggestive (Kruskal–Wallis p=0.024). Cognitive minus Social median ratio is 0.466 (95% CI 0.118–0.695; Mann–Whitney p=0.022); Social minus Economics is -0.514 (95% CI -0.809 to -0.229; p=0.025).

sub_hypo.text: On the primary absolute Fisher-z scale, Cognitive has the largest mean decrease, whereas Social has the smallest, reversing their relative-scale ordering.
sub_hypo.context: Unweighted paired original–replication comparisons in the merged dataset, with project and discipline summaries reported at separate, overlapping levels.
sub_hypo.relations: Mean fiso-fisr is 0.289 in Cognitive (paired 95% CI 0.164–0.415), 0.266 in Economics (0.084–0.447), 0.261 in Psychology overall (0.191–0.332), and 0.233 in Social (0.162–0.304). Cognitive exceeds Social in absolute decrease but has less relative contraction according to median rr/ro.

sub_hypo.text: After precision-weighted DerSimonian–Laird meta-analysis, Economics has the smallest pooled absolute decrease, and between-domain differences are not statistically significant.
sub_hypo.context: Mixed-effects meta-analysis of the 86 studies, using var_d = se_fiso² + se_fisr² and inverse-variance precision weighting, with project-level and discipline-level comparisons.
sub_hypo.relations: The pooled Economics decrease is 0.129 (95% CI 0.011–0.246). Between-project Q=2.19, df=1, p=0.139; between-discipline Q=2.21, df=2, p=0.331. Domain ordering depends on weighting as well as measurement scale.

sub_hypo.text: Social psychology has the highest frequency of original estimates exceeding replication estimates, concentrates sign reversals, and has the lowest replication rate.
sub_hypo.context: Project- and discipline-level summaries of the merged studies; ro is positive for every study, so rr < 0 identifies a sign reversal.
sub_hypo.relations: The frequency of ro > rr is 88.2% in Social, 85.3% in Psychology overall, 83.3% in Economics, and 82.4% in Cognitive. In Social, 29.4% of replication estimates are negative and the replication rate is 20.6%.

sub_hypo.text: The proposed explanation for the Cognitive–Social ranking reversal is that Cognitive original effects are larger, while Social replication effects tend toward zero or reverse sign.
sub_hypo.context: Comparison of Cognitive and Social psychology studies, each with n=34, using absolute Fisher-z decreases and signed replication-to-original correlation ratios.
sub_hypo.relations: Mean ro is 0.533 in Cognitive versus 0.346 in Social. The proposed mechanism is that the same relative contraction yields a larger absolute decrease when original effects are larger; near-zero or negative Social replication estimates depress rr/ro. This is a proposed explanation, not an established causal relationship.

sub_hypo.text: The evidence does not justify claiming a larger Fisher-z decrease in Psychology than in Economics, although greater relative contraction in Social psychology and smaller relative contraction in Economics remain plausible.
sub_hypo.context: Psychology n=68 versus Experimental Economics n=18, with Social psychology n=34 considered separately at the discipline level.
sub_hypo.relations: Economics has an imprecisely estimated mean absolute decrease of 0.266 (95% CI 0.084–0.447), precluding the asserted Psychology-greater-than-Economics absolute ordering. Relative-scale results instead support a cautious Social-greater-than-Economics contraction interpretation.

native_result.query: What is the proportion of junior professors in replicated studies in Psychology?
native_result.HypoA: In Psychology, replicated studies have a much higher proportion of junior professor (64.7%) and in the original studies the senior professors are more represented (82.4%)
native_result.HypoB: Assuming a seniority hierarchy that the dataset itself does not define (Professor > Associate Professor > Assistant Professor > Assistant > Researcher) and counting 'junior professor' as Assistant Professor or Assistant - i.e. the assistant level, with Researcher excluded as non-professorial - roughly two in five of the replicated studies in Psychology were led by a junior professor: among all 97 original-replication pairs of the Psychology replication project (project == 'rpp', all with usable seniority) 38 have a junior most-senior author on the replication line (seniority.r), i.e. 38/97 = 39.2% (Wilson 95% CI 30.1%-49.1%) - a share that rises to 16/35 = 45.7% (CI 30.5%-61.8%) if one restricts to the studies that additionally replicated successfully (replicated == 1) - whereas on the original-study line (seniority.o) not one of the 97 has an assistant-level lead (0/97 = 0%; 5/97 = 5.2% if Researcher is also counted as junior), because the replicated originals were overwhelmingly full professors (83/97), so the junior-professor share is a property of the replication teams rather than of the original papers.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded File A (meta-regression_study_data_...csv, 927x57) and File B (meta-regression_replication_success_data_...csv, 143x15). 2) Excluded study-level roll-ups (aggregated == True; 26 rows, ml1/ml3 only) to avoid double counting -> 901 rows. 3) Primary population: project == 'rpp' (Psychology project) = 97 rows, 97 unique ids, one row per O/R pair; seniority.o and seniority.r 0% missing, so N = 97. 4) Numerator: seniority.r in {Assistant Professor, Assistant} (junior definition D2, tier order assumed) = 38 -> 38/97 = 39.2%, Wilson 95% CI 30.1-49.1%. 5) Parallel column seniority.o (D1/D2 = 0/97; D3 with Researcher = 5/97) plus seniority.o x seniority.r crosstab (77/97 rows differ) and per-category distributions. 6) Sensitivity grid 5 filters (F0 all rpp 97; F1 drop==False 90; F2 replicated==1 35; F3 both 31; F4 dedupe repeated titles 95) x 3 junior definitions (D1 AsstProf; D2 +Assistant; D3 +Researcher) x 2 seniority lines, every cell reported as k/N and % with Wilson CIs. 7) Integrity checks: unique ids, no row duplicates, category counts sum to N, D1 subset D2 subset D3, integral F2 counts (10/35, 16/35, 20/35). 8) Confirmatory (not used for numbers): surname-heuristic join of File B project=='Psychology' rows onto rpp (71/73 matched, median |po - p_value.o| = 2.5e-4) to verify that 'Psychology' == project 'rpp'; File B has no seniority field. 9) Descriptive contrast: replication success 16/38 = 42.1% junior-led vs 19/59 = 32.2% senior-led, Fisher exact p = 0.388 (not significant).

native_result.query: What is the average length of original papers in Experimental Economics and that in Psychology?
native_result.HypoA: Studies in Experimental Economics tend to have longer original papers compared to Psychology. The average length of original papers in Experimental Economics is 28 pages, whereas in Psychology, the average is 11 pages.
native_result.HypoB: In these replication-project data, original papers in Experimental Economics are substantially longer than those in Psychology: on average 28.0 pages (n = 18 papers, bootstrap 95% CI [24.8, 31.3]) versus 11.2 pages (n = 97 papers, CI [10.0, 12.4]) - a difference of 16.8 pages (CI [13.5, 20.4]) and a ratio of 2.5x (CI [2.1, 2.9]). The gap holds across the whole distribution (every ee paper exceeds the rpp median; P(ee > rpp) ~ 0.96) and is robust to lab-level vs study-level rows, excluding drop==True studies, and trimmed/winsorized means (11.0-12.0 pages for Psychology, 27.7-28.0 for Experimental Economics); alternative definitions of 'Psychology' barely change it (rpp+ml1+ml3 = 11.07, n = 123). This describes the original papers sampled by the Reproducibility Project: Psychology and the experimental-economics replication project in these data - not a general law about all publications in either field - and partly reflects publication conventions (ee papers are AER/QJE articles of 16-45 pages, while the rpp set includes 8 short 1-3 page reports), with limited precision for ee because n = 18.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded the study_data CSV (927x57); verified `length` (int64, 0 missing, range 1-45, constant within each `id`); deduplicated to study level by `id` (141 studies: ee 18, rpp 97, ml1 16, ml3 10); computed mean/median/SD/min-max per project with 2000-resample percentile bootstrap CIs (seed 20261022); bootstrapped the ee-rpp difference and ratio plus a two-sided bootstrap p, cross-checked with Welch t and Mann-Whitney U; reported alternative 'Psychology' definitions (rpp+ml1+ml3; discipline Social+Cognitive) as non-main; ran sensitivity controls (no dedup, drop==True exclusion, 5% trimmed, p95 winsorized, excluding 1-3 page papers); did not join the replication_success CSV (143x15, no length column, different EERP/SSRP study set).

native_result.HypoB: En Economics (los estudios de Experimental Economics) es donde la mayoría de autores tiende a ser varón de forma consistente en el estudio original y en su replicación. Agrupando los 141 pares original/replicación (una fila por par, usando la fila agregada para Many Labs) y definiendo 'mayoría masculina' como authors_male > 0.5, Economics presenta la mayor proporción de pares con mayoría de autores varones en ambos lados: 0.556 (10/18, IC95 Wilson [0.34, 0.75]) frente a 0.367 en Cognitive (18/49) y 0.270 en Social (20/74). Es además el dominio más alto en todas las métricas: media del ratio de autores varones 0.870 en original y 0.837 en replicación (medianas 1.000 en ambos), 0.875 y 0.814 ponderando por número de autores, y 42/48 y 48/59 autores varones absolutos; es el único dominio donde el equipo de la replicación es también mayoritariamente masculino en términos medios. La conclusión no depende de las decisiones analíticas: se mantiene con umbral >=0.5 (0.833 vs 0.612 y 0.568), excluyendo los pares drop=True (131 pares), usando las 927 filas o el nivel lab_id como unidad, y eliminando por completo Many Labs (0.556 vs 0.310 y 0.164). native_result.HypoA: Gender disparities exist in median wealth in 1985 among individuals who were ever incarcerated, with males having higher median wealth than females.
native_result.HypoB: Among the 289 ever-incarcerated (1985-1994) NLS-Y79 respondents, 1985 wealth disparities track RACE rather than SEX, and take the form of a white vs non-white gap: hispanic (original label 'hipanic', henceforth hispanic) and black respondents are statistically indistinguishable (median $320 vs $0; difference $320, 95% CI -1,441 to 1,480, p=0.58), while whites hold $2,200 (white-black difference $1,880, CI -100 to 5,000; white-hispanic $2,200, CI -400 to 5,000; Mann-Whitney p=0.046 and 0.041), with 31.9% of whites versus 47.8% of blacks and 52.5% of hispanics holding zero-or-negative net wealth (17.2 pp gap for pooled non-white vs white, 95% CI 3.9-29.8 pp). The racial disadvantage persists within men: white men $2,000 vs black men $800 (0.40x, 14.2 pp more at <=0) and hispanic men $700 (0.35x, 16.3 pp more at <=0), although within-male median differences alone are not significant (p=0.15, 0.19). By contrast, the apparent sex gap (men $1,000 vs women $0; 29.0 pp more women at <=0) cannot be asserted as an independent disparity because all 37 ever-incarcerated women fall into cells of n=12/16/9 and the direction reverses among white women (median $4,100, the highest of the six race-by-sex cells). Race and sex each explain only ~1.8% of rank variation (race x sex 5.0%), so the dominant pattern is a shared floor of asset poverty - Q1=$0 in every cell and 45.0% of ever-incarcerated respondents at <=0 net wealth, versus 31.8% and a $3,600 median among the never-incarcerated - overlaid by a racial gradient that is modest in dollars ($1,200-2,200) but 3-7x in ratio and consistent across medians, winsorized means and shares at or below zero. Because ever_jailed covers 1985-1994 while wealth is measured in 1985, this disparity is best read as an associative, largely pre-existing economic disadvantage shaping who becomes incarcerated rather than a causal effect of incarceration; the data contain no residence/institution ('Jail') fields to verify incarceration status independently, and $100 value granularity plus 1,899 exact duplicate rows add only about +/- $50 of noise (jitter check), an order of magnitude below the estimated gaps. Contextually, the gap widens after the incarceration window (ever-incarcerated medians $0 in 1990 and 1996 vs $10,500 and $8,500 for the never-incarcerated), and by 1996 the internal racial gap collapses to $0 at the median because both groups hit the zero floor.

native_result.query: What changes occurred in the wealth inequality for white males and females between 1990 and 1996?
native_result.HypoA: Wealth inequality increases among white people (both men and women) in the 1990-1996 period, with the Gini coefficients for white females increasing from 0.775593 in 1990 to 0.781602 in 1996, and for white males increasing from 0.792018 in 1990 to 0.797468 in 1996.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: Wealth inequality increases among white people (both men and women) in the 1990-1996 period, with the Gini coefficients for white females increasing from 0.775593 in 1990 to 0.781602 in 1996, and for white males increasing from 0.792018 in 1990 to 0.797468 in 1996.

sub_hypo.text: Between 1990 and 1996, wealth inequality declined among white men and white women with positive wealth, excluding the all-zero placeholder block. For men, P90/P50 fell from 5.68 to 3.89 (95% bootstrap CI for change: -2.47 to -1.04), P90/P10 from 68.2 to 51.1, P75/P25 from 10.8 to 7.7, CV from 2.25 to 1.65, and Gini from 0.688 to 0.623 (n=2,452 to 1,900). For women, the corresponding changes were 4.89 to 3.74 (CI: -1.79 to -0.75), 84.0 to 55.3, 12.5 to 5.7, 2.22 to 1.60, and 0.681 to 0.599 (n=2,713 to 2,016).
sub_hypo.context: White respondents in the NLSY1979-derived dataset, analyzed separately by sex in 1990 and 1996; wealth must be positive in the analyzed year, and rows with zero wealth in 1985, 1990, and 1996 are excluded.
sub_hypo.relations: Within each sex, positive-wealth distributions became less unequal between 1990 and 1996 across percentile ratios, CV, and Gini; bootstrap intervals for P90/P50 changes exclude zero.

sub_hypo.text: In the as-reported sample treating zeros as true zero wealth, measured inequality instead appears to explode because the share with zero-or-negative wealth increased from 29.3% to 45.2% among white men and from 25.3% to 44.5% among white women. The apparent increase decomposes into mass-at-zero components of +1.45 log points for men and +1.80 for women, offset by owner-distribution components of -0.45 and -0.66.
sub_hypo.context: All as-reported white rows in the NLSY1979-derived dataset, separately by sex, comparing 1990 with 1996; zeros are retained as actual wealth values.
sub_hypo.relations: Increasing zero-or-negative wealth shares mechanically raise measured inequality despite compression among positive wealth holders; the workflow separates these effects using a Shapley-symmetric mass-at-zero versus owner-distribution decomposition.

sub_hypo.text: Among white wealth holders positive in both years, median wealth growth decreased monotonically with 1990 wealth rank, indicating convergence of the lower and middle owner distribution toward the top. Log-growth-on-rank slopes were -2.33 (s.e. 0.106) for men and -3.05 (s.e. 0.112) for women, both p<1e-16. Bottom-decile median log growth was 2.15 for men and 2.97 for women, while top-decile median dollar changes were -4,750 and -77,000, with 50.0% and 60.1% declining, respectively.
sub_hypo.context: White men and white women in the strict 1990-and-1996-positive wealth panel; person-level correspondence cannot be verified because no respondent ID is available.
sub_hypo.relations: 1990 wealth rank is negatively associated with subsequent log wealth growth: lower-ranked holders gained proportionately more, while the top decile stagnated or declined, compressing the aggregate distribution.

sub_hypo.text: Aggregate wealth compression coexisted with divergent individual trajectories and limited rank persistence: Spearman correlations between 1990 and 1996 wealth were 0.613 for white men and 0.562 for white women. Thus, the inequality decline reflects distributional homogenization rather than divergence of individual trajectories.
sub_hypo.context: White respondents positive in both 1990 and 1996, analyzed separately by sex in the unverified person-level panel.
sub_hypo.relations: Positive but limited wealth-rank persistence and heterogeneous individual changes coexist with decreasing aggregate dispersion; individual trajectory divergence does not imply increasing distributional inequality.

sub_hypo.text: The decline in owner wealth inequality persisted in the strict both-years-positive panel, after winsorizing at each sex-by-year P99, and after excluding ever-jailed respondents. In the strict panel, men's P90/P50 fell from 5.04 to 3.68 and Gini from 0.676 to 0.613; women's P90/P50 fell from 4.49 to 3.58 and Gini from 0.666 to 0.589. Excluding ever-jailed respondents yielded P90/P50 declines from 5.52 to 3.84 for men and 4.88 to 3.75 for women.
sub_hypo.context: White positive wealth holders in 1990 and 1996, separately by sex; sensitivity analyses restrict both-year positivity, winsorize at group-by-year P99, or exclude respondents jailed between 1985 and 1994.
sub_hypo.relations: The direction of the inequality decline is unchanged by panel restriction, upper-tail winsorization, or exclusion of ever-jailed respondents.

sub_hypo.text: Among white positive wealth holders, women's median wealth advantage closed toward parity: the male/female median ratio increased from 0.824 in 1990 to 0.996 in 1996, with P75 ratios increasing from 0.890 to 1.011 and P90 ratios from 0.956 to 1.035. However, a descriptive log-wealth regression with female, post-1996, their interaction, and ever_jailed (n=9,081) found no significant gender level or change term: female -0.001 (s.e. 0.050), interaction -0.028 (s.e. 0.071, p=0.70).
sub_hypo.context: White positive wealth holders in the NLSY1979-derived dataset, comparing men with women in 1990 and 1996; descriptive regression adjusts for ever-jailed status.
sub_hypo.relations: Male/female wealth quantile ratios move toward parity or slightly above it, but the descriptive regression provides no statistically significant female level effect or female-by-1996 interaction.

sub_hypo.text: Ever-jailed status was associated with substantially lower wealth, although incarceration was only a sensitivity analysis rather than the explanation for declining inequality. The descriptive log-wealth regression estimated an ever-jailed penalty of -1.71 log points. Jailed white men's median wealth increased from 7,100 to 25,400 USD, versus 49,700 to 134,000 USD for other white men. Ever-jailed descriptives were low powered (57 men and 12 women), and jailed white women were too few to analyze.
sub_hypo.context: White respondents in 1990 and 1996; ever_jailed denotes incarceration between 1985 and 1994. Regression uses positive wealth holders, and incarceration comparisons are descriptive.
sub_hypo.relations: Ever-jailed status is negatively associated with wealth, but excluding ever-jailed respondents does not remove the owner-inequality decline; small incarcerated samples limit interpretation.

sub_hypo.text: Zeros almost certainly encode item non-response rather than uniformly representing genuine zero wealth: 29.4% of white men and 32.7% of white women holding wealth in 1990 recorded exactly zero in 1996, and a 1,096-row all-zero block was 99.6% duplicated rows. These patterns make the as-reported inequality increase sensitive to zero coding and owner-sample selection.
sub_hypo.context: Zero-coding and retention diagnostics in the NLSY1979-derived dataset; white wealth holders transitioning from 1990 to 1996 and the block with zero wealth in all three recorded years.
sub_hypo.relations: Frequent positive-to-exact-zero transitions and near-duplication of the all-zero block support interpreting zeros as likely non-response, undermining an interpretation of apparent inequality growth as genuine wealth dispersion.

sub_hypo.text: When 1996 zeros among 1990 owners were imputed with their 1990 wealth, declines in P90/P50 and Gini survived: men's values changed from 5.68 to 4.62 and 0.688 to 0.658, and women's from 4.89 to 4.05 and 0.681 to 0.640. The original P90/P10 compression did not robustly survive: men's ratio increased from 68.2 to 73.3, while women's changed only from 84.0 to 82.6. Compression at the bottom of the owner distribution is therefore the least robust element.
sub_hypo.context: White positive wealth holders, separately by sex, under persistence imputation assigning 1990 wealth to 1990 owners whose reported 1996 wealth is zero.
sub_hypo.relations: P90/P50 and Gini decreases are robust to persistence imputation, but lower-tail compression measured by P90/P10 is sensitive to treatment of subsequent zeros.

sub_hypo.text: The findings are descriptive and cannot establish population-representative or composition-adjusted wealth convergence: no respondent ID verifies the person-level panel, no sampling weights establish representativeness, and no age, education, or marital controls rule out life-cycle composition.
sub_hypo.context: All 1990–1996 wealth comparisons and panel interpretations for white men and white women in the supplied NLSY1979-derived dataset.
sub_hypo.relations: Observed wealth-distribution changes and rank-growth associations remain conditional on the analyzed sample; panel identity, population generalizability, and independence from life-cycle composition are not established.

native_result.query: In which years were individuals with a criminal record found to have significantly lower wealth compared to those without?
native_result.HypoA: In 1985, 1990, and 1996, individuals with a criminal record have significantly lower wealth compared to those without.
native_result.HypoB: Individuals with a criminal record (incarcerated 1985-1994) had significantly lower wealth than those without in ALL three years — 1985, 1990 and 1996 — with the gap widening over time (mean differences ≈ -$17.2k, -$57.6k and -$85.1k; median differences -$2,880, -$10,500 and -$8,500; all Welch p<1e-19, corroborated by Mann-Whitney and negative Hodges-Lehmann shifts with CIs excluding zero, and robust to dropping negatives and 1/99% winsorization). Because ever_jailed covers 1985-1994, the 1985 gap predates most incarceration and should be read as preexisting association/selection (those later incarcerated already had lower wealth), not as a causal effect of criminal records; the 1990 and especially 1996 gaps are consistent with incarceration additionally suppressing wealth accumulation. The association persists after adjusting for race and sex (HC1-robust OLS) and within males only. Limitations: nominal (undeflated) dollars, 1,899 fully duplicated rows kept (no ID), misspelled 'hipanic' race label left as-is, and zeros possibly masking missing wealth.
native_result.WorkflowB: Per-year (1985, 1990, 1996) available-case comparison of composite_wealth by ever_jailed in the NLSY79 processed dataset (12,013 rows; 289 jailed vs 11,724 not): descriptives per group/year; primary Welch t-test (alpha=0.05, two-sided) with Mann-Whitney U corroboration and Hodges-Lehmann shift + bootstrap CI as effect size; sensitivity analyses excluding negative wealth and winsorizing at 1/99%; secondary OLS wealth ~ ever_jailed + race + sex with HC1 robust SE, plus male-only (crude and adjusted) robustness. Criterion for 'significantly lower': Welch p<0.05 AND negative mean difference, same direction in Mann-Whitney/HL; ties would be decided by the robust median-based statistic (none occurred).

native_result.query: How does the median wealth of white individuals compare to that of black and Hispanic individuals from 1985 onwards?
native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: Among NLSY79 respondents, family net wealth of the non-black non-Hispanic cohort - used here as a PROXY for 'white', because this dataset encodes race/ethnicity only as the 1979 racial/ethnic cohort (1=BLACK, 2=HISPANIC, 3=NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC) and contains no strict non-Hispanic white identifier - exceeded that of black and Hispanic respondents at the median in every wave in which wealth is observed, and the gap widened between 1985 and 1996. The white-proxy/black median wealth ratio rose from about 2.2x in 1985 (USD 3,500 vs 1,600) to 2.7x in 1990 (12,972 vs 4,800) and 4.3x in 1996 (42,600 vs 9,800), a 1996/1985 ratio-of-ratios of 2.0 (95% CI 1.7-2.5); the white-proxy/Hispanic ratio rose from 7.0x (3,500 vs 500) to 8.1x (12,972 vs 1,600) and 16.6x (42,600 vs 2,562), a ratio-of-ratios of 2.4 (95% CI 1.9-3.1). Because median wealth grew for all three groups, both the relative and the absolute gaps widened: the median difference over the white-proxy group grew from about USD 1,900 (black) and 3,000 (Hispanic) in 1985 to about 32,800 and 40,000 (1996 dollars) in 1996. The rank ordering white-proxy > black > Hispanic was stable in all three waves, and the widening is reproduced in a balanced panel of the 5,739 respondents observed in all waves and when parental-household residents are excluded, so it is not driven by composition or by the 1996 non-response (52.6% missing in the reference cohort vs 31.7%/33.4%). native_result.HypoB: The variable is SAMPLE_RACE — specifically the Black-versus-White contrast in the effect of race on BA degree completion. In logit models on the full sample (n = 8,773; 2.69% complete a BA), the Black coefficient is large and highly significant before adjustment (-1.006, p < 0.0001, race only; -0.862, p < 0.0001, adding SES alone), but once BOTH SES and academic characteristics (the ASVAB composite and class percentile) are included, the Black effect shrinks to 0.0926 (SE 0.225) and becomes statistically insignificant (p = 0.68). native_result.query: Is the relation between socioeconomic status and chances of degree completion affected by racial lines of the individual?
native_result.HypoA: The strength and significance of the relationship between socioeconomic status (SES) and BA degree completion differ across racial groups. For Whites, SES has a positive coefficient of 0.2169 (p = 0.031). For Blacks SES has a larger positive coefficient of 0.9775 (p < 0.001). For Hispanics, SES has a positive coefficient of 0.6724 (p = 0.013).
native_result.HypoB: Higher socioeconomic status is associated with substantially higher odds of completing a BA degree within every racial group (OR ~1.7-2.4 per 1 SD of SES; White 1.74 [1.48-2.05], Black 2.38 [1.66-3.18], Hispanic 1.95 [1.19-2.99], bootstrap CIs), but the relation is NOT meaningfully modified by race: the SES x race interaction is non-significant (LR chi2(2)=2.6, p=0.28; Firth p=0.28; p=0.85 with SES in quartiles), all pairwise race contrasts have overlapping CIs (Black vs Hispanic OR-ratio 1.21 [0.71-2.13]), and the apparent direction reverses between scales (steepest log-odds slope in Black respondents vs largest absolute gradient in White respondents: +5.0 vs +2.1 percentage points in predicted BA probability from SES p10 to p90). The SES gradient attenuates strongly upon adjusting academic performance (ASVAB ability, class rank; OR/SD falls to ~1.2-1.6, interaction p=0.42), indicating SES operates largely through academic performance rather than differing across races. Rare outcomes (236 events, 2.7%) imply wide intervals and low power for modest interaction.

native_result.query: Between which two races is the factor of BA degree completion -0.9568 when compared to the other?
native_result.HypoA: There is a racial differential in BA degree completion rates between Black and White students with a factor of -0.9568.
native_result.HypoB: El factor -0.9568 de finalizacion del titulo BA corresponde a la comparacion de **Hispanic frente a White**: en una regresion logística de BA DEGREE COMPLETED ~ SAMPLE_RACE con la referencia fijada en White (C(SAMPLE_RACE, Treatment(reference='White'))), ser hispano tiene coeficiente -0.9568 en escala log-odds, es decir OR = e^-0.9568 = 0.384: los encuestados hispanos tienen alrededor de un 62% menos de momios de completar un BA que los blancos (tasa observada 1.436% vs 3.541%). El contraste analogo de Black vs White es -1.0057 (OR 0.366) y la diferencia entre Black y Hispanic es nula (Wald p=0.785), de modo que -0.9568 es el factor de la desventaja no-blanca frente a White, asignable numéricamente con mayor consistencia a Hispanic.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspeccion: 8773 filas x 9 columnas, 0 NaN/inf, BA DEGREE COMPLETED recodificado True/False -> 1/0, 3 niveles limpios de SAMPLE_RACE. 2) Chequeo de cordura: logit saturado (M1) reproduce los log-OR crudos (dif ~1e-15), confirmando la recodificacion. 3) Logit (statsmodels, referencia fijada en White con C(SAMPLE_RACE, Treatment(reference='White'))) en 8 especificaciones (sin ajustar, +SES, +ABILITY, +PERCENTILE, +las tres, +SEX, +FAMILY SIZE, ambas), reportando los TRES pares por especificacion con coef, SE, z, p, IC95%, OR e IC95%(OR) via t_test, para que el signo no dependa de la codificacion. 4) Barrido sistematico del valor -0.9568: 312 especificaciones/564 coeficientes, 573 transformaciones y polinomios, 96 modelos de dos razas, 32 subconjuntos aditivos, 224 fits estratificados y Firth penalizado; cero coincidencias exactas a 4 decimales, minimo |dif|=0.0015. 5) Desempate pre-declarado por familia de especificacion (Hispanic gana 5-0) mas robustez de signo (Hispanic negativo 6/8 y nunca significativo positivo; Black se invierte y es significativo positivo en 2/8). 6) Diagnosticos: convergencia ok en las 8 specs; Firth vs MLE difieren <=0.0011 -> sin separacion pese a 19-28 eventos por nivel. 7) Control de jardin de caminos bifurcados: tasa nula de coincidencias 'exactas' con un objetivo aleatorio (0.0005-0.0009), por lo que la cercania numerica sola no se uso como prueba.

The result is invariant to the denominator (n=194 answered: 50.0%; n=276 all respondents: 35.1%; n=170 users of at least one technique: 57.1%). En los datos analizados son inequívocamente los dos formatos con menor uso y en ese mismo orden relativo: BDD_Scenarios es el menos usado (4 de 194 = 2.062%, IC bootstrap 95% [0.515, 4.124], IC exacto [0.565, 4.452]) y MLCanvas el segundo menos usado (15 de 194 = 7.732%, IC bootstrap 95% [4.124, 11.856], IC exacto [4.392, 11.812]); el tercero en adelante casi duplica el uso (Vision Document y Goal Models, 14.948% cada uno) y los más usados son Notebooks (34.021%) y User Stories (32.474%). native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Increasing government education expenditure is associated with smaller per-capita-income gains in Sub-Saharan Africa than in the broader lower-middle-income aggregate it is largely nested in, and in neither aggregate is the long-run association positive. In trend-adjusted levels the association is negative (LMC: -0.20 ln points per +1pp of GNI, p=0.002; detrended r=-0.55), but the sign reverses in year-to-year changes (LMC: +0.022, p=0.035; +0.040 with trend, p<0.001, i.e. ~+2 to +4% growth per +1pp), a fragility that disappears when the sample is shortened to 1991-2015 (-0.031, p=0.48) and is largely absorbed by enrolment controls. Sub-Saharan Africa sustained the highest expenditure shares in the panel (4.30% vs 3.50% of GNI; peak 6.10% in 1997 vs 3.87%), yet its income exists only for 2011-2015 (n=5), so its implied slope (-0.10; SSA interaction +0.35, p=0.24, N=46) is descriptive rather than estimated, and the SSA/LMC overlap attenuates any true difference toward zero. In the only comparable window (2011-2015) SSA spent more (3.41% vs 3.16%) and grew far less (+5.1% vs +13.8%), with a negative year-to-year co-movement (r=-0.47), and its 2015 income level equalled the lower-middle-income aggregate's 2009 level while the gap widened from 171 to 331 US$. The mechanism is access rather than income: SSA primary gross enrolment rose 60.6 to 97.0 and secondary 14.8 to 43.4 (still ~21pp below LMC) with no detectable enrolment payoff to spending changes (secondary -0.26, p=0.21; primary +0.25, p=0.59), whereas LMC shows a negative enrolment response (-0.79, p=0.007). Associations only: two group aggregates with 5 SSA income observations cannot support causal claims.
native_result.WorkflowB: WDI wide export (12x45) reshaped to long (group x series x year); QC of non-numeric/blank cells (0 non-numeric, 128/492 blank, no imputation). Step A: decade trends of education expenditure, enrolment, exports, LFPR and income levels; levels-vs-changes correlations and detrended correlation. Step B: within-LMC OLS with Newey-West (4 lags) in trend-adjusted levels (contemporaneous, lag 1/2/3; lag 2 primary) and in first differences, reporting Durbin-Watson and residual AR(1). Associations only: two group aggregates with 5 SSA income observations cannot support causal claims.

native_result.query: How does age influence the likelihood of withdrawing more money from savings than putting in?
native_result.HypoA: Younger individuals are more likely to withdraw more money from savings than they had put in and with a negative coefficient between age and withdrawing more than putting into savings (-0.0422).
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. One-hot encode Gender variable into MALE and FEMALE
2. Extract the independent variables ['AGE','INCOME', 'BMI', 'BLACK', 'HISPANIC', 'MALE', 'FEMALE']
3. Add dependent variable (DISSAVED) from the df
4. Add a constant term to the independent variable to account for the intercept term in the logistic regression model.
5. Fit a logistic regression model
native_result.HypoB: Age is negatively associated with the likelihood of withdrawing more money from savings than putting in (DISSAVED). In the NLSY79 1989 cross-section (n=12,686, ages 24-32, base rate 23.6%), the main model DISSAVED ~ AGE + AGE_2 + INCOME + GENDER + BLACK + HISPANIC (linear probability model, HC1-robust) gives -0.0076 per year of age, i.e. about 0.8 percentage points lower probability of dissaving per additional year (SE 0.0016, p ~ 1e-5), with a negative quadratic term AGE_2 (-0.145 pp per year^2, p = 0.059) so the decline steepens with age. The relation is approximately monotone decreasing and essentially linear inside the observed 24-32 window: predicted probability falls from 25.1% at age 24 to 18.7% at age 32, a drop of -6.4 percentage points (95% CI -9.0 to -3.9; logit -6.3 pp; flexible age dummies -7.2 pp; raw gap -7.3 pp), roughly a 26% relative reduction. Flexible age dummies show no significant departure from age 24 up to age 29 but significantly lower dissaving at 30-32 (-4.0 to -7.2 pp), and they do not improve on a single linear age term (LR = 11.1 on 7 df, p = 0.13), so no U-shaped or inverted-U pattern is supported. Robust to adding BMI, to using log income, and to logit/probit instead of the LPM. A three-state check (saved more / unchanged / dissaved) shows that with age the 'savings increased' share rises from 30% to 55% while 'unchanged' falls from 44% to 26% and 'dissaved' falls from 25% to 19%, confirming a real shift toward positive saving rather than an artefact of the dichotomy. Interpretation, not a demonstrated finding: this is consistent with age differences in time preference (younger adults discount the future more and draw down savings more often). Because it is a single cross-section in 1989, the estimate mixes age, cohort and period effects and should not be read as the causal effect of ageing; income is partly imputed (31% of rows share one value, plus top-coded values) and no survey weights are available, so magnitudes are sample-specific.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspection of data/nls_bmi_processed.csv (12,686 x 9, no missing, AGE_2 = AGE^2, DISSAVED and SAMESAVE mutually exclusive, overall P(DISSAVED)=0.2355). 2) Descriptives by age year (rates of dissaving / unchanged / saved more, income medians). 3) Hierarchical LPM (HC1) and logit (HC1) models: raw age+age^2; M1 = age+age^2+INCOME+GENDER+BLACK+HISPANIC (main); M2 = M1+BMI; M1 with log income. SAMESAVE deliberately excluded as a regressor. 4) Functional form: LPM with age dummies 25-32 (ref 24) plus M1 controls, joint F test, LR test of dummies vs a single linear age term, AGE^2 Wald test, block contrast 30-32 vs 24-29. 5) Average predicted probabilities at each age with delta-method SEs (LPM, logit, probit) and marginal effect of +1 year of age. 6) Contrast 32 vs 24 in percentage points with 95% CIs across all estimators. 7) Three-state multinomial logit (saved more / unchanged / dissaved) as an interpretation check. 8) Figure: observed rates with 95% CIs plus fitted M1 and crude age-only curves (SVG, generated without matplotlib). All steps in analysis/nls_dissave_age_analysis.py, executed end to end (exit 0); outputs in analysis/results_log.txt and the CSV tables.
